docs.title: Contour Terminal Emulator
docs.text:
Contour is modern, fast, and designed for everyday use. It's not just a terminal emulator, but a powerhouse of features tailored for those who seek efficiency and control. With GPU-accelerated rendering and high-DPI support, experience the smoothest and most responsive terminal emulator like never before.

Contour is designed with the advanced power user in mind, offering high-speed, feature-rich functionality across all major platforms. From Linux and macOS to FreeBSD, OpenBSD and Windows, we've got you covered. Contour offers a suite of unique features designed to enhance your productivity and user experience. Enjoy support for font ligatures, emoji, and Unicode grapheme clusters. Navigate quickly with vertical line markers and vi-like input modes. Control your settings with runtime configuration reload and customizable key bindings. Bring your terminal to life with color schemes, profiles, and sixel inline images. Enjoy the convenience of clickable hyperlinks, and set your clipboard with OSC 52.

This website is still in DRAFT mode, please be patient while we're building up the content.

Install Join

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text: Available on all major platforms, Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Windows. Font ligatures support (very useful for programming and scripting) Complex Unicode support, including colored Emoji (-: 🌈 💝 😛 👪 - including ZWJ, VS15, VS16 emoji :-) Persistent sessions that survive the window (daemon mode) — reattach locally or over the network Vi-like input modes for improved navigation, selection and copy'n'paste experience Vertical Line Markers (quickly jump to markers in your history!) Command blocks from shell integration: folding, an exit-status gutter, scrollbar marks and a sticky command header Profiles (grouped customization of: color scheme, login shell, and related behaviors) Sixel Image support VT320 Host-programmable and Indicator statusline support Bold and italic fonts For a full list of features, click here

docs.title: Contribution Guidelines
docs.text:
Many thanks for your interest in contributing to the Contour terminal emulator.

Any kind of contribution is welcome, let it be coding (feature, bugfixes), documentation, or just bug management / community management.

If you would like to contribute but do not know how, we welcome you to join our Discord. You can also see some live development on Twitch.

docs.title: Some general tips:
docs.text:
• Please keep in mind, this project is still in its very early stages (started August 2019) and thus under very active development. It's not perfect nor bug-free yet.
  • Please fork the main repository at github.com/contour-terminal/contour then git clone your repository into your preferred location.
  • Always work on a branch based off the master branch, if it is a feature or a bugfix.
  • Please have a look at the coding style guidelines.
  • When creating a pull request, please see if you can keep the commits as atomic as possible. That is, a single reasonably sized feature or functionality should be committed as one single commit. If you can branch out a some functionality, let it be a more generalized API or refactor of something that can stand on their own, then those deserve their own commits.
  • Every new feature should ideally be unit-testable, this isn't always possible or easy for pure GUI tasks, but the rest should ideally get one. The plus-side of this story is, that one can test their own code right with the new test case.
  • Bug fixes should ideally also result into an added or tweaked or fixed test case, if possible.

docs.title: Contributing to the Website
docs.text:
The website is living directly in the project's main repository. We are using MkDocs to create the website and have the project well documented.

Please bear with us, we just started developing this website, it is incomplete and far from perfect. This is why documentation and website development needs the most love and probably external contributions.

docs.title: Running the website locally
docs.text:
In order to contribute to the website, it's best tested locally in an iterative approach.

Have a recent Python right next to you, such as Python 3.11+ and install the module requirements:

pip install -r docs/requirements.txt

Use your editor of choice to change the content in docs/ and Running

mkdocs serve

to spawn the test HTTP server at port 8080.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
Contour reports where the terminal caret is to the operating system, so assistive technology can follow it. This is what makes a screen magnifier keep the cursor in view while you type, and what lets a screen reader know where it should be reading.

There is nothing to switch on. Reporting is always available and costs effectively nothing while no assistive client is attached; the platform activates it when one appears.

Should you ever need to rule the caret reports out — when diagnosing input latency, say — set accessibility_caret_reporting: false in contour.yml. That silences the caret reports only; the announcements below have their own setting.

docs.title: What is reported
docs.text:
Reported Meaning The caret's position and screen rectangle Where the cursor is, updated whenever it moves. The visible screen's text The grid contents, addressed by offset, rows separated by newlines. The shell prompt region Where the current prompt is — see below.

The caret is reported whenever it moves and is visible, and also whenever it becomes visible after having been hidden — so an application that hides the cursor while it redraws and then shows it again does not leave a client pointing at a stale position.

A blinking cursor is not reported on every blink. Only the focused pane reports, so a split window does not make a magnifier jump between panes.

docs.title: The prompt region
docs.text:
When your shell has OSC 133 shell integration enabled, Contour additionally exposes the live shell prompt — the one you are typing at — as its own focusable region. Assistive technology that follows focus (rather than the text caret) uses this to keep the prompt itself in view, which is usually what you want while typing a command.

While a command is running there is no prompt to report, and Contour says so rather than pointing at a stale one. Without shell integration, or with a shell that marks only prompt starts, the caret is still reported as usual — only the prompt region is unavailable.

This needs no opt-in beyond the shell integration itself: it is driven by the OSC 133 marks directly and does not require DEC mode 2034.

docs.title: The window around the terminal
docs.text: The tab bar is exposed as a tab list whose tabs announce themselves as you switch between them, the window and tab buttons say what they do rather than naming the glyph they are drawn with, and every field on the settings page carries its own label.

docs.title: Keyboard access to the window chrome
docs.text:
With defaults_edition: native2026, Ctrl+F6 moves keyboard focus out of the terminal and into the window's chrome, and on through it: the terminal, then the tab bar, then the toolbar (the host chip, the daemon version chip and the new-tab button), then back to the terminal. Ctrl+Shift+F6 walks the other way. On macOS Ctrl+F5 goes straight to the toolbar and Ctrl+F6 moves between the areas. An area that is not shown, such as a tab bar hidden by tab_bar_visibility, is skipped.

A ring marks the item that has focus: a 3 pt outline in the accent on macOS and 2 pt on Windows and Linux, and a run of selection-coloured cells under ui_style: terminal. It appears for keyboard focus only, so clicking a tab never draws it.

Where Key What it does Tab bar Left, Right Move to the previous or next tab; Home and End jump to the first or last Tab bar Return, Space Activate the tab Tab bar Backspace, Delete Close the tab; Contour asks first when a program may still be running in it Tab bar Alt+Left, Alt+Right Move the tab left or right Toolbar Left, Right Move to the previous or next item Toolbar Return, Space Press the item Either Escape Return to the terminal

A bare F6 is never taken: it reaches the shell, so mc, vim and htop keep it. The three actions, FocusNextArea, FocusPreviousArea and FocusToolbar, can be bound to other chords, on any key, and those chords keep working from inside the chrome. When the window shows no tab bar and no toolbar there is nowhere to go, and Ctrl+F6 reaches the program like any other key. Closing a tab asks whenever its foreground program is not its shell, and also when Contour cannot tell (every pane of a daemon-hosted window), because closing the tab would end whatever runs in it.

While the chrome has focus, every key binding keeps working, such as the command palette, opening a new tab or one of your own, except the keys the chrome takes for itself: the arrow keys, Home, End, Return, Space, Escape, Backspace, Delete and Tab, with no modifier or with Shift or Alt alone. A chord with Ctrl on one of those keys is still yours. Plain typing is not sent to the shell until you press Escape to return to the terminal.

docs.title: Things that are only announced
docs.text:
Some of what a terminal does has no representation in the accessibility tree at all — nothing's state changed, so nothing is reported unless it is said explicitly. Contour announces:

Event Politeness The bell Polite — it waits for your screen reader to finish its sentence A desktop notification (OSC 99, OSC 777 or OSC 9) Polite Read-only mode being switched on or off Assertive — it interrupts, because it changes what typing does

Set accessibility_announcements: false in contour.yml to switch these off. They cost nothing while no assistive client is attached.

docs.title: Reading a selection aloud
docs.text:
Select some text and press ++ctrl+shift+s++, or pick Read Aloud from the right-click menu, to have the operating system's speech synthesizer read it. ++ctrl+shift+s++ again reads the new selection.

Text is prepared before it is spoken: the blank padding every terminal line carries out to the right margin is dropped, runs of empty lines collapse to a single pause, and a very long selection is cut at a line boundary so that selecting a build log gives a readable excerpt rather than many minutes of speech.

This needs a speech engine, and it is optional

Reading aloud needs Qt's TextToSpeech module at build time and a speech engine with an installed voice at run time — on Linux that means speech-dispatcher or flite. Where either is missing the feature is simply not offered: the menu row does not appear and the shortcut does nothing, rather than appearing and staying silent.

A build that omitted it says so in its own build log, so a packager can see it without having to run the application.

docs.title: Platform notes
docs.text:
Platform Technology Notes Linux AT-SPI 2 Works with Orca and with KDE Plasma's zoom — see the note below. Windows UI Automation Works with Magnifier's follow keyboard focus / text cursor modes. macOS NSAccessibility Qt maps the text interface to AXTextArea. Not verified.

KDE Plasma: caret tracking is off by default

Plasma's zoom (Meta++ / Meta+- / Meta+0) follows the mouse pointer out of the box and ignores the text caret until you say otherwise. Turn on Enable caret tracking in System Settings → Accessibility → Screen Magnifier; without it the zoom will not follow the cursor in Contour — or in any other application — no matter what the application reports.

KWin consumes the AT-SPI object:text-caret-moved signal for this. If tracking still does not follow after enabling the option, KWIN_WAYLAND_ZOOM_FORCE_LEGACY_TEXT_CARET_TRACKING=1 forces KWin onto that AT-SPI path rather than its newer one.

Qt's own environment variables apply. In particular QT_ACCESSIBILITY=0 disables accessibility for the process, and on Linux QT_LINUX_ACCESSIBILITY_ALWAYS_ON=1 forces the AT-SPI bridge on even when no client has announced itself.

docs.title: Verifying it
docs.text:
To inspect what Contour actually exposes:

  • Linux — Accerciser. Select the Contour window; the terminal appears with a text interface, and the caret offset updates as you type. A shell prompt child appears while you are at a prompt and disappears while a command runs.
  • Windows — Accessibility Insights, or Inspect.exe from the Windows SDK.

docs.title: Control API
docs.text: Every window, tab and pane a Contour daemon hosts can be listed, driven and watched from the shell, from scripts and from coding agents, with the same contour binary that runs the terminal. The verbs below talk to the daemon's control API; contour api list shows everything the API offers, including what has no verb yet.

docs.title: Where you are
docs.text:
A shell hosted by the daemon finds its surroundings in four environment variables:

Variable Holds $CONTOUR_PANE The shell's own pane, pane:<uuid>. The default target of every verb. $CONTOUR_TAB Its tab, tab:<uuid>. $CONTOUR_WINDOW Its window, window:<uuid>. $CONTOUR_DAEMON The daemon's socket path.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
Wherever a verb takes a pane, tab or window (--pane P), P is resolved in this order, and the first kind of match wins:

  1. a full id (pane:018f3c4e-...);
  2. a label, compared case-insensitively (see contour label);
  3. a 1-based position, for tabs and windows;
  4. an id suffix of at least four hex digits.

More than one match is an error that lists the candidates, one per line. Without --pane, a verb acts on $CONTOUR_PANE; a pane that has since closed is an error (exit status 3), never a silent fallback to another pane.

docs.title: Verbs
docs.text:
Verb What it does contour ls [--window W] Lists windows, tabs and panes as a tree; ids are shortened to their last 8 hex digits and * marks the active ones. contour new [--window W \| --new-window] [--cwd DIR] [--label L] [--no-focus] [-- CMD...] Opens a tab and prints its pane id. contour split [--pane P] [--right \| --below] [--ratio PCT] [--cwd DIR] [--label L] [--no-focus] [-- CMD...] Splits a pane and prints the new pane's id. contour send [--pane P] [--enter] [--wait] TEXT...\|- Types text into a pane. --enter appends a carriage return, - reads standard input, --wait waits for the command the text starts and exits with that command's own status. contour pane capture [--pane P] [--scrollback N \| --all] Prints a pane's text. contour close [--pane P \| --tab T] Closes a pane, or a tab with all its panes. contour label OBJECT LABEL Labels a window, tab or pane (contour label pane:018f logs); an empty label clears it. contour block list [--pane P] [--limit N] Lists a pane's recent command blocks, newest first: id exit duration command. contour block read [BLOCK] [--pane P] [--prompt \| --output] Prints a block's text; without BLOCK, the pane's last finished block. With neither flag, the prompt and then the output. contour wait [BLOCK] [--pane P] [--timeout SECONDS] Waits for a block to finish and exits with the command's own status. contour events [--follow] [--kind K[,K...]] [--pane P] Prints the first matching event and exits, or with --follow every event until Ctrl+C (exit status 130). contour api list [-q] Lists the API's methods and events; -q prints names only. contour api describe NAME Prints one method's or event's schemas and examples. contour api call NAME [JSON\|@FILE\|-] Calls any method with the given request, sent as is and without context. The output is indented on a terminal and one line otherwise. contour api wit Prints the API as the WIT package terminal-extensions:control@0.1.0 a WebAssembly extension imports, exactly as wit/control/world.wit holds it. Reaches no daemon and takes none of the connection options.

contour pane capture is spelled that way because contour capture is the older verb that captures the screen of the terminal it runs in.

Options that look like words (--pane, but also the bare pane) can be mistaken for typed text: put -- before text that starts with the name of an option, as in contour send --enter -- wait.

docs.title: Connection options
docs.text:
Every verb takes:

Option Meaning --json Prints the reply JSON as received, plus a newline, instead of the human form. --daemon PATH\|HOST:PORT\|NAME\|URL The daemon. Defaults to $CONTOUR_DAEMON, then the default socket. A verb never starts a daemon. --token-file FILE The token a HOST:PORT daemon expects. --tls-ca FILE The CA certificate (PEM) a HOST:PORT daemon is verified against.

A HOST:PORT daemon without --tls-ca is refused before anything is sent, with a message naming the option: control requests, which can type into panes, never travel over an unverified connection.

A bare word (--daemon homepc) names a saved host of the configuration's hosts: section, and an ssh:// URL an ad-hoc one, exactly as contour client --host reads them (see Remote hosts): the host's own token_file and tls_ca apply, and --token-file and --tls-ca do not. A saved tls:// host without tls_ca is refused like a HOST:PORT daemon without --tls-ca. A name no saved host has exits 4 with the names that are saved.

docs.title: Windows opened by contour new --new-window
docs.text: A window created by a control connection is followed by the primary viewer, the GUI whose launch took every window, and so appears in the open GUI. With no GUI attached it appears at the next launch.

docs.title: Waiting
docs.text:
contour wait and contour send --wait exit with the finished command's own status, clamped to 0..255. A block without an exit code, with a negative one, or that was superseded by a newer prompt exits 1, with a note on standard error. contour wait with no BLOCK waits for the next block of the pane to finish; one that already finished is read with contour block read. --timeout SECONDS is kept by the client: when it runs out, contour wait prints Error: timed out and exits 1, and the command in the pane carries on.

contour send --enter 'make' && contour wait --timeout 600 || echo "make failed or took too long"

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
contour events subscribes to the daemon's events. A line reads HH:MM:SS type pane details (times are UTC; the pane is the last 8 hex digits of its id behind an ellipsis). With --json each event is printed as received, one per line, which is what scripts read:

contour events --follow --json --kind block.finished | jq -r '.payload.block | "\(.exitCode) \(.command)"'

An event of a type this release does not know, from a newer daemon, is printed raw. --kind takes a comma separated list of:

Event Fires when block.finished A command block finished. pane.bell A pane rang the bell. pane.titleChanged A pane's title changed. pane.cwdChanged A pane's working directory changed. pane.programStatusChanged A pane's program status changed. pane.created, pane.closed A pane was created or closed. tab.created, tab.closed A tab was created or closed. client.attached, client.detached A GUI client attached or detached. events.dropped The subscriber was too slow and events were dropped.

docs.title: Exit statuses
docs.text:
Status Meaning 0 Done. 1 The call failed; the reason is on standard error as Error: <message>. 2 The command line was malformed, or a setting it names cannot be used (a --tls-ca that does not parse). 3 The pane, tab, window or block named does not exist, or the name matches several. 4 No daemon could be reached. 130 Interrupted by Ctrl+C.

contour send --wait exits with the command's own status instead (0 to 255). A command with no exit code, or one that was superseded, exits 1 with a note on standard error.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: A daemon's TCP tokens carry grants (contour daemon --access-file): read for listing, screen for capturing, reading blocks and program status (pane.programStatusChanged, and the programStatus of contour ls --json), input for typing, and write for changing the workspace. A call outside the token's grants is refused as forbidden (exit status 1). The daemon's socket grants everything to its owner. A connection holds at most 64 subscriptions and 256 pending waits; one more is refused as limitReached (exit status 1). Each verb opens a connection of its own, so only a script driving contour api call over one connection meets it.

docs.title: A workflow: run the tests beside you
docs.text:
pane=$(contour split --below --no-focus --json | jq -r .pane)
contour send --pane "$pane" --enter --wait -- 'make test'   # exits with make's status
contour block read --pane "$pane" --output                   # what it printed

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
contour agent setup writes a skill that teaches coding agents to operate Contour panes: where they are, how targets resolve, every verb with its usage, the exit statuses, the run-the-tests workflow, and the whole API. The skill is generated from the verb table and the API catalog, so it always matches the binary.

contour agent setup            # Claude Code and ~/.agents
contour agent setup --agent claude --dry-run
Agent Skill file claude (Claude Code) ~/.claude/skills/contour/SKILL.md, or beneath $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when that is set agents (Codex, OpenCode and other agents reading ~/.agents) ~/.agents/skills/contour/SKILL.md

Rerun it after upgrading Contour: a file it generated is updated, one that is already current is left alone, and a file it did not generate is kept unless you pass --force. --dry-run reports what would happen, and --json prints the outcomes as an array.

docs.title: Status-line extensions
docs.text:
Experimental

Status-line extensions are new, and the interface they are written against, the terminal-extensions:statusline@0.1.0 world, may still change before it is declared stable.

A status-line extension is a small WebAssembly module that draws part of the indicator status line, or all of it. It is told what happens in its pane (the working directory changed, a program set a user variable, the pane gained the focus, ...), and it answers with the text, colours and, when it owns the whole line, images to show.

Extensions run sandboxed. A module sees no files, no network and no environment; it gets the time and the pane's state from Contour, and it can run only the commands it declared up front, and only once you said it may. Every call into an extension has a time limit, and its memory a cap.

Extensions run on a small pool of worker threads shared by every pane -- as many as the machine has cores, four at most -- and never on the threads that read the terminal's output, parse it or draw it. Each extension is handed one of the workers, in turn. A slow, frozen or crashing extension therefore never slows the terminal down: it keeps reading, parsing and drawing at full speed (see Performance). It can delay the other extensions on its worker, though, by up to its time limit per call, until it fails often enough to be disabled.

docs.title: Configuring extensions
docs.text:
Extensions are configured per profile. Each entry under extensions: is one extension; its key is the name the status line refers to it by.

profiles:
    main:
        extensions:
            clock: {}
            git:    { run_command: ask }
            plasma: { config: { text: "{mode}  {title}", speed: "2" } }
            mine:   { path: ~/wasm/mine.wasm, run_command: deny }
Key Meaning path The module to load; a leading ~ is the home directory, and a relative path is taken relative to the directory of the configuration file that declares it. Without a path the key selects the bundled extension of that name. config Text values the extension reads by key; what each extension understands is listed with it. run_command Whether the extension may run the commands its manifest declares: allow, deny or ask. Default: ask. See Permissions.

An extension shows up where the status line names it. There are two ways:

  • As a segment. {Extension:<name>} in one of the indicator status line's templates is replaced by the extension's text, with its colours and attributes. Every other placeholder keeps working beside it. The long form takes the usual formatting styles: {Extension:Name=git,Left= ,Right= }.
profiles:
    main:
        status_line:
            indicator:
                left: " {InputMode:Bold}{Extension:git}"
                right: "{Extension:clock}"
  • Taking the line over. status_line.extension names one extension that draws the whole indicator status line instead of its templates. Only an extension that takes the line over may draw images (Sixel or the kitty graphics protocol); as a segment an extension draws text only.
profiles:
    main:
        status_line:
            display: indicator
            extension: plasma

A name that is not one of the profile's extensions is reported in the log, and the templates are used.

Every pane runs its own instance of each of its profile's extensions. Changing extensions: and reloading the configuration (or switching the profile) restarts them; an unchanged set keeps running.

When an extension fails (it traps, exceeds its time limit or its memory, or writes too much output), it is restarted after a short back-off. Three failures within a minute disable it, and its place shows ⚠ <name> disabled: <reason> instead. A module that cannot be found or loaded shows the same notice right away.

docs.title: Bundled extensions
docs.text:
Contour ships these extensions. Name one under extensions: without a path to use it.

Name Shows Settings clock The local time of day, HH:MM, daylight saving included. Wakes once a minute. none git The branch of the git repository the pane's working directory is in, with * when the working tree has changes. Runs git, so it asks first. Refreshes when the directory or the foreground process changes (the latter on Linux and macOS) and when the pane gains the focus. refresh-ms: also refresh this often while focused (default 0, never) sysload The system's load: the 1, 5 and 15 minute load averages from uptime, or the processor load on Windows. Runs a command, so it asks first. refresh-ms: how often, while focused (default 5000) agent-status A badge for the state a coding agent reports in a user variable (working, waiting, done), and the progress it reports (OSC 9;4). variable: the user variable to follow (default agent_status) plasma An animated plasma drawn with Sixel across the whole line, with text on top. Meant to take the line over; animates only while the pane is focused. text: drawn on top, where {mode}, {title} and {tabs} are filled in; speed: how fast the colours cycle (default 1)

A coding agent, or a hook it runs, sets the variable agent-status follows like this:

printf '\e]1337;SetUserVar=agent_status=%s\a' "$(printf working | base64)"

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
An extension can run a program only if its module declares the command in its manifest, and only as declared: the program and its arguments are fixed, and the extension fills in only the placeholders the declaration names. No shell is involved.

What run_command says decides the rest:

  • deny: no command runs.
  • allow: every declared command runs, without asking.

  • ask (the default): the first time the extension tries to run a command, Contour asks you. The question names the extension, the module it was loaded from, and every command it declares, exactly as it would run.

  • Allow lets it run its declared commands from now on.

  • Deny refuses them from now on.
  • Closing the question answers nothing: the extension's commands keep failing, and you are asked again once the extension starts anew, in a new pane or after a configuration reload restarts it.

The call that triggered the question fails at once; nothing waits for your answer. Once you allowed it, the extension's next attempt succeeds.

Your answer is remembered for that installation of the extension and for that exact manifest: an extension configured under another name or loaded from another path, or one whose manifest changed in any way (an update that adds a command, say), is asked about again. Answers are kept beside the configuration file:

  • extension-grants.txt for the GUI;
  • extension-grants.daemon.txt for contour daemon, named after the socket it serves, so that daemons sharing a configuration directory, and the GUI, keep their answers apart:
  • extension-grants.daemon.<label>.txt for a daemon serving another socket label than the default one (every character of the label but letters, digits, ., - and _ spelled _);
  • extension-grants.daemon[.<label>].<hash>.txt for a daemon given a socket path other than its label's own, where <hash> is eight hex digits computed from that path.

A daemon's answers govern commands that run on the daemon's machine.

To take an answer back, delete its line from the file, or the whole file.

docs.title: In daemon sessions
docs.text:
A session hosted by contour daemon runs its extensions in the daemon, where the session's terminal lives, and its clients show what they draw. The profile the daemon loads decides which extensions run; a client's own profile only decides whether the status line is shown. Mirrored panes run no extensions of their own. A question about an extension's commands is asked in the attached client, and remembered in the daemon's grants file.

This works with some limits for now:

  • No font events. The daemon draws in no font, so extensions in daemon sessions are not told the font's size or the cell size, and an image an extension draws is sized for a default cell.
  • A dismissed question waits for a reattach. If you close the question instead of answering it, it is asked again only when a client attaches to the session again.
  • No tab events. The daemon does not tell its extensions about the client's tabs.

docs.title: Writing an extension
docs.text: An extension is a WebAssembly core module built for wasm32-wasip1 that implements the terminal-extensions:statusline world. The world, at wit/statusline/, is the contract, and its README spells out what the WIT text cannot: when the host calls what, what it guarantees, and how the contract is carried in the binary. Any language with a wit-bindgen generator works; the bundled extensions are written in Rust, and so is this walkthrough.

docs.title: The world in short
docs.text:
The host calls three functions of the module:

  • load(config): once, first, with the extension's config: values. It returns the event kinds the extension wants to hear about, any of title, cwd, foreground-process, input-mode, tabs, user-var, progress, focus and font. foreground-process is reported on Linux and macOS only; on Windows no such event arrives. It is always told when its own surface is resized, when a frame it asked for is due, and the terminal's replies to queries in its output.
  • update(event): once per event, in order. It answers render when what the extension shows has changed, none otherwise.
  • render(cols, rows): after load, and after an update that answered render. It returns the bytes that draw the status line on a terminal of that many cells: text, SGR colours and attributes, cursor movement and, when the extension takes the line over, images.

And the module may call four functions of the host:

  • state(): the pane's current state (working directory, title, focus, user variables, the time and the time zone's offset, the font, ...);
  • request-frame(ms): asks for a timer event; this is how an extension animates, or wakes at the next minute. It never sleeps;
  • run-command(name, args): runs a command its manifest declares, if allowed;
  • log(level, message): writes to Contour's log.

docs.title: A Rust crate
docs.text:
# Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "hello"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
wit-bindgen = { version = "0.63.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "realloc"] }

[profile.release]
opt-level = "s"
lto = true
panic = "abort"

// src/lib.rs
wit_bindgen::generate!({
    path: "wit/statusline", // a copy of Contour's wit/statusline directory
    world: "statusline",
});

struct Hello;

impl Guest for Hello {
    fn load(_config: Vec<(String, String)>) -> EventKinds {
        EventKinds::CWD
    }

    fn update(_event: Event) -> RenderRequest {
        RenderRequest::Render
    }

    fn render(_cols: u32, _rows: u32) -> Vec<u8> {
        let cwd = terminal_extensions::statusline::host::state().cwd;
        format!("\x1b[1m{cwd}\x1b[m").into_bytes()
    }
}

export!(Hello);

Build it with the wasm32-wasip1 target, and point a profile at the module:

rustup target add wasm32-wasip1
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1
# target/wasm32-wasip1/release/hello.wasm

profiles:
    main:
        extensions:
            hello: { path: ~/src/hello/target/wasm32-wasip1/release/hello.wasm }
        status_line:
            indicator:
                right: "{Extension:hello}"

The module stays a plain core module: do not componentize it. The bundled extensions under extensions/bundled/ are complete examples; clock is the smallest.

Keep the limits in mind: each call (load included) has a deadline (50 ms for update and render), the module's memory is capped at 32 MiB, one render may return at most 1 MiB, and renders are at least 16 ms apart. Events are coalesced under load, so an extension sees the latest working directory rather than every one in between.

docs.title: The manifest
docs.text:
A module that runs commands declares them in a custom section named terminal-extension-manifest, which Contour reads before it runs any of the module's code:

name = git
version = 1
command status = git --no-optional-locks -C {cwd} status --porcelain=v2 --branch

run-command("status", [("cwd", "/home/me/src")]) then runs exactly that argv, the whole value of cwd as one argument. In Rust, the manifest crate under extensions/manifest emits the section:

manifest::declare_manifest!(
    "name = git\nversion = 1\ncommand status = git --no-optional-locks -C {cwd} status --porcelain=v2 --branch\n"
);

A module without a manifest loads and runs; every command it tries fails. The manifest's full grammar, and the rules for the values filled into a command, are in the world's README.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Extensions run on a small pool of worker threads, never on the threads that read the terminal's output, parse it or draw it, and nothing on those threads ever waits for an extension: an event an extension's queue cannot take is dropped, not waited for. A profile without extensions starts none of their machinery: no WebAssembly runtime, no worker thread, no timer.

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text:
Measured on a 32-thread Linux machine with bench-headless throughput, a release build, 16 MiB per workload fed from memory, the indicator status line shown and the terminal focused. Each cell is the faster of two rounds, run interleaved (one configuration after the other, twice), each round the fastest of 5 runs. The misbehaving guest spins until its time limit stops it, on every call, for the whole run (the benchmark restarts it at once and never disables it):

Workload (primary screen) No extensions configured plasma animating + a guest spinning to its time limit Four such guests, every worker busy ascii 238 MiB/s 238 MiB/s 239 MiB/s colored 161 MiB/s 160 MiB/s 160 MiB/s sgr 95 MiB/s 95 MiB/s 94 MiB/s utf8 36 MiB/s 36 MiB/s 36 MiB/s tui 261 MiB/s 262 MiB/s 261 MiB/s

The one dip that repeated is on the alternate screen, which the table does not show: with four guests keeping every worker busy, sgr there ran about 4 % slower in both rounds (98 against 94 MiB/s).

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Each extension runs as its own instance in every pane: its WebAssembly memory, and a small private terminal its output is drawn on. Measured with bench-headless memory (a release build on Linux, each pane 120×40 with 1000 lines of scrollback, the indicator shown and focused, refreshed at 60 Hz for 5 s, the process's resident set before and after):

Panes No extensions All five bundled extensions (plasma taking the line over and animating) Cost of the extensions 1 4.5 MiB 13.2 MiB 8.7 MiB 10 21.0 MiB 104.2 MiB 8.3 MiB per pane

One extension costs about 1.6 MiB per pane, plasma about 2.3 MiB (its image is drawn on its surface, and again in the pane's status line). An empty module costs 1.4 MiB per pane too: most of an extension's cost is the private terminal and the runtime's per-instance state every extension has, not what it does. Shared by all panes, once, are the runtime and its workers: well under 1 MiB.

docs.title: Without extensions
docs.text: A build without extensions compiled in runs within the same few percent: its parser executes the same number of instructions (Callgrind) as one with them. An idle Contour with no extensions configured wakes up exactly as often as one built without them (measured on Qt's offscreen platform).

docs.title: The WebAssembly runtime
docs.text: Extensions run on WAMR's fast interpreter, but nothing in Contour that hosts them names it. They are loaded, instantiated and called through a runtime-neutral interface (src/vtextension/wasm/WasmRuntime.hpp), and the runtime behind it is a backend chosen when Contour is built: the CMake cache variable CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME (today its one value is wamr) selects the target vtextension_<runtime>. Only what composes a program links that backend, through vtextension_runtime, and creates it with vtextension::wasm::makeDefaultBackend(): the GUI, contour daemon, bench-headless and the test suites. The extension engine and the daemon's session host see only the interface. The check_wasm_runtime_containment lint gate (ctest -L lint) holds them to it: it fails when a file under src/ outside the backend directory includes WAMR's C headers or the backend's own headers, or when the vtextension or vthost library links WAMR. Bringing in another runtime is adding a backend directory beside src/vtextension/wasm/wamr/ and a value of CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME; the behaviour an extension sees is pinned by the backend contract tests every backend must pass.

docs.title: Adding a backend
docs.text:
A backend for a runtime <runtime> is the directory src/vtextension/wasm/<runtime>/, and it must provide all of the following; src/vtextension/wasm/wamr/ is the one to copy from.

  • A CMakeLists.txt defining the target vtextension_<runtime>, which links vtextension publicly and the runtime itself privately. src/vtextension/CMakeLists.txt adds the directory named by CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME and links its target into vtextension_runtime; nothing else may link the runtime.
  • A value of CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME: <runtime> added to _CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIMES in the top-level CMakeLists.txt, which refuses any value not on that list.
  • vtextension::wasm::makeDefaultBackend() (declared in src/vtextension/wasm/DefaultBackend.hpp), defined in the backend's target and returning its IWasmBackend (WAMR: DefaultBackend.cpp).
  • vtextension::wasm::testing::preparedGeneration() (declared in src/vtextension/wasm/testing/PreparedGeneration.hpp), defined in a PreparedGeneration.cpp added to vtextension_test only: the runtime generation the calling thread was prepared for, 0 if none.
  • The contract suite, instantiated in vtextension_test: a *_test.cpp the directory adds to vtextension_test, holding a traits struct whose make() returns a new backend and the line CONTOUR_WASM_BACKEND_CONTRACT(Traits) (from src/vtextension/wasm/testing/BackendContract.hpp). Every case tagged [wasm-contract] must pass, among them the two rules no backend is exempt from: the runtime generation increases on each bring-up, and entering a thread guard fails RuntimeUnavailable while no runtime is up.
  • A passing containment gate: ctest -L lint (check_wasm_runtime_containment) must pass. The gate knows WAMR's C headers, backend directory and link target by name (scripts/check-wasm-runtime-containment.py); teach it the new runtime's alongside, so that they too stay inside the backend directory.

docs.title: Main Features
docs.text: Available on all 4 major platforms, Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, Windows. GPU-accelerated rendering. Terminal tabs and split panes, with colored tabs, tab badges and drag-and-drop rearranging of panes and tabs Layouts: named sets of tabs and panes that open together Native window chrome on Windows 11, macOS and Linux, in light and dark, with a Settings window, a command palette and a character-cell Terminal style Persistent sessions that survive the window (daemon mode) — reattach locally or over the network, and interoperate with tmux in both directions Font ligatures support (very useful for programming and scripting) Unicode: Emoji support (-: 🌈 💝 😛 👪 - including ZWJ, VS15, VS16 emoji :-) Unicode: Grapheme cluster support Bold and italic fonts Nerd Fonts glyphs (Powerline, Font Awesome, Material Design, Devicons, ...) with whichever font you choose: a symbols font is bundled High-DPI support. Vi-like input modes for improved navigation, selection and copy'n'paste experience Hint mode for keyboard-driven selection of URLs, file paths, git hashes, and more Drag and drop: drop a tab on a pane edge to split it, or files to type their escaped paths Clickable links: URLs, file paths and your own patterns in whatever a program prints, opened with Ctrl+click A find bar with a live match count, floating over the pane being searched Control API and the contour ls, new, split, send, pane capture and block commands to script the daemon's windows, tabs, panes and command blocks Sandboxed WebAssembly status-line extensions Quick terminal: a global hotkey slides a terminal down from the top of the screen Vertical Line Markers (quickly jump to markers in your history!) Command blocks: an exit-status gutter, line numbers, per-line timestamps, folding, scrollbar marks and a sticky command header Restored sessions: history comes back above a "Restored" divider, with one toast saying what was restored Offer to install shell integration for bash, zsh and fish, showing the one line it adds, also in Settings Notifications when a long-running command finishes in a tab you are not looking at Shell integration for bash, zsh, fish, tcsh and PowerShell Blurred behind transparent background when using Windows 10 or KDE window manager on Linux. Blurrable Background image support. Runtime configuration reload 256-color and Truecolor support Key binding customization Color Schemes Profiles (grouped customization of: color scheme, login shell, and related behaviors) Synchronized rendering (via SM ? 2026 / RM ? 2026) Text reflow (configurable via SM ? 2028 / RM ? 2028) Clickable hyperlinks via OSC 8 Clipboard setting via OSC 52 Sixel Image support ReGIS vector graphics Terminal page buffer capture VT extension to quickly extract contents. Builtin Fira Code inspired progress bar support. Read-only mode, protecting against accidental user-input to the running application, such as Ctrl+C. VT320 Host-programmable and Indicator statusline support Size indicator on resize

docs.title: Input Modes
docs.text:
Normally, a terminal emulator only knows about one input mode, so there is no need of distinction.

Inspired by Vi/Vim, the Termite terminal emulator started to introduce so called Vim-modes, where the user can use the keyboard only to screen text selection, amongst other things. So users can press Ctrl+Shift+Space to enter the vim mode. You can then move the cursor using vim motion keys and then start selecting.

docs.title: Contour introduces multiple Vim-like input modes:
docs.text:
• insert mode: This is the default input mode. Everything is forwarded to the application.
  • normal mode: Use motion keys to move the cursor and operators to act
  • visual mode: Linear selection, use motion keys to alter the selection.
  • visual line mode: Line based selection, use motion keys to alter the selection.
  • visual block mode: Block based selection, use motion keys to alter the selection.
  • hint mode: Overlay alphabetic labels on detected patterns (URLs, file paths, etc.) and type a label to act on it.

docs.title: Supported operators (Normal Mode)
docs.text:
• Normal: [count] p (paste primary clipboard count times)
  • Normal: yy (yank current line to primary clipboard)
  • Normal: y {motion} (yank given motion to primary clipboard)
  • Normal: y {TextObject} (yank given textObject to primary clipboard, such as yiw, yaw, yip, yap, ...)
  • Visual: y (yank current selection into primary clipboard)
  • v enables/disables visual mode
  • V enables/disables visual line mode
  • i activates insert mode
  • Ctrl+v enables/disables visual block mode
  • Normal: o {motion} (opens resource by given motion, this can be a URL or local file)
  • Normal: o {TextObject} (opens resource by given textObject, such as oiw, oaw, oiW, ...)
  • Visual: o (open current selection into primary clipboard)
  • Normal: gh (enter hint mode — copy selected match to clipboard)
  • Normal: gH (enter hint mode — open selected match)
  • Normal: gx (opens the link under the cursor: a URL, a path, or a custom pattern)
  • Normal: mm (set or clear a user mark on the cursor line)
  • Normal: za / zo / zc (toggle / open / close the command block under the cursor)
  • Normal: zM / zR (close / open every command block)

docs.title: Supported motions
docs.text:
Moving the cursor outside of the current view using a motion, will cause the terminal to scroll the view to make that target line visible.

  • [count] h
  • [count] j
  • [count] k
  • [count] l
  • [count] w
  • [count] b
  • [count] e
  • [count] |
  • 0
  • $
  • gg
  • G
  • { & }
  • [m & ]m (previous / next mark: a prompt or a user mark)
  • [count] ]x (next link)
  • [count] [x (previous link)

docs.title: Supported text objects
docs.text:
• i<, a< - angle brackets enclosed text
  • i{, a{ - curly brackets enclosed text
  • i", a" - double quotes enclosed text
  • ip, ap - backtick enclosed string
  • i(, a( - round brackets enclosed string
  • i', a' - single quoted string
  • i`, a` - backtick enclosed string
  • i[, a[ - square bracket enclosed string
  • iw, aw - regular word
  • iW, aW - space delimited word
  • im, am - the lines between two marks, without / with the marked lines

docs.title: Opening local files and URLs
docs.text:
Contour finds URLs, file paths and patterns of your own in the output and underlines them (see Links in Terminal Output). In normal mode, ]x and [x move the cursor from one link to the next, scanning beyond the screen when needed, and gx opens the link under the cursor as Ctrl+click would. A path counts once Contour has found that it exists.

You can also open what is not detected as a link by moving the cursor onto a resource (URL or local file) and then pressing oiW (open in (space separated) word) or use any of the other supported text objects to denote what to open.

You may as well type oo to open the URL under the current line. This works if no other information is on this current line, while spaces are trimmed left and right of the given URL in this line.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Installation

contour is packaged and available for installation on multiple distributions.

docs.title: Windows 10 or newer
docs.text: Please download Contour for Windows (the .msi file) from our release page, and double click on it to install.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: brew install contour

docs.title: Fedora Linux
docs.text:
Use the official package

sudo dnf install contour-terminal

docs.title: Arch Linux
docs.text:
Use the official package

sudo pacman -S contour

docs.title: Ubuntu Linux
docs.text:
Please download Contour for Ubuntu Linux (the .deb files) from our official release page, and then use the following command to install:

sudo dpkg -i ~/Downloads/contour-0.3.12.262-UBUNTU_VERSION-ARCH.deb

If you want to provide feedback in case of any crashes, also install the debug symbols (.ddeb-file), e.g.:

sudo dpkg -i ~/Downloads/contour-0.3.12.262-UBUNTU_VERSION-ARCH.ddeb

docs.title: Flatpak
docs.text: Contour is available at the Flathub store.

docs.title: Installing from source
docs.text: Contour is best installed from supported package managers, but you can build from source by following the instruction below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
./scripts/install-deps.sh

This script might ask you for the administrator password if a package dependency can be installed via the system package manager.

docs.title: Compile
docs.text:
You can use cmake presets to compile contour. The full list of available presets can be seen using cmake --list-presets. To compile release build for linux clang-release or gcc-release, or appleclang-release on macOS accordingly.

cmake --preset clang-release
cmake --build --preset clang-release

# Optionally, if you want to install from source
cmake --build --preset clang-release --target install

Please note, if you want to install into a system root, e.g. /usr/local, you may need to prefix the install command with sudo.

Also, ensure that the terminfo file is correctly resolved, as the terminfo library is very limited in locating the correct terminfo files (e.g. it does not search in /usr/local), you can symlink into ~/.terminfo however.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
For Windows, you must have Windows 10, 2018 Fall Creators Update, and Visual Studio 2019, installed. It will neither build nor run on any prior Windows OS, due to libterminal making use of ConPTY API.

  1. Set up vcpkg, preferably somewhere high up in the folder hierarchy, and add the folder to your PATH.
cd C:\
git clone git clone https://github.com/Microsoft/vcpkg.git
.\vcpkg\bootstrap-vcpkg.bat
  1. Install Visual Studio Build Tools (make sure to select the CLI tools for C++, which you might need to do in the separate components tab).
  2. Install Qt6 (i.e. to C:\Qt)
  3. Open the developer version of Powershell.
  4. In the contour source folder execute .\scripts\install-deps.ps1. This step may take a very long time.

docs.title: Compile
docs.text:
In the developer version of Powershell:

# change paths accordingly if you installed QT and vcpkg to somewhere else
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=C:\vcpkg\scripts\buildsystems\vcpkg.cmake -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=C:\Qt\6.5.0\msvc2019_64\lib\cmake
cmake --build build/

# Optionally, if you want to install from source
cmake --build build/ --target install

docs.title: Persistent sessions (daemon mode)
docs.text:
Experimental

Daemon mode is new in 0.7.0 and still settling. It is built into every Contour and covered by the test suite, but its command-line flags and its wire protocol may change between releases.

Contour already gives you tabs and split panes inside one window. Daemon mode is different: it moves your sessions into a background process, so they survive the window that shows them. Close the window, reattach later, or attach from another machine — the shells keep running either way.

That buys you three things:

  • A long build, a database migration or a training run keeps going after you close the window — deliberately or by accident.
  • Work done over SSH survives the link dropping. Reconnect, reattach, carry on.
  • The same sessions are reachable from a second machine, over an encrypted connection.

If you have used tmux or screen, this is the same idea, with two differences: the sessions are rendered by a real Contour window (images, hyperlinks, sized text and all), and Contour can speak tmux's own protocol in both directions — so it interoperates with tmux rather than replacing it.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
contour client

That is the whole thing. contour client looks for a daemon, starts one if none is running, and opens a window showing its sessions. Close the window and the shells stay alive; run contour client again to pick them back up — with their scrollback, so you can scroll back through what the session did while nothing was watching.

To manage the daemon yourself, start it first:

contour daemon &      # runs in the FOREGROUND; background it or use a service manager
contour client        # attaches to the daemon you started

The distinction matters, because the two daemons have different lifetimes:

How it started When it exits Auto-started by contour client 10 seconds after it has no sessions and no clients — it belongs to the clients that needed it, so nothing is left behind Started by you (contour daemon) Never on its own. It keeps serving with zero sessions, ready for the next client Started by the OS (contour daemon-service) Never on its own, see Starting the daemon at login

Closing the last window therefore keeps your sessions: the auto-started daemon stays up as long as any session lives, and for 10 seconds after the last one is gone and the last client has disconnected. A client that attaches within those 10 seconds keeps the daemon alive.

The policy is the daemon's --lifecycle option, and it rides on the daemon, not on the client that started it:

--lifecycle The daemon ends persistent (default for contour daemon) never on its own exit-with-last-session once its last hosted session is gone (tmux spells this exit-empty) exit-when-idle (what contour client starts on demand) 10 seconds after it has no session and no client

--exit-with-last-session is kept as an alias for --lifecycle=exit-with-last-session. Stating both is an error only when they differ. A status probe (contour daemon status) is not a client and never keeps an idle daemon alive.

contour daemon does not detach by itself

It runs in the foreground and logs to standard error, which is what you want under a service manager or in a container. Background it with &, or let contour client start it for you.

docs.title: Detaching versus ending a session
docs.text:
Because sessions outlive the window, "close" needs two answers — and Contour gives you both. Which one you get depends on what you close:

What you close What happens to the shell The window (its close button, or quitting Contour) Detach. It keeps running; the next contour client shows it again A pane — Close Pane in the right-click menu, or the ClosePane action Ends. That session is closed on the daemon and does not come back A tab — its ✕, or the CloseTab action Ends, together with every pane in it Typing exit in the shell Ends, as always — the shell decided

This is the same split tmux draws between detaching a client and kill-pane, and it works the same for a local session as for one hosted by a daemon: a pane you end is ended everywhere, including for any other client attached to that daemon.

Neither ClosePane nor CloseTab ships with a default key binding — bind them yourself if you want one:

input_mapping:
    - { mods: [Ctrl, Shift], key: 'W', action: ClosePane }

Ending a whole daemon's worth of sessions

Closing panes one at a time is the fine-grained way. To end everything at once, stop the daemon — see Stopping a daemon.

docs.title: Running several daemons side by side
docs.text:
Daemons are told apart by a label, exactly as tmux's -L does:

contour daemon --label work
contour client --label work

The label names a socket under your per-user runtime directory. Resolution order:

  1. --socket PATH — used verbatim.
  2. An explicitly given --label NAME (the value default included) — the label's own socket, exactly as tmux's -L beats $TMUX.
  3. $CONTOUR_MUX — used verbatim (analogous to tmux's $TMUX).
  4. $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/contour/<label> (the default label when none was given).
  5. <temp>/contour-<uid>/<label> when there is no runtime directory (tmux's /tmp/tmux-<uid>/<label> shape).

A daemon exports $CONTOUR_MUX into every shell it hosts, so a command typed in one of its panes reaches that same daemon without a flag. That is why it ranks above the default label: a sandboxed (Flatpak) shell cannot derive where its daemon lives, and a plain contour client there still finds it. It ranks below an explicit --label, so contour daemon --label work status from inside a pane asks the work daemon rather than the one hosting the pane.

The daemon binds three endpoints, all derived from that one path: the control socket itself, <socket>-native for Contour's own clients, and <socket>-tmux for the tmux binary.

The socket directory is created 0700 and checked on every bind: it must be a real directory, owned by you, and must not be world-accessible. Group access is permitted, matching tmux.

Keep socket paths short

A Unix socket path is limited to roughly 100 bytes by the operating system, not by Contour. A deeply nested --socket path will fail to bind.

docs.title: contour daemon options
docs.text: Option What it does --socket PATH Path of the control socket file. Defaults to the configuration's daemon.socket, else $CONTOUR_MUX when no --label is given, else $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/contour/LABEL. --label NAME Socket label distinguishing daemon instances. Default default. Given, it beats $CONTOUR_MUX. --config FILE Configuration file whose profile supplies the hosted sessions' terminal settings — including history.limit, which is how much scrollback a session keeps for clients that attach later. --profile NAME Which profile of that configuration to take them from. Defaults to the configuration's default profile. --lifecycle POLICY When the daemon ends on its own: persistent (the default), exit-with-last-session or exit-when-idle. See Quick start. --exit-with-last-session Alias for --lifecycle=exit-with-last-session. --size-policy POLICY Which attached client's size the shared grid takes when clients of different sizes are attached: latest, smallest or largest. Mirrors tmux's window-size. Defaults to the configuration's daemon.size_policy (latest unless set). --background Relaunches the command detached and returns once the daemon accepts connections. Without --log-file the daemon logs beside its socket (SOCKET.log), since a detached process has no console. --stdio Relays the native protocol between standard input/output and this user's daemon, starting it if needed: what contour client --host runs over ssh. Honours --label, --socket, --config, --profile, --log, --log-file and --size-policy (forwarded to a daemon it starts); cannot be combined with --listen-tcp, --background or --tmux-compat-socket. --in-place Runs from the installed binary instead of a per-version copy. See After upgrading Contour. --tmux-compat-socket LABEL Additionally binds tmux's own discovery path /tmp/tmux-<uid>/<LABEL>, so a plain tmux -L LABEL -C attach-session finds this daemon. --listen-tcp HOST:PORT Also serve the native protocol over TCP. Opt-in; always TLS-encrypted and token-authenticated. See Remote access. --token TOKEN Preshared token every TCP client must present. Required with --listen-tcp. Visible to other local users through the process list — prefer --token-file. --token-file FILE Reads the token from FILE instead, so the secret is protected by that file's permissions. Trailing newlines are ignored. --access-file FILE Further TCP tokens with narrower grants, one per line. Needs --listen-tcp. See Narrower tokens. --tls-cert FILE, --tls-key FILE PEM certificate and matching private key for the TCP listener. Omit both to have the daemon generate an ephemeral self-signed certificate. --log TAGS Enable logging for a comma-separated list of tags, or all. See Diagnostics. --log-file FILE Append log output to FILE instead of standard error; - means standard error explicitly.

docs.title: Hosting from a plain contour
docs.text:
The thin client is the default: a plain contour shows sessions that a daemon hosts, starting that daemon when none runs. contour client always attaches; a plain contour decides by daemon.mode in the configuration, or by --daemon-mode on its command line:

Mode Where the sessions run auto (the default) In the daemon, started if none runs; when none can be had, in the window's process, with a bar saying why — those shells end when the window closes in_process In the window's own process, as before daemon mode existed required In the daemon, or not at all: the launch ends with the reason before any window opens 
daemon:
  mode: auto          # auto, in_process or required
  socket: ""          # the daemon's socket path; empty selects the default
  size_policy: latest # whose size wins when clients disagree: latest, smallest or largest
  history_limit: 1000 # scrollback lines per session, -1 for unlimited; unset follows the profile

contour --daemon-mode in_process   # this launch only: keep the sessions in this window
contour --daemon-mode required     # this launch only: fail rather than fall back

docs.title: What a launch opens
docs.text:
An attaching launch opens one new window beside whatever the daemon already shows. When no other window is attached to the daemon, it instead brings every window the daemon holds back, so reopening Contour after closing its last window finds your sessions where you left them.

A launch that names a program (-e, or a command after the options) runs it in the window's own process under auto; under required it ends before any window, since a daemon session runs the host's profile.

docs.title: When the connection is lost
docs.text: A window attached to a daemon keeps its panes when the connection drops. They show "Reconnecting…" while the window reconnects with backoff (250 ms doubling to 5 s) and picks its windows up again. A connection gone half-open — a laptop that changed networks — is noticed by a heartbeat within about 15 s instead of whenever TCP gives up. Input typed while disconnected is dropped rather than replayed into whatever shell answers next. A launch that falls back to in_process has no connection to lose.

docs.title: contour client options
docs.text: Option What it does --socket PATH, --label NAME Which daemon to attach to; same resolution as above, daemon.socket of the client's configuration included. --window ID Show only the daemon window ID instead of opening a new one; fails, naming it, when the daemon has no such window. --size-policy POLICY The policy a daemon this client auto-starts runs with; defaults to daemon.size_policy. --tmux Attach to a real tmux server instead of a Contour daemon. See tmux interoperability. --tmux-socket PATH The tmux server socket (tmux's -S) for --tmux. --profile NAME Config profile the window renders remote sessions with. --config FILE Configuration file to load. --host NAME\|URL Attach to a remote host: a name saved under hosts:, or an ad-hoc ssh://[USER@]HOST[:PORT] (a tls:// host needs its token, so it must be saved). The remote daemon is started there when none runs; every one of its windows is shown, and the window title and the tab strip name the host. A host's profile: is used unless --profile names one. Cannot be combined with --socket, --connect-tcp, --token, --token-file, --tls-ca or --tmux. See Remote hosts. --connect-tcp HOST:PORT Connect to a remote daemon over TLS instead of a local socket. --token TOKEN, --token-file FILE The preshared token to present, inline or read from a file. --tls-ca FILE PEM trust anchor pinning the daemon's certificate. Omitted means encrypt-but-do-not-verify. --log TAGS, --log-file FILE As above — and passed on to a daemon this client auto-starts, which is otherwise the one instance nobody can configure.

docs.title: tmux interoperability
docs.text: Contour speaks tmux's control-mode protocol in both directions, pinned to tmux 3.7b semantics.

docs.title: Attach tmux tooling to a Contour daemon
docs.text:
<socket>-tmux speaks the binary protocol the stock tmux client uses, so the real tmux binary can attach to a Contour daemon:

tmux -S "$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/contour/default-tmux" -C attach-session

To let tmux find the daemon by label alone, have the daemon bind tmux's own discovery path too:

contour daemon --tmux-compat-socket mine
tmux -L mine -C attach-session

--tmux-compat-socket is opt-in for a reason

That path is where tmux looks for its server. With the Contour daemon down, a new-session against it would silently start a real tmux server there instead.

Control mode (-C) is supported; -CC is not — Contour never renders a full terminal client for tmux. Arbitrary startup commands are refused; the endpoint accepts attach- and new-session-shaped startup only.

docs.title: Show a real tmux server in a Contour window
docs.text:
The other direction: point Contour at a tmux server and mirror it.

contour client --tmux                       # the default tmux server
contour client --tmux --tmux-socket /tmp/x  # a specific one

tmux windows become Contour tabs, tmux panes become splits, and input travels back as send-keys. Content mirrors live.

tmux replay carries text, not images

Contour replays each pane's full history through capture-pane, so scrollback survives a reattach on this path too. Images do not, and that is a tmux limitation rather than Contour's: capture-pane serialises text and colour, never image data. Images drawn while you are attached display normally; images drawn before you attached cannot be recovered. Contour's own native protocol has no such gap — it transfers images by id.

docs.title: Remote access over TCP
docs.text:
By default a daemon is reachable only through its Unix socket, where the filesystem permissions are the access control. --listen-tcp additionally exposes the native protocol over the network:

# On the host running the sessions:
umask 077 && openssl rand -base64 32 > ~/.contour-token
contour daemon --listen-tcp 127.0.0.1:9090 --token-file ~/.contour-token

# On the machine you are sitting at:
contour client --connect-tcp server.example.com:9090 --token-file ~/.contour-token

Properties worth knowing before you open a port:

  • TLS is not optional. The TCP endpoint is always encrypted; there is no plaintext mode.
  • A token is required. TCP has no filesystem gate to fall back on, so --listen-tcp without --token/--token-file refuses to start rather than serving anonymously.
  • Prefer --token-file. A token passed as --token is readable by every other user on the machine through the process list; a file carries permissions.
  • Without --tls-cert/--tls-key the daemon generates an ephemeral self-signed certificate, and without --tls-ca the client encrypts but does not verify who it is talking to. That is a trust-on-first-use posture: it stops passive eavesdropping, not an active machine-in-the-middle. For anything beyond a trusted network, pass a real certificate on the daemon and pin it with --tls-ca on the client — the certificate must then also be issued for the host you connect to, not merely signed by that CA.
  • Bind deliberately. 127.0.0.1 reaches only the local machine; 0.0.0.0 reaches everyone who can route to you. Prefer forwarding the loopback port over SSH to exposing it directly.
  • Control requests need a verified daemon. A client of the control API refuses to send a single request over TLS it has not verified: without --tls-ca it stops before connecting. With the control API a token types into and reads every pane, so it must not be handed to whoever answers.

docs.title: Narrower tokens for scripts
docs.text:
--token grants everything. A script that only needs to read a pane can be given a token of its own that grants less, through --access-file FILE, one entry per line:

# grants   token (to the end of the line)
read,screen ci-reader s3cret
all admin-token

A line is a grant list — all, or a comma list of read (look at the workspace), screen (read what is on screen and in command blocks), input (type into a pane) and write (change the workspace, stop the daemon) — one space, then the token, which may contain spaces. Carriage returns and trailing whitespace are dropped, as for --token-file; blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored. An unknown grant, an empty token or a token that appears twice stops the daemon from starting, naming the line. The file adds tokens beside --token/--token-file, never instead of them: a hello may present either, and the --token keeps granting everything, so moving everyone to the access file means removing --token as well. A line that repeats the --token stops the daemon from starting too, since its narrower grants would silently read as everything.

Running a program is typing it: tab.create and pane.split with a command need input as well as write, so a token granted read,screen,write can open shells and rearrange the workspace but cannot run a program of its choosing in it. Events follow the same grants: block.finished carries the command line and needs screen, so a subscription of a read token is handed every other kind but that one, and a subscribe naming only kinds the token may not see is answered forbidden.

A call outside a token's grants is answered forbidden and the connection stays open. Viewing the sessions needs every grant, so a contour client with a narrower token is refused exactly as with a wrong one.

To attach over ssh instead, with no port to open, to save hosts by name, or to reach a home PC from the office over Tailscale, see Remote hosts.

docs.title: Starting the daemon at login
docs.text:
Instead of letting contour client start a daemon when it is needed, you can have the operating system start one for you when you log in:

contour daemon-service install      # register it (and start it with your next login)
contour daemon-service status       # registered? running? what does it run?
contour daemon-service start        # start it now
contour daemon-service stop         # stop it, leaving it registered
contour daemon-service restart
contour daemon-service uninstall    # stop it and remove the registration

Each verb takes --label NAME (default default). install additionally takes --socket, --config, --profile, --size-policy, --log and --log-file, which are recorded in the registration. A socket path is made absolute at install time, because the registration outlives the shell that wrote it. Unless you give --log-file the daemon logs to SOCKET.log.

OS What is registered Runs as Linux the systemd user unit contour-daemon.service (contour-daemon-LABEL.service for other labels), written to ~/.config/systemd/user and enabled you, no elevation macOS the LaunchAgent org.contourterminal.contour-daemon in ~/Library/LaunchAgents you, no elevation Windows a Scheduled Task triggered by your logon you, no elevation

Packages for Linux also ship a contour-daemon.service unit file. It is not enabled by the package; contour daemon-service install writes your own copy, which takes precedence.

A service-managed daemon runs with --lifecycle=persistent: it never exits on its own, not even with zero sessions and zero clients. contour client finds the registration and starts it before it falls back to spawning a daemon on demand. A registration made by an older release under another name is found as well.

--start boot and --start manual (a Windows service) are not implemented yet.

docs.title: Stopping a daemon
docs.text:
Ask it to stop, from anywhere:

contour daemon stop           # asks first when the daemon hosts sessions
contour daemon stop --yes     # does not ask
contour daemon status         # is one running? version, uptime, socket, sessions, clients
contour daemon logs           # the last 100 lines of its log
contour daemon logs --follow --lines 20

All of them accept --label and --socket, written before or after the verb. Giving the same option before and after the verb with different values is a usage error, so that stop never silently targets another daemon than the one you named. When no daemon answers, status and stop exit with status 4. stop asks for confirmation only when sessions exist; without a terminal it refuses unless you pass --yes. logs shows the file the daemon reports as its log; if none is running it falls back to the default SOCKET.log beside the socket, and says so.

A daemon started from a terminal also stops on SIGINT or SIGTERM — Ctrl+C if it is in the foreground, or kill <pid>. On Windows, a console-control event does the same. A daemon that predates contour daemon stop answers that it does not support it; stop it where it runs, or end its process.

For a service-managed daemon, prefer contour daemon-service stop, which lets the service manager know it was stopped on purpose rather than restarting it.

Shells do not survive the daemon

Persistence is against the client, not against the daemon process. Stopping the daemon ends every shell it hosts. Shutdown is abrupt by design — attached clients see the connection close with no goodbye, exactly as a real tmux kill-server looks to them. What comes back after a reboot, a crash or an upgrade is the workspace — see Surviving reboots.

docs.title: Surviving reboots
docs.text:
A daemon keeps a snapshot of its workspace, so that after a reboot, a crash or an upgrade the next daemon brings it back. The shells themselves cannot survive their daemon; what returns is:

  • every window, tab and split, with its ratios, the active tab and pane, and a zoomed pane;
  • tab titles and the tab colours you set;
  • each pane's working directory and profile;
  • the newest lines of each pane's scrollback, under a dim marker row such as ── restored · snapshot of 2026-10-24 09:15 ──, followed by a fresh shell.

The snapshot is written every interval seconds while the workspace changes, at once when you close a pane or a tab, and once more as the daemon ends. It is restored when a daemon starts and finds one: after a reboot, a crash, a SIGTERM, an idle exit, or the restart the drift chip offers after an upgrade (see After upgrading Contour). It is not restored after a plain contour daemon stop, which empties it, and panes and tabs you closed are not brought back.

contour daemon stop                   # ends the shells and discards the workspace
contour daemon stop --keep-snapshot   # ends the shells; the next daemon restores the workspace

With no daemon running, contour daemon stop still offers to empty the saved workspace, so a daemon started later does not bring back what you meant to end. Since a crash may have left that workspace as all you have, it asks first, unless --yes is given, and without a terminal to ask on it clears nothing and tells you to pass --yes. It exits with status 4 as before, whether it cleared the workspace or you kept it; with nothing saved it says so and creates no file. A daemon from a release before this feature keeps no workspace: --keep-snapshot then says so and stops it plainly.

A program is never started again by itself. Only one you list in rerun_programs is run once more when its pane was running it, and only when its command line holds nothing a shell would expand. When the saved directory no longer exists, the pane opens in the shell's default directory and the daemon logs it.

daemon:
  restore:
    scrollback: true          # bring the scrollback back
    scrollback_lines: 1000    # the most lines kept per pane, 0 to 100000
    rerun_programs: []        # e.g. [vim, htop]; nothing is re-run unless listed
    interval: 30              # seconds between writes of a changed workspace, at least 5

scrollback_lines bounds the snapshot only; how much scrollback a session holds while it runs stays daemon.history_limit.

The snapshot is <state-dir>/sessions/<label>.snapshot (the state directory is listed under Platform notes); a daemon started with --label work keeps work.snapshot. A daemon given a socket of its own, by --socket or $CONTOUR_MUX, keeps <label>@<hash>.snapshot instead, the hash naming its socket, so it never restores or overwrites the workspace of the daemon its label runs; contour daemon stop --socket finds the same file. The file is your user's alone: mode 0600 in a 0700 directory on Linux, macOS and BSD, and a protected ACL granting only your account on Windows. It is replaced atomically and durably: each write is flushed to the disk before it replaces the previous snapshot, and the replacement is flushed in turn, so a daemon crash, a power loss or a kernel crash in the middle of a write leaves either the previous snapshot or the new one, whole.

The snapshot may hold secrets

Restored scrollback is whatever was on screen: a password echoed by mistake, a token printed by a tool. It is written to disk in the clear. Set scrollback: false to keep only the layout and the directories, or scrollback_lines: 0 for the same.

A snapshot that cannot be read is renamed <label>.snapshot.corrupt and the daemon starts with its startup layout, logging why; one written by a newer release is left in place. A restore that brought nothing back is tried once more at the next start, then set aside as <label>.snapshot.failed.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
The daemon logs through Contour's category system; contour list-debug-tags prints every tag. The vthost.* categories are the daemon's:

Category Default What it records vthost.daemon on Endpoints bound, listeners started, signals, shutdown vthost.conn off Per-connection accept, handshake, disconnect vthost.session off Session spawn, resize, exit vthost.tmux off Control-mode and tmux-binary attach or rejection vthost.client off The client side of the native protocol vthost.trace.proto off One line per protocol message, both directions vthost.trace.tmux off Every control-mode line, both directions 
contour daemon --log 'vthost.conn,vthost.session'
contour daemon --log 'vthost.*' --log-file /var/log/contour-daemon.log

Three behaviours to know:

  • * is a plain prefix match, so vthost.* sweeps in the verbose vthost.trace.* tier as well. Name vthost.trace.* to select the trace tier alone.
  • A filter is a selection: it disables the categories it does not name. Real failures are exempt — asking for extra detail never takes error reporting away.
  • --log-file appends and never writes colour escapes, so restarting a daemon against the same file does not erase why the previous run died.

Traces report sizes, never payloads: a keystroke message shows a byte count, a screen update a line count, and a token only as present or absent. A trace of a busy session must not become a transcript of what you typed.

docs.title: Platform notes
docs.text:
Contour keeps what outlives a daemon in a per-user state directory, separate from the runtime directory the sockets live in:

OS State directory Linux, macOS, BSD $XDG_STATE_HOME/contour when set and absolute, otherwise ~/.local/state/contour Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\contour

Without a usable home directory the fallback is <temp>/contour-state-<user>. That directory is shared ground, so a daemon never runs from a copy staged there: it runs in place instead.

Daemon mode works on Linux, macOS, BSD and Windows 10 1803 or newer, over Unix domain sockets everywhere. On Windows, sessions are backed by ConPTY, the socket directory is governed by NTFS ACLs rather than POSIX permission bits, and the tmux-binary (<socket>-tmux) endpoint is absent — it needs file-descriptor passing, which Windows sockets do not have.

docs.title: After upgrading Contour
docs.text:
An upgrade never touches the running daemon. The daemon keeps serving, and the client you start next may be newer than the daemon it attaches to.

Where an upgrade would disturb a running binary, the daemon does not run from the installed binary at all. On Windows (the installer replaces contour.exe and the Restart Manager kills whoever holds it), on macOS (swapping the .app breaks the lazy loading of its frameworks) and for an AppImage (its mount vanishes when the AppImage process exits), a daemon runs from a copy of its own release under <state-dir>/bin/<version>-<id>/. It is made the first time that release starts a daemon, and removed again once no daemon runs from it.

What the copy costs
