Appending a * at the end of a debug tag will enable all debug tags that match prefix its prefix. The list of available debuglog tags can be found via CLI flag -D (--list-debug-tags).
  • Adds support for different font render modes: lcd, light, gray, monochrome in profiles.NAME.font.render_mode (default: lcd).
  • Adds support for different text render engines: OpenShaper, DirectWrite and CoreText for upcoming native platform support on Windows (and later macOS).
  • Adds support for different font location engines: fontconfig (others will follow).
  • Adds experimental text reflow.
  • Adds OpenFileManager action to configuration.
  • Adds terminal identification environment variables TERMINAL_NAME, TERMINAL_VERSION_TRIPLE and TERMINAL_VERSION_STRING.
  • Adds config option mode to input modifiers for additionally filtering based on modes (alt screen, app cursor/keypad, text selection modes, ...).
  • Adds config option profile.*.terminal_id: STR to set the terminal identification to one of VT100, VT220, VT340, etc.
  • Adds config option profile.*.maximized: BOOL to indicate maximized state during profile activation.
  • Adds config option profile.*.fullscreen: BOOL to indicate fullscreen state during profile activation.
  • Adds config option profile.*.font.strict_spacing: BOOL to indicate that only monospace fonts may be used.
  • Adds config option profile.*.font.TYPE.weight: WEIGHT and profile.*.fonts.TYPE.slant: SLANT options (optional) along with profile.*.fonts.TYPE.family: STRING.
  • Adds config option profile.*.font.dpi_scale: FLOAT to apply some additional DPI scaling on fonts.
  • Adds config option profile.*.font.builtin_box_drawing: BOOL to use pixel-perfect builtin box drawing instead of font provided box drawing characters.
  • Adds config option profile.*.refresh_rate: FLOAT to configure how often the terminal screen will be rendered at most when currently under heavy screen changes. A value of "auto" will use the currently connected monitor's refresh rate.
  • Adds configuration's action ToggleAllKeyMaps to enable/disable intercepting and interpreting keybinds. The one that did toggle it will not be disabled.
  • Adds configuration's action ClearHistoryAndReset to clear the history, and resetting the terminal.
  • Adds VT sequence for enabling/disabling debug logging. CSI ? 46 h and CSI ? 46 l and CLI option -d.
  • Adds VT sequence for querying/setting current font OSC 50 ; ? ST and OSC 50 ; Font ST (and OSC 60 Ps Ps Ps Ps Ps ST for a more fine grained font query/setting control).
  • Adds VT sequence CSI 18 t and CSI 19 t for getting screen character size. Responds with CSI 8 ; $columns ; $rows t and CSI 9 ; $columns ; $rows t respectively.
  • Adds VT sequence to capture the current screen buffer CSI > LineMode ; StartLine ; LineCount t giving the response back on stdin via OSC 314 ; $screen_buffer ST, and feature detection via DA1 number 314.
  • Adds VT sequence DECSNLS for setting number of lines to display.
  • Adds VT sequence CSI Ps b (REP) for repeating the last graphical character Ps times.
  • Adds VT sequence OSC 4 ; INDEX ; COLOR ST for setting or querying color palette (if COLOR is ? instead of a color spec).
  • Adds VT sequence OSC 104 ; INDEX ST for resetting color palette entry or complete palette (if no (index is given).
  • Adds VT sequence DECCRA to copy a rectangular area.
  • Adds VT sequence DECERA to erase a rectangular area.
  • Adds VT sequence DECFRA to fill a rectangular area.
  • Adds VT sequence CSI > q (XTVERSION) to query terminal identification (name and version). Response comes as DCS >| Contour ContourVersion ST.
  • Adds VT sequence DECRQM to request ANSI/DEC modes states (set / unset / not recognized).
  • Adds new CLI command: contour capture ... to capture the screen buffer.
  • Adds new CLI command: contour set profile to NAME to change the profile on the fly.
  • Adds new CLI command: contour generate terminfo output OUTPUT_FILE to create a Contour terminfo file.
  • Adds new CLI command: contour generate config output OUTPUT_FILE to create a new default config.
  • Adds new CLI command: contour generate integration shell SHELL output OUTPUT_FILE to create the shell integration file for the given shell (only zsh supported for now). Also adds a pre-generated shell integration file for Linux (and macOS) to /usr/share/contour/shell-integration.zsh.
  • Unicode data updated to version 14.0 beta.
  • Adds support for building with Qt 6 (disabled by default).
  • Adds support for building with mimalloc (experimental, disabled by default).

• Fixes race condition when displaying image animations (e.g. gifs via sixel).
  • Fixes NewTerminal action to also inherit the active configuration file.
  • Fixes restoring cursor position in RM ?1049.
  • Fixes DECSTR resetting saved-cursor state and active cursor-position.
  • Fixes selecting text not being pushed into the selection-clipboard.
  • Adds VT sequence OSC 7 (set current working directory).
  • Adds VT sequence DCS $ p $Name ST to change config profile name to $Name.

• Available on all 3 major platforms, Linux, macOS, Windows.
  • Emoji support (-: 🌈 💝 😛 👪 :-)
  • Font ligatures support (such as in Fira Code).
  • Bold and italic fonts
  • GPU-accelerated rendering.
  • Vertical Line Markers (quickly jump to markers in your history!)
  • Blurred behind transparent background when using Windows 10 or KDE window manager on Linux.
  • Runtime configuration reload
  • 256-color and Truecolor support
  • Key binding customization
  • Color Schemes
  • Profiles (grouped customization of: color scheme, login shell, and related behaviors)
  • Clickable hyperlinks via OSC 8
  • Sixel inline images

docs.title: Remote hosts
docs.text:
A Contour window can show the sessions of a daemon running on another machine: your home PC from the office, a build server, a workstation under your desk. The sessions keep running there; the window here is a client of that daemon, exactly as it is of a local one (see Persistent sessions).

There are two ways to reach a remote daemon:

Transport What it needs Authentication ssh (ssh://) An OpenSSH client here, Contour on the remote machine. Nothing listens on the network besides sshd. ssh's own: keys or an agent. TLS (tls://) A daemon on the remote machine started with --listen-tcp. A token, over TLS.

If you can already ssh to the machine, use ssh: it needs no open port, no token and no certificate.

docs.title: Saved hosts
docs.text:
Hosts you attach to often are saved in the configuration under hosts:, by name (reference):

hosts:
  home:
    url: "ssh://me@homepc"
  studio:
    url: "tls://studio.tailnet.ts.net:7297"
    token_file: "~/.config/contour/studio.token"
    tls_ca: "~/.config/contour/studio-ca.pem"

Hosts can also be added in Settings › Hosts, without editing the file: each one is written to hosts/<name>.yml beside contour.yml, with the same keys as an entry of hosts:. Its page shows the SSH or TLS fields its address calls for, says under a field what would keep the host from loading, and saves nothing until it is fixed; Attach opens a window attached to it. Hosts written in contour.yml are listed there too, read-only, with Duplicate to Edit.

Then attach in any of these ways:

  • "Attach to Host" in the command palette lists the saved hosts; pick one.
  • The same list is in the terminal's context menu and the title-bar menu.
  • From a shell:
contour client --host home                     # a saved host, by name
contour client --host ssh://me@homepc:2222     # an ssh URL that is not saved

An ad-hoc tls:// URL is refused: a TLS host needs its token_file, so save it first.

A window attached to a remote host says so in its chrome, so it is never mistaken for a local one: its title reads home — <session title>, and the tab strip starts with the host's name.

docs.title: Choosing where a window lives: the Connect picker
docs.text:
The Connect picker is one question before a window opens: where do its sessions live? It lists

  • This computer: Persistent sessions, the local daemon, with its state (running · 3 sessions, or not running · starts on connect), and This window only, with no daemon: its shells end when the window closes (daemon.mode: in_process);
  • Saved hosts: each host of hosts:, tagged SSH or TLS;
  • and, while you type an ssh:// or tls:// address in the field, a leading Connect to ADDRESS row for it. The address is not saved.

Open it from File › New Window to… (Ctrl+Shift+K, ⇧⌘K on macOS; the NewWindowTo action), from contour connect with no target, from the launchers below, or at every plain start, with Ask every time Contour starts (connect_picker_on_start, also in Settings › General). A launch with command-line arguments never shows it.

The field has the focus. Type to filter by name or address; ↑ and ↓ move, Return connects and Esc cancels, which quits when no other window is open. Every row shows a key, Alt+1 to 9 (⌘1 to ⌘9 on macOS), that connects to it at once; plain digits stay typable, for addresses and ports. Filtering renumbers the rows, so star then Alt+1 reaches a host named starfive. Ctrl+L (⌘L) puts the caret back in the field. The selection starts on the target you used last, which Contour remembers in gui-state.yml, not in contour.yml.

A host that cannot be reached stays in the picker: the reason is shown under its row, in the words Attach to Host uses (an unknown host key, an authentication failure, Contour missing on the host, an unreachable host), with Retry and Edit Host…, which opens Settings › Hosts on it. Manage Hosts… opens Settings › Hosts.

docs.title: contour connect
docs.text:
contour connect                     # the picker
contour connect daemon              # this computer's daemon; daemon:LABEL for another one
contour connect local               # this window only, no daemon
contour connect starfive            # a saved host, by name
contour connect ssh://me@pi4.lan    # an ssh:// or tls:// address
contour connect --list [--json]     # the targets the picker would show

A target opens the window as contour client does (--label, --host), or contour terminal --daemon-mode in_process for local; no target shows the picker. --config FILE names the configuration that holds the hosts. --list prints each target, as contour connect reads it, with its detail, or a JSON array with --json. An ad-hoc tls:// address is refused, as for contour client --host: a TLS host needs its token file, so save it first.

docs.title: From the launchers
docs.text:
• Linux: the desktop entry has a Connect… action (contour connect) beside Open a New Window, and org.contourterminal.Contour.Connect.desktop is a launcher of its own, "Contour — Connect…", for menus that show no actions.
  • macOS: the Dock menu has New Window to… and each saved host.
  • Windows: the jump list has the task Connect… and one per saved host, and the installer adds a Contour (Connect…) Start menu shortcut.

docs.title: Over SSH
docs.text:
Contour runs, for every attach and every reconnect:

ssh -T -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o ServerAliveInterval=15 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 \
    [-p PORT] -- [USER@]HOST contour daemon --stdio

On the remote side, contour daemon --stdio reaches your daemon there — starting it if none runs, the same way a local contour client does — and relays the session between it and ssh.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• An OpenSSH client on this machine (ssh on PATH). On Windows, the built-in OpenSSH client ("OpenSSH Client" optional feature) works.
  • Contour on the remote machine, findable by a non-interactive login — which often has a shorter PATH than your interactive shell. Check with:
ssh me@homepc contour version

If that says command not found, give the full path in the saved host:

hosts:
  home:
    url: "ssh://me@homepc"
    remote_command: "/opt/contour/bin/contour daemon --stdio"
  • Key or agent authentication. Contour never answers a prompt: there is no terminal to type a password, a key passphrase, a second factor or a host-key confirmation into. Load your key into the agent (ssh-add) or use a key without a passphrase.
  • The host key accepted once. The first connection to a new host asks whether to trust its key. Run this once in a terminal and answer yes, then attach from Contour:
ssh me@homepc

Your ~/.ssh/config applies as usual: host aliases, User, Port, ProxyJump and IdentityFile all work, so url: "ssh://homepc" can rely on what that file says about homepc.

docs.title: When it does not connect
docs.text:
Contour reads what ssh reports and says what to do. The messages, and the fix for each:

Message (abridged) Cause Fix ssh could not log in to ssh://me@homepc without a prompt … Run this once in a terminal, then attach again: ssh me@homepc The host key is not known yet, or no key/agent identity was accepted. Run the command shown in a terminal. Accept the host key; if it asks for a password, set up a key (ssh-copy-id me@homepc) or load yours into the agent (ssh-add). The host key of ssh://me@homepc has changed … The remote machine's key differs from the one in ~/.ssh/known_hosts: a reinstalled machine, or someone in between. If you expected it, remove the old key with ssh-keygen -R homepc and run ssh me@homepc once. If you did not, do not connect. ssh could not reach ssh://me@homepc: … The name does not resolve, nothing answers on the port, or there is no route. ssh's own words follow. Check the name, the port and the network (VPN, Tailscale). Contour retries this on its own while a window waits. Contour was not found on ssh://me@homepc by a non-interactive ssh login … contour is not installed there, or not on the non-interactive PATH. Install it, or set remote_command: to its full path (see above). Contour on ssh://me@homepc is too old for ssh attach … The remote Contour has no contour daemon --stdio. Upgrade Contour on the remote machine. ssh://me@homepc: daemon did not start within 5 seconds. (or another reason) The remote relay ran, but could not reach or start the daemon there. Run ssh me@homepc contour daemon --stdio in a terminal and read what it says; check the daemon's log on that machine. ssh://me@homepc printed more than 64 KiB before Contour answered … A login script on the remote machine prints output on non-interactive logins. Make .bashrc / profile scripts quiet when not interactive (e.g. wrap output in [[ $- == *i* ]] && …). A short banner is skipped; only a long one fails. ssh to ssh://me@homepc ended before Contour answered (exit code N): … ssh ended for a reason Contour does not recognize. Run ssh me@homepc contour daemon --stdio in a terminal to see the whole output. Contour retries this one too. ssh://me@homepc did not answer within 30 seconds The connection hangs (a firewall that drops packets, a stuck login). As for "could not reach". ssh was not found on PATH; install the OpenSSH client No ssh client on this machine. Install OpenSSH.

A connection that drops mid-session — the laptop sleeps, the Wi-Fi changes — is reconnected with a fresh ssh, while the window shows that it is reconnecting. A failure that retrying cannot fix (a refused login, a host key, a missing Contour) ends the attempt with its message instead of repeating it.

docs.title: Over TLS
docs.text:
The daemon on the remote machine listens on a TCP port itself; every connection is TLS-encrypted and must present a token.

On the remote machine:

umask 077 && openssl rand -base64 32 > ~/.config/contour/daemon.token
contour daemon --background --listen-tcp 192.0.2.10:7297 --token-file ~/.config/contour/daemon.token

Copy the token file to the machine you sit at (for example with scp), keeping it private (chmod 600), and save the host:

hosts:
  studio:
    url: "tls://studio.example.net:7297"
    token_file: "~/.config/contour/studio.token"

docs.title: Unverified TLS, and a pinned CA
docs.text:
Without tls_ca, the daemon presents a certificate it generated itself and the client does not check it. The connection is encrypted, which stops anyone merely listening, but an active man-in-the-middle can pose as the daemon and take the token, and with it your sessions. Use this only on a network you trust, such as a tailnet (below).

To have the client verify the daemon, give the daemon a certificate issued by a CA of your own, for the name you connect to, and pin that CA on the client:

# Once, anywhere: a CA of your own.
openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -days 3650 \
    -subj "/CN=My Contour CA" -keyout ca.key -out ca.pem

# For the remote machine: a certificate for the name the client connects to.
openssl req -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes \
    -subj "/CN=studio.example.net" -keyout daemon.key -out daemon.csr
printf 'subjectAltName=DNS:studio.example.net\n' > daemon.ext
openssl x509 -req -in daemon.csr -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -days 825 \
    -extfile daemon.ext -out daemon.pem

Start the daemon with --tls-cert daemon.pem --tls-key daemon.key, copy ca.pem (never ca.key) to the client, and add tls_ca: "~/.config/contour/studio-ca.pem" to the saved host. The certificate must name the host in the url: one merely signed by the CA, for another name, is refused.

Contour's control commands — the contour verbs that change a daemon's state from a script — need tls_ca: they refuse a TLS host whose certificate is not verified.

docs.title: Reaching a home PC from the office with Tailscale
docs.text:
Tailscale puts your machines on a private network (a tailnet) wherever they are, without opening ports on your router. Contour does not bundle Tailscale or talk to it; it simply connects to an address on the tailnet like any other.

  1. Install Tailscale on both machines from https://tailscale.com/download and log in to the same tailnet on each.
  2. Find the home PC's tailnet address — on the home PC:
tailscale ip -4          # e.g. 100.101.102.103

With MagicDNS on (the default), the machine is also reachable as <machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net, e.g. homepc.tail1234.ts.net; the admin console shows the exact name.

  1. The simplest way is ssh over the tailnet. If the home PC runs sshd, nothing else is needed:
hosts:
  home:
    url: "ssh://me@homepc.tail1234.ts.net"
  1. Or listen with TLS on the tailnet address only — on the home PC:
umask 077 && openssl rand -base64 32 > ~/.config/contour/daemon.token
contour daemon --background --listen-tcp 100.101.102.103:7297 \
    --token-file ~/.config/contour/daemon.token

Binding to the 100.x.y.z address, not to 0.0.0.0, keeps the port off every other network the PC is on. contour daemon-service install does not record --listen-tcp, so start this listener yourself (or from your login scripts). Then, at the office, with the token file copied over:

hosts:
  home:
    url: "tls://homepc.tail1234.ts.net:7297"
    token_file: "~/.config/contour/home.token"

Tailscale already encrypts and authenticates the traffic between your machines, which is what makes unverified TLS a reasonable choice here. For the control commands, or for defense in depth, add tls_ca as above, with the certificate issued for homepc.tail1234.ts.net.

  1. Attach: "Attach to Host" → home, or contour client --host home.

docs.title: Foreign paths
docs.text: The sessions of a remote host run on that machine, so the directories and files they report — the current directory a shell announces (OSC 7), a command block's working directory, a link to a file — are that machine's paths. A window attached to a remote host shows them, but never opens them here: it does not open such a file, start a program in such a directory, or offer "open folder" for it, since on this machine the path names nothing, or something else.

docs.title: Secure input
docs.text: While a program in a pane hides what you type, as sudo and ssh do when they ask for a password, Contour shows a lock for that pane. On macOS it also turns on Secure Keyboard Entry for as long as that pane has focus, which keeps other applications from reading your keystrokes.

docs.title: The setting
docs.text:
secure_input: auto
Value Meaning auto Lock and, on macOS, Secure Keyboard Entry while a pane asks for hidden input. off Never. false and no read as off.

A new configuration (defaults_edition: native2026) uses auto; the Classic edition keeps off. Reloading the configuration applies the change at once: turning it off releases Secure Keyboard Entry immediately.

docs.title: What counts as a password prompt
docs.text: A pane is locked when its terminal has echo off and canonical (line) mode on: the state sudo, readpassphrase(3), ssh and read -s put it in. A program that clears echo for its own screen, such as an editor, htop, less or the line editor of your shell, also turns canonical mode off, so it shows no lock. Ghostty reads the same two flags (password_input in its termio/Exec.zig); xterm has no automatic detection and only a manual Secure Keyboard menu entry.

docs.title: What it cannot see
docs.text:
Contour looks at the terminal's flags and nothing else, so it misses a password reader that clears both echo and canonical mode. Those readers show no lock and turn nothing on:

  • sudo with pwfeedback, and sudo-rs with its feedback option
  • pinentry-curses
  • sudo and similar asked over ssh, where the prompt runs on another machine's terminal
  • panes whose program runs on a host Contour cannot read flags from (an SSH pane, a Windows ConPTY pane)

For these, the lock is simply absent: a lock means the program hides the typing, and no lock means only that Contour could not tell.

docs.title: How quickly it notices
docs.text:
Contour re-reads the flags when output reaches the pane, before each key and paste is sent, and on focus. For two seconds after the pane's last output or key it also checks every 100 ms while the pane has focus, then stops: an idle pane wakes nothing. A program that turns echo off only after more than two quiet seconds is noticed at the first key you type. That key has already reached the system by then, so Secure Keyboard Entry protects the keys after it, not that one. The opposite case leans safe: a program that turns echo back on silently, more than two seconds after the last key or output, leaves the lock and Secure Keyboard Entry on until the next key or output.

Panes hosted by a daemon report the same state over the native protocol, so the lock works under daemon.mode: auto as well.

docs.title: Where the lock shows
docs.text:
Wherever something showing the pane is on screen: in the pane's header, on its tab, in a chip in the title band, and, when none of those is on screen, in a small pill over the pane's blank cells at the top right. The pill avoids the prompt and yields to the link pill and the find bar; if a full-screen program leaves no blank place, it covers a few cells rather than disappear.

The words beside the lock read Secure input on only for the pane the system's Secure Keyboard Entry protects: on macOS, the focused pane of the front application. Every other locked pane (an unfocused split, a background tab) and every other platform read Input hidden, which says only that the terminal hides what you type. Screen readers announce the same words.

docs.title: Configuring Contour
docs.text:
Contour offers a wide range of configuration options that can be customized, including color scheme, shell, initial working directory, and more. The configuration options can be categorized into several groups:

  • Global options: These settings determine the overall behavior of the terminal and apply to all profiles.
  • Profiles: With profiles, you can configure the terminal more granularly and create multiple profiles that can be easily switched between.
  • Color scheme: Contour allows you to define different color schemes for the terminal and choose which one to use for each of the profiles.

On Unix systems, the main configuration file is located at ~/.config/contour/contour.yml and is both read from and auto-generated there. On Windows systems, the file is located at %LocalAppData%\contour\contour.yml.

Please note that on Unix systems, the environment variable XDG_CONFIG_HOME (by default set to ~/.config) is taken into account.

By default, on Unix systems, Contour is executed with the following arguments contour config ~/.config/contour/contour.yml profile main. If the configuration file includes a default_profile variable, it will be used as the default profile. Otherwise, the first profile listed in the file will be the default one.

docs.title: Load specific configuration file
docs.text: contour config /path/to/file/with/configuration.yml

docs.title: Set profile for current session
docs.text: you can utilize the profile parameter with the contour command contour profile one_of_profiles

docs.title: Global options
docs.text: Let's go through the different sections of the global configurations in the file:

docs.title: defaults_edition
docs.text: option names the generation of built-in defaults the configuration file is written against, so a setting the file does not spell out keeps the value it had when the file was written. classic is the defaults of every release before the 2026 redesign, and is what a file without the key gets. native2026 is the redesign's: JetBrains Mono (Cascadia Mono on Windows) at 13pt on macOS and 12pt elsewhere, a 100x30 page with 8x6 margins, the contour-dark/contour-light color schemes, the status line without hard-coded colors, a silent bell, 10000 lines of scrollback, a steady block cursor, links decorated while the follow modifier (Command on macOS) is held, unfocused panes dimmed, a tab bar shown only for two or more tabs, a scrollbar that follows the system's scroll bar setting (scrollbar.mode: system, where classic always shows it), a hovered link's target shown only while the follow modifier is held (hyperlink_hover_tooltip: false), and GUI chrome that follows the terminal background (theme: terminal, where classic follows the OS). Under native2026 colors: default, the stock scheme left unmodified, also means the contour-dark/contour-light pair, so an existing configuration follows dark mode; naming any other scheme keeps it fixed. Under native2026 the default profile's contour-dark and contour-light palettes come from the built-in schemes: a color_schemes: entry of either name takes effect only when a profile names it in colors:. A freshly generated configuration states native2026. A settings.yml beside the file may set the key too, and wins.

docs.title: platform_plugin
docs.text: option allows you to override the auto-detected platform plugin to be loaded. You can specify values like auto, xcb, cocoa, direct2d, or winrt to determine the platform plugin. The default value is auto.

docs.title: renderer
docs.text: section contains configuration options related to the VT Renderer, which is responsible for rendering the terminal onto the screen. It includes the backend option to specify the Qt RHI graphics API, with possible values of auto (the native backend per platform), OpenGL, vulkan, direct3d11, direct3d12, metal, or software. The other options in this section control the tile mapping and caching for performance optimization.

docs.title: word_delimiters
docs.text: option defines the delimiters to be used when selecting words in the terminal. It is a string of characters that act as delimiters.

docs.title: extended_word_delimiters
docs.text: option defines the delimiters to be used when selecting words in the second time. It is a string of characters that act as delimiters. By default word delimiters are used.

docs.title: command_palette_recent_count
docs.text: option sets how many recently used commands the command palette pins above its alphabetical list. The palette is opened with the OpenCommandPalette action (bound to Ctrl+Shift+P by default), and the list of recent commands is remembered across restarts in the command-history.yml file beside your configuration file. Set it to 0 to turn the "recently used" section off entirely. The default value is 5.

docs.title: pty_read_buffer_size
docs.text: option sets the most bytes taken from the PTY in one read, and so the most parsed in one go. Larger batches parse output faster; smaller ones show a flood of it in smaller steps. It is an advanced option and should be used with caution. The default value is 65536. A change applies to sessions opened afterwards.

docs.title: pty_buffer_object_size
docs.text: option sets the size in bytes per PTY Buffer Object. It is an advanced option for internal storage and should be changed carefully. The default value is 1048576. A change applies to sessions opened afterwards.

docs.title: default_profile_name
docs.text: option determines the default profile to use in the terminal.

docs.title: early_exit_threshold
docs.text: option determines the early threshold time. If the shell ends earlier than the specified threshold without a successful exit status, its pane stays open with the shell's last output and a footer naming how it ended (its exit code or signal): Return restarts the shell in the same pane, and the ClosePane binding (Ctrl+Shift+X by default) closes it. A shell that exits successfully -- exit or Ctrl+D -- closes the pane at once.

docs.title: spawn_new_process
docs.text: flag determines whether a new process should be spawned when creating a new terminal. The default value is false.

docs.title: reflow_on_resize
docs.text: option controls whether or not the lines in the terminal should be reflowed when a resize event occurs. The default value is true. A change applies to sessions opened afterwards.

docs.title: snap_to_rows
docs.text: option aligns startup and manually resized window heights to complete terminal rows. The default is false. Applies to a single visible pane, including a zoomed split pane. Font metrics, window chrome and configured margins are taken into account. Windows snaps during resizing; macOS snaps when manual resizing ends; X11 uses window-manager size hints. Wayland has no resize-increment hint, so only startup sizing is supported there. Maximized and fullscreen sizes are unrestricted. Fractional scaling can leave less than one logical pixel of rounding slack. A change applies at the next startup or manual resize.

docs.title: connect_picker_on_start
docs.text: option makes a plain launch, one with no command-line arguments such as a Dock, Spotlight or launcher start, show the Connect picker first: a small window asking whether the new window's sessions live in this computer's daemon, in this window only, or on a saved host. The default is false. contour connect shows the picker whatever this says, and a launch with arguments never does. Also the "Ask every time Contour starts" switch of the picker and of Settings.

docs.title: remember_window_position
docs.text: option remembers the last normal window position and monitor, without saving window size. The default is true on Windows and false on other platforms. Enable it to opt in on macOS and X11; Wayland leaves placement to the compositor. The first window restores its location at startup. The window-position.yml side file stores monitor-relative x/y coordinates and a zero-based monitor index. Disabling the option stops reading and writing position state.

docs.title: tab_switch_on_horizontal_wheel
docs.text: option controls whether a horizontal mouse wheel tilt (or a horizontal trackpad swipe) over the tab strip or the terminal switches to the previous/next tab. An application that has requested mouse reporting keeps receiving the horizontal wheel; holding the bypass modifier switches tabs anyway. An explicit WheelLeft/WheelRight entry in input_mapping takes precedence. The default value is true.

docs.title: hyperlink_hover_tooltip
docs.text: Whether hovering a link (OSC 8 or detected) shows its target without holding the follow modifier. While the modifier is held the target always shows. A local file:// target is shown as a plain path. Defaults to false; a configuration written before the 2026 defaults keeps true.

docs.title: progress_timeout
docs.text:
How long an application's progress indicator (OSC 9;4) stays on screen without being updated, in milliseconds.

0 (the default) disables expiry entirely: the indicator persists until the application clears it with state 0, which is what the sequence specifies and what ConEmu and Windows Terminal do. The terminal cannot tell a long-running operation from an application that died holding one, so a non-zero value trades that fidelity for a guard against a bar left stranded on screen. Applications using the protocol are expected to refresh it about once a second, so a timeout well above that -- 15000 or so -- is the useful range.

docs.title: notification_close_timeout
docs.text:
How long after showing a desktop notification that asked to hear of its close (c=1) the terminal waits before assuming the desktop closed it, in milliseconds.

This only applies where a close cannot be observed. Contour normally learns that a notification was dismissed or expired from the desktop itself and reports it back to the application as the OSC 99 p=close event. Inside a Flatpak sandbox that is impossible: the only reachable service is the org.freedesktop.portal.Notification portal, which has no close signal of any kind, so an application that asked for close events (c=1) would otherwise wait forever.

A notification that states its own lifetime through w= is answered after that instead -- the application already said what it wanted. Only w=-1, "whatever the desktop does", falls back to this value.

Two cases are deliberately never answered, because there is no moment at which an answer would be true: 0 here, which disables the assumption outright, and w=0 on the notification, which asks for a popup that never expires on its own. An application that requested close events in either case is not told.

A notification that asked for no close event -- a command's finish notice among them -- is never assumed closed: assuming it would only make it impossible to withdraw, and its click, from the desktop's notification history, would go unanswered.

Read once per terminal session, so a changed value reaches sessions opened after the reload.

Because the report is a timer rather than an observation, it is marked untracked on the wire, so an application can tell the two apart.

docs.title: accessibility_announcements
docs.text: Whether events with no representation in the accessibility tree -- the bell, a desktop notification, a mode change -- are announced to assistive technology. Costs nothing while no assistive client is attached. See Accessibility.

docs.title: accessibility_caret_reporting
docs.text: Whether the terminal reports where the caret is to assistive technology, which is how a screen magnifier follows what you are typing. Costs nothing while no assistive client is attached. Turn it off to rule the caret reports out when diagnosing input latency. See Accessibility.

docs.title: tab_bar_position
docs.text:
Selects where the GUI tab strip (tab bar) is placed within the window. Valid values (ignore-case):

  • Top — the tab strip is drawn above the terminal content. This is the default.
  • Bottom — the tab strip is drawn below the terminal content.

docs.title: tab_bar_visibility
docs.text:
Selects when the GUI tab strip (tab bar) is shown. Valid values (ignore-case):

  • Always — the tab strip is always shown. This is the classic default.
  • Never — the tab strip is never shown.
  • Multiple — the tab strip is shown only when the window has more than one tab, and hidden while a single tab remains. This is the native2026 default.

docs.title: gui_config_locked
docs.text: flag, when true, opens the in-app settings page read-only and prevents the GUI from writing any of its side files (profiles/, colorschemes/, settings.yml), so this hand-maintained configuration file stays the single source of truth. The default value is false.

docs.title: theme
docs.text: option selects the light/dark appearance of the GUI chrome (title bar, tab strip, command palette, settings pages, dialogs) independently of the operating system. Possible values are terminal (follow the terminal's background), system (follow the OS color scheme), dark, and light. The terminal grid keeps following the OS light/dark preference through its own color scheme. The default value is terminal under defaults_edition: native2026 and system under classic.

docs.title: ui_style
docs.text:
Selects how the application's own chrome is painted: the tab strip and title bar, and the controls (buttons, fields, menu entries, combo boxes) inside menus, popups and the settings page. This selects a shape, not a color: both styles take their colors from the operating system palette and follow the theme setting. Valid values (ignore-case):

  • native — platform-native GUI chrome. This is the default.
  • terminal — the chrome is quantized to whole character cells of a monospace font and its corners are squared off, so the window reads as one continuous TUI rather than as a GUI wrapped around a terminal. Tabs keep every GUI affordance (drag to reorder, tear off, rename, close, context menu); only their appearance changes.

This is the recommended way to get the terminal look now that a window can hold split panes: the indicator status line's {Tabs} item still works, but it is drawn per pane, so a split window would show one tab list per pane instead of one per window.

The Qt Quick Controls half of the style is selected once, before the first control is created, so a change takes effect on the next start rather than live.

docs.title: window_control_style
docs.text:
Selects how the window's own minimize/maximize/close controls are drawn, and which side of the tab bar they sit on. These are drawn only while the native title bar is hidden (show_title_bar is false, the default), which is when the tab bar doubles as the title bar; with the native frame shown, the operating system draws them itself. Valid values (ignore-case):

  • auto — match the host: macOS gets macos, Windows gets windows, and anything else (KDE Plasma included) gets linux. This is the default.
  • windows — trailing (right) edge, flush rectangular buttons in minimize/maximize/close order, with a red close hover.
  • macos — leading (left) edge, traffic lights in close/minimize/zoom order. The dots reveal their glyphs while the group is hovered and grey out while the window is inactive.
  • plasma — trailing (right) edge, like windows but with the circular hover fills of KDE Plasma's Breeze decoration.
  • linux — round buttons with the desktop's themed icons, in the order and on the side (or sides) the desktop's own button layout names: GNOME's button-layout, KWin's ButtonsOnLeft and ButtonsOnRight, or GTK's gtk-decoration-layout. Where none is set, minimize, maximize and close sit at the trailing (right) edge.

Independent of ui_style: every value works in both the native and the terminal chrome, and takes its extents from whichever of those is active — so under ui_style: terminal the controls stay quantized to whole character cells, and the traffic lights are drawn as coloured cell-wide dots.

Unlike ui_style, this applies immediately when changed from the settings page.

docs.title: chrome_density
docs.text:
Selects how much room the window chrome takes. Valid values (ignore-case):

  • comfortable — once a tab is split, its panes are cards with a header each and a 6 pt gap between them. This is the default.
  • minimal — panes are separated by 1 pt lines and carry no header; hold Alt (Option on macOS) for half a second to show the headers. On macOS a tab that is not split gets a bare 28 pt band.

A change is applied live.

docs.title: secure_input
docs.text: Shows a lock while the program in a pane hides what you type (a password prompt) and, on macOS, turns on Secure Keyboard Entry while that pane has focus. auto or off.

docs.title: ui_font_family
docs.text: Font family the terminal-style chrome is drawn with. When empty (the default) the chrome inherits the regular font family of the profile the window is running (-p/--profile, else default_profile), which is what makes it match the terminal grid below it. Ignored while ui_style is native, where the chrome uses the platform UI font. Takes effect on the next start.

docs.title: ui_font_size
docs.text: Font size, in points, the terminal-style chrome is drawn with. When 0 (the default) the chrome inherits the font size of the profile the window is running. Ignored while ui_style is native. Takes effect on the next start.

docs.title: grapheme_clustering
docs.text: Whether DEC mode 2027 starts out set. While set, a late codepoint may widen its grapheme cluster -- U+FE0F widens a cluster to two columns -- but a cluster never narrows again. While unset, a cell is measured by plain wcwidth() with no clustering. Applications may still toggle the mode at runtime. A change applies to sessions opened afterwards.

docs.title: text_scaling_method
docs.text: How a glyph is enlarged for scaled text (kitty text sizing protocol, OSC 66). stretch magnifies the ordinary-size glyph: free to rasterize, no extra atlas entries, but softer at large scales. rerasterize asks the font for the glyph at the larger size: crisp at any scale, at the cost of a rasterization and an atlas entry per glyph and scale.

docs.title: bypass_mouse_protocol_modifiers
docs.text: option specifies the keyboard modifier (e.g., Shift) that can be used to bypass the terminal's mouse protocol and select screen content.

docs.title: mouse_block_selection_modifiers
docs.text: option determines the modifier (e.g., Control) that needs to be pressed to initiate block selection using the left mouse button.

docs.title: on_mouse_selection
docs.text: option selects the action to perform when a text selection has been made. Possible values include None, CopyToClipboard, and CopyToSelectionClipboard.

docs.title: live
docs.text: option determines whether the instance should reload the configuration files whenever they change. The default value is false.

docs.title: images
docs.text: section contains configuration options related to inline images. It includes options like sixel_scrolling, sixel_register_count, and good_image_protocol to control various aspects of image rendering. The maximum image size is derived from the screen size; max_width and max_height are deprecated and ignored.

docs.title: daemon
docs.text:
section decides whether sessions are hosted by a daemon process, so they outlive the window. 

daemon:
  mode: auto
  socket: ""
  size_policy: latest
  history_limit: 1000
  restore:
    scrollback: true
    scrollback_lines: 1000
    rerun_programs: []
    interval: 30
mode in_process keeps sessions in the GUI process, auto uses a daemon and falls back to in-process with a notice, required fails when no daemon can be reached. socket The daemon's socket path; empty selects the default. size_policy Which client's size wins when several are attached: latest, smallest or largest. history_limit Scrollback lines per session, -1 for unlimited; unset uses the hosting profile's history.limit. restore.scrollback Whether a restored pane gets its scrollback back; the snapshot file may hold secrets that were on screen, and is readable by your user only. restore.scrollback_lines The most scrollback lines kept per pane, from 0 to 100000; the live scrollback stays history_limit. restore.rerun_programs Programs a restored pane runs again when it was running one of them, such as [vim, htop]; nothing is re-run unless listed. restore.interval How often, in seconds, a changed workspace is written; at least 5.

docs.title: quick_terminal
docs.text:
section sets a global hotkey that slides a terminal down from the top of the screen under the pointer, full width and 40 % of its height, in Minimal density. 

quick_terminal:
  hotkey: { mods: [Control], key: '`' }
  hide_on_focus_loss: true
hotkey The chord, spelled as an input mapping spells it; it needs at least one of Control, Alt and Super. Unbound (~) by default. hide_on_focus_loss Whether the quick terminal hides when it loses the focus.

docs.title: folding
docs.text:
configuration controls output folding: collapsing a finished command's output down to the prompt line it was entered at, and expanding it again. 

folding:
  enabled: true
  show_markers: true
  auto_collapse_on_new_command: false
  on_jump_into_fold: expand
Folding is driven entirely by the OSC 133 semantic marks a shell with shell integration emits, so no additional escape sequence is involved and any shell that already speaks OSC 133 works. Only FINISHED commands fold, which is why the prompt you are typing at never does. enabled Whether folding is available at all. When false the actions below do nothing and no fold markers are drawn. show_markers Whether the gutter's block column, left of the grid, draws fold markers: a boxed minus on a foldable prompt line whose output is showing, a boxed plus once it is collapsed, and a bar down the side of the block joining the two. Clicking anywhere on that column toggles the fold. Note that the column costs one column of terminal width; it is reserved while this, gutter.exit_status or gutter.user_marks is on. auto_collapse_on_new_command Whether a command's output is collapsed automatically as soon as the next prompt appears, so that only the command you are running now is shown in full. on_jump_into_fold What a Vi-mode jump that targets a line inside a collapsed block does: expand opens the block so the cursor lands on what it was aiming at, skip leaves it collapsed and stops at its prompt line instead. Plain motions (j, k, {, }, ++ctrl+d++, ++ctrl+u++) always step over a collapsed block regardless of this setting.

The actions CollapseAllFolds, ExpandAllFolds, CollapseLastFold, ToggleLastFold and ToggleFold can be bound to keys; ScrollMarkUp and ScrollMarkDown already move the viewport from one prompt to the next.

docs.title: gutter
docs.text:
configuration controls the gutter: the strip left of the grid that carries per-line timestamps, line numbers and the block column. 

gutter:
  exit_status: true
  user_marks: true
  block_column_width: 2
  bold_on_hover: true
  line_numbers: off
  line_number_width: 6
  timestamps: false
  timestamp_format: '%H:%M:%S'
The gutter's width follows this configuration and never its content, so a growing line number cannot resize the page in the middle of a command's output. The block column is reserved while fold markers (folding.show_markers), exit status or user marks are on, block_column_width cells wide. exit_status Colour each command's fold controls by how it ended -- the colour scheme's block_status colours -- draw a triangle beside a running command, and a dot beside a finished one that shows no fold control: one with nothing to fold, or any one while fold markers are off. Hovering the block column shows the exit code, duration, start time, working directory and command line. user_marks Draw a diamond beside every row marked with vi-mode mm. block_column_width The block column's width in cells, 1 or 2. At 2, the default, its fold controls and marks are drawn across both cells at twice the size, and a click anywhere in the column -- the blank strip left of it included -- lands on it. bold_on_hover Draw the fold under the pointer -- its line, its box and its end -- one stroke heavier, as well as at full strength: a failed command's, already heavy, heavier still. Its colours are the color scheme's fold_marker.hover and block_status_hover. line_numbers off, absolute (every row's number, counted from the session's first row, so the numbers stay put while history scrolls away), relative (every row's distance from the cursor row, counting a collapsed block as one row -- exactly what j and k count) or hybrid (the cursor row's own number, every other row's distance), as vim's nu and rnu. In vi mode the distance counts from the vi cursor. line_number_width Columns the line numbers take, 3 to 10. A longer number shows its last digits after an ellipsis. timestamps Show the time each row was first reached. A row shows it only where it differs from the row above, so a long output does not repeat one second. timestamp_format A std::format chrono specification in local time, such as %H:%M or %a %H:%M:%S. It must begin with a % conversion, so a leading literal such as [%H:%M] is refused, and so is a leading width or alignment such as 8%H or >%H, which std::format would pad the timestamp with. Every character it spells must take exactly one column, so a double-width character (a CJK ideograph, say) or a combining mark is refused as well. A format that cannot be drawn is reported when the configuration loads, and the default is kept.

In vi normal mode, za, zo, zc, zM and zR toggle, open and close the block under the cursor, and close or open all of them, as in vim.

docs.title: osc_context
docs.text:
configuration controls whether Contour reads OSC 3008, systemd's hierarchical context signalling (UAPI.15): the nested stack of contexts a shell, run0, ssh or a container runtime opens around whatever runs inside it. 

osc_context:
  enabled: true
  max_depth: 16
  max_retained_contexts: 256
  derive_markers: when_alone
  tinting: boundaries
systemd 258 and later ship a shell snippet that emits these sequences around every interactive command with no configuration at all, so on such a system Contour learns command boundaries, exit statuses (including whether a command crashed or was interrupted, which OSC 133 cannot express) and working directories without any shell integration being installed. enabled Whether the sequences are read at all. When false nothing is tracked, nothing is derived and nothing is tinted. max_depth How deep the context stack may grow. Beyond it, further contexts are ignored -- the NEWER ones, so that a program cannot push the context established above it out of the stack. max_retained_contexts How many contexts are remembered for scrolled-back output that still refers to them. Older ones are forgotten, and output belonging to them simply stops being attributed. derive_markers Whether OSC 3008 may stand in for a shell integration that is not installed. when_alone derives prompt and command marks from it only while OSC 133 has said nothing; once a shell integration speaks, it owns the marks for the rest of the session. never leaves marks entirely to OSC 133. tinting Which contexts may tint the page background. The colours themselves come from the colour scheme's tint: map, which no shipped scheme sets, so nothing is tinted until you choose a colour there. Note that a context is something the session announced: anything that can write to your terminal can announce one, or fail to announce one, so the absence of a tint is not a statement that nothing is elevated.

docs.title: command_blocks
docs.text:
configuration controls what the terminal remembers about each shell command it saw run. 

command_blocks:
  max_records: 1000
  pager: less -R
  pager_format: sgr
A command block is one prompt and the output of the command run at it, delimited by the OSC 133 marks a shell with shell integration emits -- or, without one, by systemd's OSC 3008 contexts. For each block the terminal keeps its command line, exit status, duration, start time and working directory, even after the block's rows have left the scrollback. max_records How many blocks one session remembers; the oldest are forgotten first. At least 1, at most 1000000. A change applies to sessions opened afterwards. pager The program the OpenCommandOutput action ("Open Output in Pager", Ctrl+Shift+G) opens a command's output with when its binding names none. It is read as a profile's shell: is: a string naming a program runs as it is; otherwise its first word is the program and the rest its arguments -- on Windows passed on as written, so C:\Tools\less.exe -R needs no quoting. A binding's own program: is read the same way. The output is written to a private file that is appended as the last argument and deleted when the pane closes. Defaults to less -R (more on Windows). pager_format Whether the pager renders colours: sgr writes the output with its SGR sequences, plain as text only. Defaults to sgr, which both less -R and Windows more (inside the terminal's pseudo console) render. A binding's own format: wins, and a binding that names its own program: gets sgr.

docs.title: default_layout_name
docs.text: Name of the layout to open at startup, instead of a single default tab. Saved remote hosts that "Attach to Host" lists.### git_drawings fmt formatted doc thin

docs.title: box_arc_style
docs.text: fmt formatted doc round

docs.title: braille_style
docs.text: fmt formatted doc circle

docs.title: Default global parameters
docs.text:
platform_plugin: auto
renderer:
    backend: auto
    tile_hashtable_slots: 4096
    tile_cache_count: 4000
    tile_direct_mapping: true
word_delimiters: " /\\()\"'-.,:;<>~!@#$%^&*+=[]{}~?|│"
read_buffer_size: 65536
pty_buffer_size: 1048576
default_profile: main
spawn_new_process: false
reflow_on_resize: true
bypass_mouse_protocol_modifier: Shift
mouse_block_selection_modifier: Control
on_mouse_select: CopyToSelectionClipboard
live_config: false
images:
    sixel_scrolling: true
    sixel_register_count: 4096

The default profile is automatically the top (first) defined profile in the configuration file, but can be explicitly set to an order-independent name using default_profile configuration key.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Profiles is the main part of user specific customizations, you can create more than one profile and chose which you want to use during startup or define in configuration file.

By default each profile inherites values from default_profile. This means that you can specify only values that you want to change in respect to default profile, for example you can create new profile to use bash as a shell preserving other configuration from main profile 

profiles:
    main:
    # default profile here
    bash:
        shell: "/usr/bin/bash"

For the full list of options see generated configuration file on your system or Profiles section of documentation.

docs.title: Color Schemes
docs.text:
In contour you can specify different colors inside terminal, for example text background and foreground, cursor properties, selection colors and plenty others. You can configure your color profiles, whereas a color can be expressed in standard web format, with a leading # followed by red/green/blue values, 7 characters in total. You may alternatively use 0x as prefix instead of #. For example 0x102030 is equal to '#102030'.

Syntax for color schemes repeat the one of profiles. First color scheme inside configuration file must be named default, each other color schemes inherit values from default color scheme. Example of configuration for color_schemes 

color_schemes:
    default:
    # values for default color scheme
    different_selection:
      selection:
        background: '#fff0f0'

For the full list of options see generated configuration file on your system or Colors section of documentation.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text: Color scheme configure colors that are used inside terminal. To specify which color scheme you want to use you need to define the name of the scheme inside profile configuration or inline colors inside profile.

docs.title: Color scheme configuration
docs.text: Color configuration is set under profiles with colors. Then the scheme is defined under color_schemes.

docs.title: default
docs.text:
section defines the default colors used in the terminal. 

color_schemes:
  default:
    default:
      background: '#1a1716'
      foreground: '#d0d0d0'
      bright_foreground: '#ffffff'
      dimmed_foreground: '#808080'
background determines the default background color of the terminal. foreground option sets the default foreground text color of the terminal. bright_foreground option sets the default foreground text color of the terminal when text text is instructed to be bold (/bright). This is only used if profile option draw_bold_text_with_bright_colors is set to true dimmed_foreground option sets the default foreground text color of the terminal when text text is instructed to be dimmed.

docs.title: background_image
docs.text:
section in the configuration file allows you to control various aspects of the background image feature. 

color_schemes:
  default:
    background_image:
      path: '/path/to/image.png'
      opacity: 0.5
      blur: false
path To specify the image file to use as the background, you need to provide the full path to the image. Both ~ (home directory) and ${VAR} (environment variable) expansion are supported — see Path Handling for details. By default, the path option is set to an empty string, indicating that background image support is disabled. opacity option controls the opacity of the background image. It determines how transparent or intense the image appears. The default value is 0.5, which provides a moderately transparent background. You can adjust this value to make the image more or less prominent, depending on your preferences. blur option applies a blur effect to the background image. This can help reduce distractions and keep the focus on the terminal contents. By default, the blur option is set to false, indicating that background image blurring is disabled. If you want to enable it, set the value to true.

docs.title: cursor
docs.text:
section in the configuration file let you customize the color of the cursor and optionally override the text color. 

color_schemes:
  default:
    cursor:
      default: CellForeground
      text: CellBackground
default option allows you to specify the color of the cursor shape. By default, the default value is set to CellForeground, which means the cursor color will be the same as the cell's foreground color. You can change this value to any valid RGB color or use the special options CellForeground or CellBackground. text allows you to specify the color of the characters that would be covered by the cursor shape. This is useful for ensuring readability when the cursor overlaps with the text. By default, the text value is set to CellBackground, which means the overridden text color will be the same as the cell's background color. Similarly to the default option, you can specify any valid RGB color or use the CellForeground or CellBackground options.

docs.title: hyperlink_decoration
docs.text:
allows you to customize the colors used for hyperlink decoration when hovering over them. These colours apply to the links Contour detects in output as well as to OSC 8 hyperlinks. 

color_schemes:
  default:
    hyperlink_decoration:
      normal: '#f0f000'
      hover: '#ff0000'
normal defines the color to be used for hyperlink decoration in its normal state (not being hovered). hover determines the color to be applied to hyperlink decoration when it is being hovered over.

docs.title: vi_mode_highlight
docs.text:
customize the colors used for highlighting in Vi mode. 

color_schemes:
  default:
    vi_mode_highlight:
      foreground: CellForeground
      foreground_alpha: 1.0
      background: '#ffa500'
      background_alpha: 0.5
foreground section specifies the color to be used for the foreground of the highlighted text. foreground_alpha option determines the transparency level of the foreground color. It accepts a value between 0.0 (fully transparent) and 1.0 (fully opaque). This option allows you to control the visibility of the highlighted text. background option in the vi_mode_highlight section defines the color to be used for the background of the highlighted text. background_alpha option controls the transparency level of the background color. It accepts a value between 0.0 (fully transparent) and 1.0 (fully opaque).

docs.title: vi_mode_cursorline
docs.text:
customize the colors used for the cursor line in Vi mode. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight. 

color_schemes:
  default:
    vi_mode_cursorline:
      foreground: CellForeground
      foreground_alpha: 1.0
      background: '#ffa500'
      background_alpha: 0.5

docs.title: selection
docs.text:
section customize the colors used for text selection. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight. 

color_schemes:
  default:
    selection:
      foreground: CellForeground
      foreground_alpha: 1.0
      background: '#4040f0'
      background_alpha: 0.5

docs.title: search_highlight
docs.text:
section customize the colors used for search highlight. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight. 

color_schemes:
  default:
    search_highlight:
      foreground: CellForeground
      foreground_alpha: 1.0
      background: '#4040f0'
      background_alpha: 0.5

docs.title: search_highlight_focused
docs.text:
section customize the colors used for focused search highlight. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight. 

color_schemes:
  default:
    search_highlight_focused:
      foreground: CellForeground
      foreground_alpha: 1.0
      background: '#4040f0'
      background_alpha: 0.5

docs.title: word_highlight_current
docs.text:
Coloring for the word that is highlighted due to double-clicking it. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight. 

color_schemes:
  default:
    word_highlight_current:
      foreground: CellForeground
      foreground_alpha: 1.0
      background: '#4040f0'
      background_alpha: 0.5

docs.title: word_highlight_other
docs.text:
Coloring for the word that is highlighted due to double-clicking another word that matches this word. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight. 

color_schemes:
  default:
    word_highlight_other:
      foreground: CellForeground
      foreground_alpha: 1.0
      background: '#4040f0'
      background_alpha: 0.5

docs.title: indicator_statusline
docs.text:
Defines the colors to be used for the Indicator status line. Configuration entry consist of following sections, namely default, inactive, insert_mode, normal_mode, visual_mode. Each section have foreground and background options. You can specify only the sections you want to customize after configuring the default section. Minimal configuration looks like this: 

color_schemes:
  default:
    indicator_statusline:
        default:
          foreground: '#808080'
          background: '#000000'

docs.title: fold_marker
docs.text:
Defines the colors of the fold markers drawn in the gutter's block column, left of the grid, when output folding is enabled (see folding.show_markers). Two independent sections, default and hover, each with foreground and background; hover applies to the whole run of the fold the pointer is currently over, not just the row under it.

Both are optional, and left unset by default. When a section is missing, its colors are derived from this scheme's own default foreground and background: at rest the glyph is faded partway toward the background so it stays quieter than the text beside it, and on hover it comes up to the full foreground. Only the glyph changes — the background stays the page's own in both states, so the gutter never paints over a transparent window. That is what lets a scheme which has never heard of folding still draw a legible, obviously-clickable column, in light and dark themes alike — so only set these if you actively want something else.

color_schemes:
  default:
    fold_marker:
        default:
          foreground: '#7e7c7c'
          background: '#1a1716'
        hover:
          foreground: '#d0d0d0'
          background: '#1a1716'

default Colors of the fold column at rest. Set the background to this scheme's own background to keep the gutter transparent along with the rest of the window. hover Colors of the fold run under the pointer — the whole run of the hovered fold, not just the row beneath it.

docs.title: block_status
docs.text:
Defines the colors of a command block's marks by how its command ended (see Command blocks): what the gutter's block column draws beside it while gutter.exit_status is on (the default), and its tick on the scrollbar. Each is a single color, and all three are optional, left unset by default. A missing one is derived from this scheme, so a scheme that has never heard of them still shows them legibly:

  • success — a command that exited with 0, or whose exit status is unknown. Derived from the fold marker's color, so a successful block looks exactly as the fold column always has.
  • failure — a command that exited non-zero, or was killed. Derived from this scheme's normal red (normal color 1).
  • running — a command that has not finished yet. Derived from this scheme's normal yellow (normal color 3).

Under the pointer, failure and running — and a success set here — are lifted halfway toward the text color; an unset success comes up to full strength, as the fold column does.

color_schemes:
  default:
    block_status:
        success: '#7E7C7C'
        failure: '#C63939'
        running: '#A0A000'

The values shown are what the default scheme derives.

docs.title: gutter_text
docs.text:
The color of the gutter's line numbers and timestamps, and of the chip a collapsed fold carries (1,234 lines hidden ⌄), lifted where it would not read on the chip's band. Optional, and unset by default: it is then this scheme's foreground faded toward its background, as the resting fold markers are, so the numbers stay quieter than the text beside them.

color_schemes:
  default:
    gutter_text: '#7E7C7C'

docs.title: sticky_header
docs.text:
Defines the colors of the sticky command header (see the profile key sticky_header): the band pinned over the top row while you read a command's output with the command itself scrolled out of view, and the one-pixel line along its bottom edge.

Both are optional, and unset by default. A missing one is derived from this scheme's own default colors: the band is the background lifted a tenth of the way toward the foreground, the line about a third of the way — quiet in every theme, yet distinct from the page.

color_schemes:
  default:
    sticky_header:
        background: '#2C2928'
        separator: '#595757'

background The band's color. The command copied into it keeps its own colors; only the cells the shell left on the default background take this one. separator The one-pixel line along the band's bottom edge.

docs.title: Palette Presets
docs.text:
When choosing a palette from a preset as the color scheme (in profiles) it is possible to tweak any configuration: 

color_schemes:
  one-light:
      word_highlight_other:
          foreground: CellForeground
          background: CellBackground
          foreground_alpha: 1.0
          background_alpha: 1.0

Complete configuration looks like this: 

color_schemes:
  default:
    indicator_statusline:
        default:
          foreground: '#FFFFFF'
          background: '#0270C0'
        inactive:
          foreground: '#FFFFFF'
          background: '#0270C0'
        insert_mode:
          foreground: '#FFFFFF'
          background: '#0270C0'
        normal_mode:
          foreground: '#0F0002'
          background: '#0270C0'
        visual_mode:
          foreground: '#FFFFFF'
          background: '#0270C0'

Normal colors

      black:   '#000000'
      red:     '#c63939'
      green:   '#00a000'
      yellow:  '#a0a000'

docs.title: bright

Bright colors

docs.title: Writing a palette
docs.text:
normal, bright and dim each take their eight colors either by name, as above, or as a list in the order black, red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan, white: 

color_schemes:
  default:
    bright: ['#707070', '#ff0000', '#00ff00', '#ffff00', '#0000ff', '#ff00ff', '#00ffff', '#ffffff']
A list may stop short: the colors it leaves out keep their values. Either way, each color is written as '#rrggbb' (quoted, since # would otherwise start a YAML comment) or as 0xrrggbb. A bare decimal number is not a color, and leaves its slot as it was.
