docs.title: Hosts
docs.text: A saved host is a remote machine whose daemon Contour can attach to by name: "Attach to Host" lists them, and contour client --host NAME attaches to one. How remote attach works, and how to set the far side up (including over Tailscale), is described in Remote hosts.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Hosts are configured under the top-level hosts entry, a map of host name to its settings. Listings are sorted by name.

hosts:
  home:
    url: "ssh://me@homepc"
    remote_command: "/opt/contour/bin/contour daemon --stdio"
    profile: "remote"
  studio:
    url: "tls://studio.tailnet.ts.net:7297"
    token_file: "~/.config/contour/studio.token"
    tls_ca: "~/.config/contour/studio-ca.pem"
Key Meaning url Where the host is: ssh://[user@]host[:port] or tls://host:port. Required. token_file The file holding the remote daemon's token. Required for tls://, unused for ssh://. tls_ca A CA certificate to verify the daemon's TLS certificate against (tls://). Without it the connection is encrypted but the daemon's certificate is not checked. remote_command Replaces the whole command run on the remote side of ssh:// (default: contour daemon --stdio). Use it when contour is not on the remote non-interactive PATH. It reaches the remote shell verbatim, so quote a path with spaces inside the YAML string yourself ("'/opt/my apps/contour' daemon --stdio"). profile The profile the remote sessions are created with; empty selects the default one.

Paths in token_file and tls_ca expand ~ and ${VAR}, as every path in the configuration does.

docs.title: Key binding
docs.text:
The AttachToHost action opens a new window attached to the saved host its name names, as the "Attach to Host" entries do; a binding without name is skipped.

input_mapping:
  - { mods: [Control, Shift], key: H, action: AttachToHost, name: home }

docs.title: ssh://
docs.text:
hosts:
  home:
    url: "ssh://me@homepc:2222"

Contour runs ssh <target> contour daemon --stdio; ssh does the authentication, with keys or an agent only (no password or host-key prompt is answered from the GUI). The user and the port are optional; ssh's own configuration (~/.ssh/config) applies as usual. A host or user that begins with - is refused.

docs.title: tls://
docs.text:
hosts:
  studio:
    url: "tls://studio.tailnet.ts.net:7297"
    token_file: "~/.config/contour/studio.token"

A daemon listening with contour daemon --listen-tcp always requires a token, so a tls:// host must name its token_file; a tls:// host without one is skipped with a warning, and an ad-hoc tls:// URL (one not saved under hosts:) is refused. The port is required, and a tls:// URL takes no user: the token authenticates.

An entry that cannot be used — no url, a malformed one, a tls:// host without token_file — is reported in the log and skipped; the other hosts still load.

docs.title: Indicator Statusline
docs.text: The indicator statusline used to be a feature, from the old DEC VT level 4 terminals. Contour revives this feature to prominently show the terminal status.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
profiles:
    your_profile:
        status_line:
            indicator:
                left: "{InputMode:Bold,Left= ,Right= ,Chip,Hide=Insert}{Context:Left= }{Cwd:Color=success,Left= }{Git:Left=  }"
                middle: "{LastCommand}{Selection:Left=  }{SearchPrompt:Color=warning,Left=  }"
                right: "{Progress:Color=accent,Right=  }{Scroll:Right=  }{Clock:Faint,Right= }"

This is the default of a configuration with defaults_edition: native2026: the vi mode as a chip (hidden while typing), the directory and Git branch, how the last command went, the selection and search, and the scroll position and clock. Its colours are roles, so it follows the color scheme.

A configuration with defaults_edition: classic (one written before the redesign) keeps the earlier default, with the tabs, the title and fixed colors:

profiles:
    your_profile:
        status_line:
            indicator:
                left: " {InputMode:Bold,Color=#FFFF00}{TraceMode:Bold,Color=#FFFF00,Left= │ }{Tabs:ActiveColor=#FFFF00,Left= │ }{ProtectedMode:Bold,Left= │ }{Context:Left= │ }"
                middle: "« {Title} »"
                right: "{HistoryLineCount:Faint,Color=#c0c0c0} │ {Clock:Bold}"

Each segment, left, middle, and right may contain text to be displayed in the left, middle, or right segment of the indicator statusline.

This text may contain placeholders to be replaced by their respective dynamic content.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text: Variable Description {Clock} current clock in HH:MM format {Cwd} the working directory the shell reports, with the home directory as ~ when it is on this machine; at most MaxWidth= columns (default 40), eliding the middle directories (/…/d59) {Command} yields the output of the given command, as specified via parameter Program=... (or the {Command:<command>} shorthand), re-run every Interval=... seconds {Extension} what the status-line extension named by parameter Name=... (or the {Extension:<name>} shorthand) draws {Git} the branch of the Git repository the shell's directory is in (a ref outside refs/heads/ as remotes/origin/x, a detached HEAD as its first 7 hex digits in parentheses, (a1b2c3d)), read from .git/HEAD or a worktree's .git file; empty outside a repository or in a directory on another machine. It is looked up in the background, so it shows a moment after the directory does, and again only after a command ends or the shell reports its directory, never per frame. As git does by default, the search for the repository stops at a filesystem boundary. The directory is walked as the shell reports it: in a symlink to a directory inside a repository, no branch shows. A repository using the reftable ref backend (git init --ref-format=reftable) shows no branch for now. {HistoryLineCount} number of lines in history (only available in primary screen) {Hyperlink} reveals the hyperlink at the given mouse location {LastCommand} how the last command went, from the shell integration's command blocks (OSC 133): ✓ make · 4ms after a success, ✗ exit 8 ctest · 12s after a failure; the status drawn in the success or danger role and the duration in muted, unless the item names a Color= of its own. Empty while a command runs, and when a newer prompt ended one that reported no exit status. A multi-line command's line breaks and tabs read as spaces. The command text is at most MaxWidth= columns (default 32), cut at its end with … {InputMode} current input mode (e.g. INSERT, NORMAL, VISUAL); see Hide= and Chip below {ProtectedMode} indicates protected mode, if currently enabled {Scroll} how far the view is scrolled back into the history, out of how far it can be: ↑ 1 240 / 10 000, thousands grouped by a space. Empty at the bottom, and while the view cannot scroll (the alternate screen) {SearchMode} indicates search highlight mode, if currently active {SearchPrompt} the active search pattern, if any (read-only; search is typed into the find bar) {Selection} how much the selection holds, as y would copy it: 12 lines · 418 chars, thousands grouped by a space (1 240). Empty without a selection. The characters are those a copy yields: each row up to its last non-blank cell, the spaces between words included, a wide character once. They are counted only while the selection spans fewer than 10 000 cells (its rows at the page's width, or at a rectangle's own width); a larger one shows its lines alone, 1 240 lines {Tabs} indicates active tabs {Text} given text (makes only sense when customized with flags) {Title} current window title {VTType} currently active VT emulation type

docs.title: Formatting Styles
docs.text:
Each Variable, as specified above, can be parametrized for customizing the look of it. The common syntax to these variables and their parameters looks as follows:

{VariableName:SomeFlag,SomeKey=SomeValue}

So parameters can be specified after a colon (:) as a comma separated list of flags and key/value pairs. A key/value pair is further split by equal sign (=).

The following list of formatting styles are supported:

Parameter Description Left=TEXT text to show on the left side, if the variable is to be shown Right=TEXT text to show on the right side, if the variable is to be shown Color=COLOR text color: #RRGGBB, or one of the roles accent, success, danger, warning, muted BackgroundColor=COLOR background color: #RRGGBB, or one of the roles accent, success, danger, warning, muted Bold text in bold font face Italic text in italic font face Underline underline text (only one underline style can be active) CurlyUnderline curly underline text (only one underline style can be active) DoubleUnderline double underline text (only one underline style can be active) DottedUnderline dotted underline text (only one underline style can be active) DashedUnderline dashed underline text (only one underline style can be active) Blinking blinking text RapidBlinking rapid blinking text Overline overline text Inverse inversed text/background coloring

These parameters apply to all variables above.

{Cwd}, {Context} and {LastCommand} additionally take this attribute:

Parameter Description MaxWidth=N the widest the item may draw, in columns; beyond it the middle is elided and both ends kept. Default 40 for {Cwd}, 32 for {Context} and for {LastCommand}'s command text, which is cut at its end instead; a value that is not a number > 0 keeps the default.

A role names a color by what it means rather than by its value, and takes it from the active color scheme when the line is drawn, so it follows a scheme change: accent is palette color 4 (blue), success 2 (green), danger 1 (red), warning 3 (yellow) and muted 8 (bright black). The scheme is the configured one: a program changing the palette (OSC 4) recolours its own text, not the status line. Where a role's color would not read on the bar it is drawn on (at 4.5:1; muted, secondary text, at 3:1), the role's text takes the bar's legible ink instead -- the scheme's foreground or background, bright white, then black or white -- so it stays readable in every input mode and scheme; a #RRGGBB color is drawn as written. Roles are read in any case and written lowercase. A value that is neither a role nor a color leaves the color unset. The same values are accepted by the Tabs attributes ActiveColor and ActiveBackground.

The InputMode variable additionally takes these attributes:

Parameter Description Hide=<mode> shows nothing, Left=/Right= included, while the terminal is in that mode: Normal, Insert, Visual, VisualLine, VisualBlock or Hint, read in any case. An unknown mode hides the item in none. Chip draws the item, Left= and Right= included, as a chip filled with its mode's colors (indicatorStatusLine*Mode of the color scheme), while the rest of the line keeps the idle (Insert) colors in every mode. The chip's text takes the fill's legible ink where the scheme's own would not read at 4.5:1. Only the focused pane's chip is colored, and an item naming Color= or BackgroundColor= takes those instead. Without Chip, the whole line takes the mode's colors.

They are written after the other attributes:

{InputMode:Bold,Left= ,Right= ,Chip,Hide=Insert}

The Command variable additionally takes these attributes:

Parameter Description Program the command to execute (required, unless the shorthand below is used) Interval seconds between runs; default 10. An invalid value or one <= 0 selects the default. 
{Command:Program=git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD,Interval=30,Bold}

Shorthand. {Command:<command>} takes everything after Command: verbatim as the command, so it may contain commas and =, but no styling and no Interval=: {Command:git log -1 --format=%h,%s}. A template naming Program= or Interval= is read in the attribute form instead; anything else is the shorthand, so {Command:Bold} runs a program named Bold (a style flag needs Program=). A command cannot contain }.

Execution. Commands run asynchronously in the background, so they never slow down rendering and, on Windows, never open a console window. The item shows the output of the previous run until a new one arrives, and is empty before the first run completes. A command that is still running after 5 seconds (or after its Interval, if that is shorter) is killed together with its child processes, and the previous output is kept.

Only the first line of the command's standard output is shown. Standard error and the exit status are ignored, and a command that cannot be started shows the operating system's error message.

Unlike popen, background processes a command leaves behind are killed as soon as the command finishes, even when it succeeds (the process group on Unix, the job object on Windows): a command like start notepad starts nothing that outlives it.

docs.title: Tabs formatting extensions
docs.text:
The Tabs key allows additional styling through the following attributes:

Parameter Description ActiveColor color of the active tab ActiveBackground background color of the active tab

{Tabs} versus the GUI tab bar

The indicator status line belongs to a pane, so with split panes a window draws one {Tabs} list per pane rather than one per window — several tab lists side by side, each describing the same tabs.

If what you want is the terminal look rather than the placement, set the global ui_style to terminal. That keeps the single window-level tab bar and every one of its affordances (drag to reorder, tear off, rename, close, context menu) but draws it cell-quantized, in the terminal font, with square corners and box-drawing separators.

{Tabs} remains fully supported, and the two can be used together.

docs.title: Key Mapping
docs.text:
To customize key mappings, you need to configure input_mapping yaml entry

Defining input_mapping replaces the built-in bindings — it does not add to them

As soon as an input_mapping section is present in your contour.yml, Contour's built-in defaults (Ctrl+Shift+C/Ctrl+Shift+V, the Ctrl+Shift+P command palette, the tab and pane shortcuts, …) are discarded, and only the entries you list are active. Writing an input_mapping section is a declaration that you are defining the full set of bindings.

The contour.yml that Contour generates on first run already contains every default binding written out in full, so editing that section keeps the defaults you did not touch. If you are writing a configuration by hand and want to keep the defaults, start from a generated one (contour generate config) and add your entries to the existing list.

docs.title: Built-in bindings
docs.text:
A small number of bindings are built in and do not appear in input_mapping:

Binding Action Ctrl+Tab / Ctrl+PageDown Switch to the tab on the right (wrapping around) Ctrl+Shift+Tab / Ctrl+PageUp Switch to the tab on the left (wrapping around) Ctrl+Shift+G Open the last command's output in the pager named by command_blocks.pager (needs a shell that marks its commands with OSC 133). With nothing to open the chord is swallowed rather than sent to the shell as ^G; on the alternate screen it goes to the application Alt+Shift+Arrow (Linux, Windows) / Cmd+Option+Arrow (macOS) Move the focus to the pane on that side. Some desktops and keyboard-layout switchers grab Alt+Shift; if the chord never reaches Contour, bind another one to FocusPaneLeft/Right/Up/Down in input_mapping Ctrl+Shift+E / Ctrl+Shift+O (Linux, Windows) Split the active pane side by side / stacked Cmd+D / Cmd+Shift+D (macOS) Split the active pane side by side / stacked Cmd+Shift+Enter (macOS) Zoom the active pane to fill the tab, and back Ctrl+Shift+K (Linux, Windows) / Cmd+Shift+K (macOS) NewWindowTo: open the Connect picker to choose where a new window's sessions live Right mouse button Open the terminal's context menu Ctrl + triple-click with the Left mouse button Select the output of the command under the pointer (needs a shell that marks its commands with OSC 133; on the alternate screen, which has no commands, the click selects as usual) Horizontal wheel / two-finger sideways swipe Switch tabs

These are consulted only when your input_mapping does not claim the same key or button (for the triple-click, the same button and click count), so binding one of them yourself replaces it.

They are built in rather than listed as defaults for the reason given in the warning above: an input_mapping section replaces the built-in list wholesale, and the generated contour.yml writes every default into that section. A binding added to Contour after your configuration file was written would therefore be shadowed by your own file forever. Consulting these after yours is what lets a new binding still reach you, while anything you bind explicitly keeps winning.

Ctrl+Tab is taken from the application

Like Windows Terminal, GNOME Terminal and Konsole, Contour claims Ctrl+Tab for tab switching, so a terminal application that wants it (via the Kitty keyboard protocol) will not receive it. Bind it in your own input_mapping to give it back to the application.

docs.title: Writing bindings
docs.text:
Each element in the input_mapping represents one key binding, whereas mods represents an array of keyboard modifiers that must be pressed - as well as the key or mouse - in order to activate the corresponding action. Additionally one can filter input mappings based on special terminal modes using the modes option:

  • Alt : The terminal is currently in alternate screen buffer, otherwise it is in primary screen buffer.
  • AppCursor : The application key cursor mode is enabled (otherwise it's normal cursor mode).
  • AppKeypad : The application keypad mode is enabled (otherwise it's the numeric keypad mode).
  • Select : The terminal has currently an active grid cell selection (such as selected text).
  • Insert : The Insert input mode is active, that is the default and one way to test that the input mode is not in normal mode or any of the visual select modes.
  • Search : A search term is currently set. It outlives the find bar, so this stays true for as long as the matches are still highlighted; an open bar with nothing typed into it does not match.
  • Trace : The terminal is currently in trace-mode, i.e., each VT sequence can be interactively single-step executed using custom actions. See TraceEnter/TraceStep/TraceLeave actions.

You can combine these modes by concatenating them via | and negate a single one by prefixing with ~. The modes option defaults to not filter at all (the input mappings always match based on modifier and key press/mouse event). key represents keys on your keyboard, and mouse represents buttons as well as the scroll wheel.

Modifiers, which are case-insensitive (Control, control and CONTROL are the same modifier):

  • Shift
  • Alt
  • Control — may also be written Ctrl
  • Super — may also be written Meta. This is the Windows key on Windows, the Command key on macOS, and the Super key on anything else.
  • Hyper

Note

Meta is a synonym for Super for historical reasons: contour.yml has spelled the Windows/Command key Meta since before a separate Meta modifier existed. There is currently no configuration spelling for the distinct Meta modifier that the extended CSI u keyboard protocol reports.

An entry naming a modifier that is not in this list is rejected as a whole — the binding is dropped rather than bound with a partial chord — and the reason is reported on startup.

Keys can be expressed case-insensitively symbolic:

APOSTROPHE, ADD, BACKSLASH, COMMA, DECIMAL, DIVIDE, EQUAL, LEFT_BRACKET, MINUS, MULTIPLY, PERIOD, RIGHT_BRACKET, SEMICOLON, SLASH, SUBTRACT, SPACE Enter, Backspace, Tab, Escape, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, DownArrow, LeftArrow, RightArrow, UpArrow, Insert, Delete, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown, Numpad_Divide, Numpad_Multiply, Numpad_Subtract, Numpad_Add, Numpad_Decimal, Numpad_Enter, Numpad_Equal, Numpad_0, Numpad_1, Numpad_2, Numpad_3, Numpad_4, Numpad_5, Numpad_6, Numpad_7, Numpad_8, Numpad_9

or in case of standard characters, just the character.

A single-character key also matches case-insensitively: key: 'q' and key: 'Q' bind the same chord. Shift is carried by mods, not by the letter's case, so writing an uppercase letter does not mean "with Shift" — use mods: [Shift] for that.

Mouse buttons can be one of the following self-explanatory ones:

Left, Middle, Right, WheelUp, WheelDown, WheelLeft, WheelRight

A mouse binding may also name a click count with clicks (1 to 4). Such a binding fires on that click of a multi-click sequence only, and it is consulted before Contour's own double-, triple- and quadruple-click selection, so it replaces that selection for the chord it names:

input_mapping:
    - { mods: [Control], mouse: Left, clicks: 3, action: SelectCommandBlock, target: pointer, part: output }

A binding without clicks fires on every press that no clicks binding claimed. Like the selection it replaces, a clicks binding never takes a click that an application asked for, unless the bypass_mouse_protocol_modifier is held.

clicks applies to the Left, Middle and Right buttons only: a wheel step is never more than a first click. An entry that gives it to a key or a wheel, or a count other than 1 to 4, is dropped and the reason is reported on startup.

List of supported actions for key mappings.

Action Description CancelSelection Cancels currently active selection, if any. ChangeProfile Changes the profile to the given profile name. ClearHistoryAndReset Clears the history, performs a terminal hard reset and attempts to force a redraw of the currently running application. CopyPreviousMarkRange Copies the most recent range that is delimited by vertical line marks into clipboard. CopySelection Copies the current selection into the clipboard buffer. With fallback: last_command_output and nothing selected, copies what the last command printed instead (requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks). CreateDebugDump Create dump for debug purposes CreateSelection Creates selection with custom delimiters configured via delimiters member. DecreaseFontSize Decreases the font size by 1 pixel. DecreaseOpacity Decreases the default-background opacity by 5%. FocusNextSearchMatch Focuses the next search match (if any). FocusPreviousSearchMatch Focuses the next previous match (if any). FollowHyperlink Follows the hyperlink that is exposed via OSC 8 under the current cursor position. HintMode Activates hint mode: scans the terminal for regex-matched patterns (URLs, file paths, git hashes, etc.), renders short alphabetic labels on each match, and lets the user type a label to act on that match (copy, open, paste). Parameter patterns selects which pattern set to use, hint_action specifies the action (Copy, Open, Paste, CopyAndPaste, Select), and scope selects how much to scan: Visible (the default, the current viewport) or Scrollback (the viewport plus up to hint_scrollback_lines rows of history, whose labels stay put while you scroll to reach them). A pattern that wraps across a line break is matched as one hint. IncreaseFontSize Increases the font size by 1 pixel. IncreaseOpacity Increases the default-background opacity by 5%. NewTerminal Spawns a new terminal at the current terminals current working directory. NewWindowTo Opens the Connect picker as a sheet: choose where the new window's sessions live (this computer's daemon, this window only, a saved host, or a typed ssh:// or tls:// address), then the window opens attached there. NoSearchHighlight Disables current search highlighting, if anything is still highlighted due to a prior search. OpenCommandPalette Opens the command palette: a searchable popup listing every runnable command with its description and key binding. Recently used commands are listed first, then all commands alphabetically. OpenConfiguration Opens the Settings window (profiles, color schemes, global settings). Set in_editor: true on the binding to instead open the configuration file in an external editor. OpenFileManager Opens the current working directory in a system file manager. OpenSelection Open the current terminal selection with the default system application (eg; xdg-open) PasteClipboard Pastes clipboard to standard input. Pass boolean parameter 'strip' to indicate whether or not to strip repetitive whitespaces down to one and newlines to whitespaces. PasteSelection Pastes current selection to standard input.Option evaluate_in_shell specify if pasted text must be appended with linefeed and used as an input for the running shell Quit Quits the application. ReloadConfig Forces a configuration reload. ResetConfig Overwrites current configuration with builtin default configuration and loads it. Attention, all your current configuration will be lost due to overwrite! ResetFontSize Resets font size to what is configured in the config file. ScreenshotVT Takes a screenshot in form of VT escape sequences. SaveScreenshot Takes a screenshot and saves it into a file. CopyScreenshot takes a screenshot and puts it into the system clipboard CollapseAllFolds Collapses every finished command, hiding all of their output (requires shell integration) CollapseLastFold Collapses the most recently finished command, hiding its output ExpandAllFolds Expands every collapsed command again ScrollDown Scrolls down by the multiplier factor. ScrollMarkDown Scrolls one mark down (if none present, bottom of the screen) ScrollMarkUp Scrolls one mark up ScrollOneDown Scrolls down by exactly one line. ScrollOneUp Scrolls up by exactly one line. ScrollPageDown Scrolls a page down. ScrollPageUp Scrolls a page up. ScrollToBottom Scrolls to the bottom of the screen buffer. ScrollToTop Scrolls to the top of the screen buffer. ToggleFold Collapses or expands the command block the cursor is in ToggleFoldAt Collapses or expands the command block covering a given grid line (used by the context menu) ToggleLastFold Collapses or expands the most recently finished command FocusPreviousCommand Focuses the command block before the focused one (else the last one in view), scrolls it into view and announces how it went. FocusNextCommand Focuses the command block after the focused one (else the first one in view), scrolls it into view and announces how it went. SelectPreviousCommandOutput Focuses the previous command block, as FocusPreviousCommand does, and selects its output. SelectNextCommandOutput Focuses the next command block, as FocusNextCommand does, and selects its output. OpenBlockMenu Opens the menu of the focused command block. Bind it with the BlockFocus mode, so the key keeps reaching the application otherwise. ClearCommandBlockFocus Takes the keyboard focus off the command block. Bind it with the BlockFocus mode, so the key keeps reaching the application otherwise. ScrollUp Scrolls up by the multiplier factor. SearchReverse Opens the find bar, searching upwards from the current cursor position. SearchSelection Searches for the selected text: its first line becomes the find bar's pattern, escaped when the bar searches by regular expression. SendChars Writes given characters in chars member to the applications input. ToggleAllKeyMaps Disables/enables responding to all keybinds (this keybind will be preserved when disabling all others). ToggleFullscreen Enables/disables full screen mode. ToggleInputMethodHandling Enables/disables IME (input method editor) handling. ToggleInputProtection Enables/disables terminal input protection. ToggleStatusLine Shows/hides the VT320 compatible Indicator status line. ToggleTitleBar Shows/Hides titlebar TraceBreakAtEmptyQueue Executes any pending VT sequence from the VT sequence buffer in trace mode, then waits. TraceEnter Enables trace mode, suspending execution until explicitly requested to continue (See TraceLeave and TraceStep). TraceLeave Disables trace mode. Any pending VT sequence will be flushed out and normal execution will be resumed. TraceStep Executes a single VT sequence that is to be executed next. ViNormalMode Enters/Leaves Vi-like normal mode. The cursor can then be moved via h/j/k/l movements in normal mode and text can be selected via v, yanked via y, and clipboard pasted via p. WriteScreen Writes VT sequence in chars member to the screen (bypassing the application). CreateNewTab Creates a new tab in the terminal emulator. CloseTab Closes current tab. MoveTabTo Moves current tab to the given position (starting at number 1). MoveTabToLeft Moves current tab to the left. MoveTabToRight Moves current tab to the right. SwitchToTab Switch to absolute tab position (starting at number 1) SwitchToPreviousTab Switch to the previously focused tab SwitchToTabLeft Switch to tab to the left SwitchToTabRight Switch to tab to the right SetTabTitle Rename the current tab inline (opens the tab-title editor) SplitVertical Splits the active pane into two side-by-side panes (a vertical divider). SplitHorizontal Splits the active pane into two stacked panes (a horizontal divider). ClosePane Closes the active pane (or the tab if it is the last pane). FocusPaneLeft Moves pane focus to the left. FocusPaneRight Moves pane focus to the right. FocusPaneUp Moves pane focus up. FocusPaneDown Moves pane focus down. SwapPaneLeft Swaps the active pane with its left neighbor. SwapPaneRight Swaps the active pane with its right neighbor. SwapPaneUp Swaps the active pane with its upper neighbor. SwapPaneDown Swaps the active pane with its lower neighbor. MovePaneLeft Moves the active pane past its left neighbor. MovePaneRight Moves the active pane past its right neighbor. MovePaneUp Moves the active pane past its upper neighbor. MovePaneDown Moves the active pane past its lower neighbor. ToggleSplitOrientation Flips the orientation of the active pane's split (horizontal <-> vertical). TogglePaneZoom Zooms the active pane so it alone fills the tab, hiding its siblings; toggles back to the tiled layout. While zoomed, moving pane focus keeps the zoom and shows the newly focused pane. ResizePane Grows or shrinks the active pane in the given direction (by an optional percent). LaunchLayout Opens a named layout, appending its tabs to the current window. SaveLayout Saves the current window's tabs as a named layout in layouts.yml. Without a name it opens a prompt to type one in (which is how the command palette offers it). AttachToHost Opens a new window attached to the saved host name (see hosts:). OpenContextMenu Opens the terminal pane's context menu. Bound to the right mouse button by default, and only fired when the running application has not asked for the mouse itself (hold Shift to open it anyway). SelectAll Selects everything the terminal holds: the whole scrollback and the whole screen. SoftReset Performs a terminal soft reset (DECSTR): resets modes, rendition and cursor state, while keeping the screen contents and the scrollback. CopyLastCommandPrompt Copies the prompt line(s) of the most recently finished command into the clipboard. Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks (see Contour's shell integration). CopyLastCommandOutput Copies what the most recently finished command printed into the clipboard. Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks (see Contour's shell integration). CopyLastCommandBlock Copies both the prompt and the output of the most recently finished command into the clipboard. Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks (see Contour's shell integration). CopyHyperlink Copies the URI of the hyperlink under the mouse cursor into the clipboard. SetTabColor Colorize the current tab. Without a color, this opens the tab's color picker; with one (e.g. color: '#ff0000') it applies that color right away. ResetTabColor Removes the color you gave the current tab, restoring its default look (or the color the running application assigned, if it assigned one). CloseAllTabs Closes every tab in this window. With only one window open, that closes Contour. SetTabBarVisibility Sets when this window's tab bar is shown (mode: always, never or multiple). Applies to this window until it is closed; the settings page is where the choice is made permanent. SetTabBarPosition Places this window's tab bar above or below the terminal (position: top or bottom). Applies to this window until it is closed; the settings page is where the choice is made permanent. SpeakSelection Reads the selected text aloud through the operating system's speech synthesizer. Available only where a speech engine and a voice are installed. StopSpeaking Stops reading aloud. SelectCommandBlock Selects one part of a command block as whole lines (target: pointer, cursor or last; part: output, input or all). Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks. CopyCommandBlock Copies one part of a command block into the clipboard as plain text (target: pointer, cursor or last; part: output, input or all). Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks. CopyCommandLine Copies the command line of a command block into the clipboard, with the control characters that would be unsafe to paste removed (target: pointer, cursor or last). Requires a shell that reports its command lines (OSC 133;C cmdline_url). RerunCommand Runs the command line of a command block again: typed at the shell's prompt and entered, once the command it would run has been shown and confirmed (target: pointer, cursor or last). Requires a shell that marks its prompts (OSC 133) and reports or shows its command lines; refused while a command is running, and for a command line that cannot be typed as it is. ToggleCommandFold Collapses or expands a command block's output (target: pointer, cursor or last). Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks, and folding to be enabled. ClearToPrompt Clears the scrollback and the screen above the current prompt. A prompt on the screen moves to its top, with a running command's output; one in the scrollback becomes the oldest line kept. Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks. OpenCommandOutput Opens a command's output in a pager (target: pointer, cursor or last; program: the pager, read as command_blocks.pager is, which it replaces when given; placement: split, tab or detached; format: sgr or plain, by default command_blocks.pager_format for the configured pager and sgr for a named program). Detached pipes plain text into the program's standard input instead of opening a pane, and is the one placement a daemon-attached session offers. Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks. CloseOtherTabs Closes every tab in this window except the current one. CloseTabsToRight Closes every tab to the right of the current one. MoveTabToNewWindow Moves the current tab into a new window of its own. Does nothing with a single tab. ShowAbout Shows the version of Contour. MinimizeWindow Minimizes this window. ZoomWindow Maximizes this window, or restores it when it is maximized (the macOS Zoom). FocusNextArea Moves keyboard focus to the next area of the window: terminal, tabs, toolbar, and back. FocusPreviousArea Moves keyboard focus to the previous area of the window: terminal, toolbar, tabs, and back. FocusToolbar Moves keyboard focus to the window's toolbar.

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text: A layout is a named set of tabs that are opened together. Each tab can change into a directory, run a specific command instead of your shell, carry a name and a color, and optionally be split into a tree of panes. Layouts let you reproduce a working set of tabs — for example an editor, a chat/agent tool, and a couple of monitoring panes — with a single action instead of opening and arranging them by hand every time.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Layouts are configured under the top-level layouts entry, a map of layout name to its list of tabs. An optional top-level default_layout names a layout to open automatically at startup instead of the usual single default tab.

layouts:
  work:
    tabs:
      - title: "editor"
        color: "#d75f00"
        directory: "~/proj/foo"
        command: "nvim"
        arguments: ["."]
        profile: "dark-big"

      - title: "claude"
        color: "#00af5f"
        directory: "~/proj/foo"
        command: "claude"

      - title: "servers"
        split:
          orientation: vertical
          panes:
            - { command: "npm run dev", directory: "~/proj/foo", ratio: 0.6 }
            - split:
                orientation: horizontal
                panes:
                  - { command: "htop" }
                  - { command: "journalctl -f" }

  dev:
    tabs:
      - title: "shell"
        directory: "~/proj/bar"

default_layout: work

docs.title: Tab options
docs.text:
Each entry under tabs describes either a single-pane tab (leaf fields) or a split tab (a split node). A tab uses leaf fields or split, not both.

Option Description title Optional. Seeds the tab's name. color Optional. Hex in '#RRGGBB' form (e.g. '#d75f00'); sets the tab's user color. directory Optional working directory for the tab. Falls back to the profile's configured directory when omitted. command Optional. Replaces the shell — the program to run in the pane. May be a full command line (see Command lines below). When omitted, the effective profile's shell is used. arguments Optional list of extra arguments, appended after any arguments already given in command. profile Optional per-tab profile override (see Per-tab profile below). split Optional. Turns the tab into a split node instead of a single pane; see Split panes.

docs.title: Command lines
docs.text:
command may be written as a full command line. It is kept as written and read when the pane starts, the way a profile's shell is read: when it names a program to run — a file at that path, or a name found on PATH — it runs as it is, spaces and all; otherwise its first word is the program and the rest are its arguments. So both of these are equivalent:

- command: "emacs -nw"
# is the same as
- command: "emacs"
  arguments: ["-nw"]

How the words are read depends on the platform:

  • On Linux, macOS and FreeBSD, as a POSIX shell reads them: whitespace separates words; double quotes ("...", allowing \" and \\) or single quotes ('...', literal) keep spaces inside one word; a backslash outside quotes escapes the next character.
  • On Windows, as CreateProcess reads a command line: the program runs up to the first space at which what precedes it names a program — so C:\Program Files\Git\bin\bash.exe --login runs bash.exe — or up to its closing double quote, and a backslash separates directories. What follows the program is handed to it as written, for it to split itself: cmd.exe /s /c ""C:\Tools x\app.exe" --flag" reaches cmd.exe unchanged.
  • A program path with spaces in it that names no file is split like any other command line; quote it to keep it whole — e.g. command: '"/opt/My App/bin/foo" --flag'.
  • In the Flatpak build, where a pane runs on the host, Contour cannot see the host's files: a command holding whitespace is always read as a command line there, so quote a program path with spaces in it.
  • Any entries in a separate arguments: list are passed after the words of command.
  • ${NAME} inside command or arguments expands to the environment variable NAME. To pass a literal ${...} through to the program (e.g. for template tooling), escape it as $${...}.

SaveLayout (below) writes command: back as the pane was started with it, and arguments: after it — escaping any literal ${ — so everything round-trips.

docs.title: Split panes
docs.text:
A split node replaces the leaf fields (command, directory, ...) with:

Option Description orientation vertical or horizontal (case-insensitive). vertical arranges panes side by side; horizontal stacks them. panes A list of child panes. Each child is either a leaf (with command, directory, arguments, profile, ratio) or another split node, nested recursively. ratio Optional, set on a child pane/split. The fraction of the parent split's space (between 0 and 1) that child occupies; children without a ratio share the remaining space equally. In the example above, ratio: 0.6 gives the first pane 60% and leaves 40% for its unspecified sibling.

Splits can be nested arbitrarily deep, as shown in the servers tab of the example above: a vertical split whose second pane is itself a horizontal split.

docs.title: Per-tab profile
docs.text: A tab (or an individual pane) may set profile to use a different profile than the window's own profile for that tab/pane. The override is terminal-level only — it affects things like the shell, fonts, colors, and scrollback of that pane. Window-level settings (window size, decorations, and similar) always come from the profile that launched the window itself.

docs.title: Opening a layout
docs.text: There are four ways to open a layout:

docs.title: At startup
docs.text:
Set default_layout to a layout name; it opens automatically when Contour starts, replacing the usual single default tab.

default_layout: work

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
Pass --layout NAME to open a layout in the newly launched window:

contour terminal --layout work

docs.title: From a keybinding
docs.text:
Bind the LaunchLayout action to a key, passing the layout's name:

input_mapping:
  - { mods: [Control, Shift], key: L, action: LaunchLayout, name: work }

Unlike the startup and CLI cases, LaunchLayout appends the layout's tabs to the current window rather than opening a new one.

docs.title: From the command palette
docs.text: Open the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P by default) and pick the Launch Layout: name entry — one is listed for every saved layout, so no keybinding is required. Picking one appends that layout's tabs to the current window, exactly like the LaunchLayout action.

docs.title: Saving the current window as a layout
docs.text:
The SaveLayout action captures the active window's current tabs and panes — their directories, the command each pane was started with, titles, colors, and split structure — and writes them out as a named layout.

input_mapping:
  - { mods: [Control, Shift], key: S, action: SaveLayout, name: work }

SaveLayout never modifies your hand-written configuration file. Instead it writes a machine-managed layouts.yml file next to your main configuration file, in the same directory. Layouts from layouts.yml are merged with any layouts defined inline in your main configuration; if a name exists in both, the layouts.yml version wins, since it reflects the most recently saved state.

You don't need a keybinding to save: open the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) and pick Save Layout. Because saving needs a name, that entry opens a small prompt for you to type one in, then saves exactly as the SaveLayout action does. A key bound to SaveLayout with no name opens the same prompt.

docs.title: Tab colors
docs.text:
A tab's color is what makes it findable in a long tab bar. A new tab takes the tab_color of the profile it starts with:

profiles:
  main:
    tab_color: '#2E3440'

Like a layout's color, tab_color is a hex '#RRGGBB' value; null, the default, means no color. A color from a layout, one an application sets for its own tab, or one you pick from the tab's context menu takes precedence over the profile's, and clearing it brings the profile's color back. A split tab keeps the color of the profile that created it.

docs.title: Links in Terminal Output
docs.text:
Contour underlines URLs, file paths and patterns you define in the output of your programs, the way it shows OSC 8 hyperlinks, about 100 ms after the output goes quiet. Ctrl+click opens them.

profiles:
  main:
    hyperlink_decoration:
      mode: always              # always | hover | modifier | never
      normal: dotted-underline
      hover: underline
    link_detection:
      primary_screen: { urls: true, file_paths: true }
      other_screens:  { urls: true, file_paths: false }
    file_opener:
      command: 'code --goto {path}:{line}:{column}'
      placement: detached       # detached | split | tab
    hint_patterns:
      - name: url
        clickable: false        # stops underlining URLs: a built-in, changed by its name alone
      - name: jira
        regex: '\b[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\d+\b'
        clickable: true
        url: 'https://jira.example.com/browse/{0}'

Everything here has a default, so a configuration without any of these keys detects links as described below.

docs.title: What is detected
docs.text:
• URLs with the schemes http, https, ftp, file and mailto. Trailing punctuation is left out of the link, so the full stop after a URL at the end of a sentence is not part of it; a closing bracket the URL opened itself is kept, as in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foo_(bar). A file:// URL is the file it names, and is a path in all that follows: underlined only once it is found on this machine, and opened as a file is. Contour never runs it; without a file_opener it goes to the application your system associates with it, which on Windows and macOS may run a program.
  • File paths: absolute (/usr/include/stdio.h, C:\Users\me\notes.txt), relative (src/main.cpp, ../build/log.txt), home-relative (~/notes.md), and bare file names (Makefile, main.cpp). A location printed after a path, :line[:column] or (line[,column]) as compilers print them, is kept and passed on when the file is opened.
  • Patterns of your own, see below.

A path is underlined only once Contour has checked that it exists on this machine. A relative path is resolved against the directory of the command that printed it, which the shell reports through shell integration (OSC 133 and OSC 7), so a cd since then does not change what an earlier command's output names. A path printed by a command that ran on another machine, over ssh or in a container, names a file there and is never underlined, once Contour can tell: the remote shell reports the directory it runs in, with its host, through its own shell integration (OSC 7). Without that, everything an ssh session prints belongs to the local ssh command, and its paths are looked up on this machine.

docs.title: Where links are detected
docs.text:
link_detection switches the automatic detection per screen. OSC 8 hyperlinks are always links, and hint mode always offers everything; only the underlining of text found by scanning is affected.

Key Default Meaning primary_screen.urls true URLs and your own patterns on the shell screen primary_screen.file_paths true file paths on the shell screen other_screens.urls true URLs and patterns on the alternate screen other_screens.file_paths false file paths on the alternate screen

other_screens covers the alternate screen (vim, less, htop, ...) and every further page. A key you leave out keeps its default, or the value it inherits from a parent profile.

Your own patterns follow the urls switch, unless they open a file: URL, which follows the file_paths switch.

docs.title: When links are shown
docs.text:
hyperlink_decoration decides when links are decorated, for OSC 8 hyperlinks and detected links alike:

mode Links are decorated always always (the default) hover only the one under the mouse pointer modifier all of them while the modifier of Ctrl+click is held never never; Ctrl+click still opens them

normal is the decoration of a link at rest and hover the one of the link under the pointer. Each is one of underline, dotted-underline, double-underline, curly-underline, dashed-underline, overline, crossed-out, framed and encircle. The colours of both live in the colour scheme, see hyperlink_decoration.

docs.title: Opening links
docs.text:
• Ctrl+click: the FollowHyperlink mouse binding. Inside an application that uses the mouse itself, such as vim or tmux with mouse support, add the global bypass_mouse_protocol_modifier (Shift by default): Shift+Ctrl+click.
  • The context menu: right-click a link for Open Link and Copy Link Address.
  • Vi normal mode: gx opens the link under the cursor, and ]x / [x move the cursor to the next / previous link (see Input Modes).
  • Hint mode: gH in vi normal mode, or a HintMode binding with hint_action: Open (see Hint Mode).

A web URL opens in your browser. A path, or a file:// URL, opens as what it names: a directory in your file manager, and a file with file_opener, or with the application your system associates with it. That application is the system's choice: on Windows and macOS, a program it is handed may run.

docs.title: file_opener
docs.text:
file_opener says how a detected file opens. The string form is the command alone; the map form adds where it runs:

profiles:
  main:
    file_opener: 'code --goto {path}:{line}:{column}'

profiles:
  main:
    file_opener:
      command: 'nvim +{line} {path}'
      placement: split    # detached (the default), split or tab
  • {path} is the file's absolute path, {line} and {column} the location printed after it, 1 where none was printed.
  • No shell is involved: the command line is split into arguments once, and each placeholder is filled in inside its own argument, so a file name with spaces or quotes in it stays one argument and cannot run anything.
  • placement: detached starts the command as a program of its own; split and tab run it in a new Contour pane, in the directory a relative path was resolved against or, for an absolute path, the file's own directory.
  • A directory always opens in the file manager. Without file_opener, a file opens with the system's default application.
  • Write the program out, without a placeholder. A program path with a space in it is read as one program where that path exists on this machine; where it does not, or under flatpak with escape_sandbox, it is split at the space. Use a wrapper script on a path without spaces in that case.
  • On Windows, name an .exe as the program. A .cmd or .bat file is run by cmd.exe, which parses its command line again, so a file name could change what it runs.

docs.title: Your own clickable patterns
docs.text:
The patterns of hint mode, hint_patterns, are detected in output too when you say so:

profiles:
  main:
    hint_patterns:
      - name: jira
        regex: '\b[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\d+\b'
        clickable: true
        url: 'https://jira.example.com/browse/{0}'
      - name: commit
        regex: '\b[0-9a-f]{7,40}\b'
        clickable: true
        url: 'https://github.com/contour-terminal/contour/commit/{0}'
  • clickable: true detects the pattern in output, decorates it and opens it with Ctrl+click. Your own patterns are hint-mode-only unless they say so.
  • url is what is opened: {0} is the whole match, {1} to {9} its capture groups. Without it, the match is opened as printed. A url naming a group the regex does not have is reported when the configuration is loaded and disables the pattern.
  • Where the printed text chooses the scheme, there is a link only for a scheme Contour opens in URLs it finds itself: http, https, ftp, mailto or file. That is so without a url, and with a url that does not start with a scheme of its own, such as {0} or {1}:{2}. Printed text cannot open a smb: share or a ms-msdt: handler. A url that writes its scheme itself, as https://jira.example.com/browse/{0} does, may open any scheme: you chose it. Hint mode still offers such a match, to copy, and opens nothing.
  • A group is percent-encoded only where a URL cannot hold a character: spaces, control characters and "#<>[\]^`{|}. / ? & = + @ : % pass through, so a group placed in a query can add parameters, and one placed before the host can change it. Write the scheme and the host in the template, groups after them.
  • An entry named like a built-in (url, filepath, githash, ipv4, ipv6) changes only the keys it gives, and may leave out its regex. A built-in takes no url; a url given to one is reported and ignored.
profiles:
  main:
    hint_patterns:
      - name: filepath
        clickable: false   # stop underlining paths; hint mode still offers them

A regex that overrides filepath names the path with capture group 1, and its location with groups 2 and 3 (:line[:column]) and 4 and 5 ((line[,column])).

Patterns are ECMAScript regular expressions, with these limits:

  • Back-references (\1 to \9) are not supported: a pattern using one is reported when the configuration is loaded and disabled, on every platform.
  • A non-ASCII character inside […] matches byte by byte, not as one character; such a pattern is reported with a warning.
  • On Linux, Contour is built with libstdc++, whose matcher runs breadth-first: where one alternative's match is a prefix of another's at the same place, as in foo|foobar, it takes the longer one, and lazy quantifiers may stop elsewhere, where macOS (libc++) and Windows take the first alternative ECMAScript names. Write patterns whose result does not depend on which alternative or which repetition count wins.
  • A clickable pattern must not match the empty string; one that can is disabled.

docs.title: The settings page
docs.text: Under Profiles, the Links group holds Show links (hyperlink_decoration.mode), Normal style, Hover style, Open files with (file_opener.command) and Open in (file_opener.placement). The Links: opening and patterns section names the gesture that opens links and lists the patterns: the built-ins, whose Clickable switch you can change, and the profile's own, which you can add, edit and remove. Below the list, a sample text shows what the selected pattern finds, checked and matched as the terminal does; a problem with a pattern is shown under it.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Detection stays off the path the terminal reads output on:

  • The output is scanned once it has gone quiet, at most once a second under continuous output, on a background thread. The parser never runs a pattern.
  • Whether a path exists is checked on a thread of its own, so a slow network mount delays the underlines and nothing else.

docs.title: Path Handling in Configuration
docs.text: Contour supports special syntax in configuration file paths to make configs portable across machines and platforms.

docs.title: Tilde Expansion
docs.text:
Use ~ at the start of a path to refer to the user's home directory:

profiles:
  main:
    shell:
      initial_working_directory: ~/workspace

On Linux/macOS this expands to e.g. /home/user/workspace, on Windows to C:\Users\user\workspace.

docs.title: Environment Variable Expansion
docs.text:
Use ${VAR_NAME} to reference environment variables:

color_schemes:
  default:
    background_image:
      path: '${HOME}/Pictures/terminal-bg.png'

This resolves ${HOME} to its value at config load time.

docs.title: Multiple Variables
docs.text:
You can use several variables in the same value:

profiles:
  main:
    shell:
      program: '${MY_SHELL_DIR}/${MY_SHELL_NAME}'

docs.title: Combining with Tilde
docs.text:
Environment variables are expanded before tilde resolution, so both syntaxes compose correctly:

profiles:
  main:
    shell:
      initial_working_directory: '~/${PROJECT_DIR}'

This first resolves ${PROJECT_DIR} (e.g. to workspace), then resolves ~ to the home directory, yielding /home/user/workspace.

docs.title: Where Expansion Applies
docs.text:
The following configuration values support both ~ and ${VAR} expansion:

Configuration value Example background_image.path '${HOME}/Pictures/bg.png' shell.program '${MY_SHELL}' shell.arguments (each entry) '--config=${XDG_CONFIG_HOME}/shell.conf' shell.initial_working_directory '~/${PROJECT_DIR}' Any std::filesystem::path config entry General file path values

docs.title: Cross-Platform Configuration
docs.text:
A primary motivation for environment variable expansion is writing configs that work on multiple operating systems without modification:

# Works on both Linux and Windows — no hardcoded paths
color_schemes:
  default:
    background_image:
      path: '${HOME}/Pictures/terminal-bg.png'

profiles:
  main:
    shell:
      initial_working_directory: '${HOME}/projects'

docs.title: Edge Cases
docs.text:
• Undefined variables expand to an empty string and a warning is logged.
  • Malformed markers like ${UNCLOSED (missing closing }) pass through the string unchanged — no partial substitution occurs.
  • No markers — strings without any ${...} syntax are passed through unchanged.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
All profiles inside configuration files share parent node profiles. To create profile you need to specify child node 

profiles:
    main:
    #default configuration
    profile_for_windows:
    # windows specific entries
    profile_for_macos:
    # macos specific entries

docs.title: shell
docs.text:
configuration section allows you to specify the process to be started inside the terminal. It provides flexibility to override the default login shell and supports logging in to a remote host. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    shell: "/bin/bash"
    arguments: ["some", "optional", "arguments", "for", "the", "shell"]
arguments (optional) Allows you to provide additional command-line arguments to the shell executable. These arguments will be passed to the shell when it is started inside the terminal.

docs.title: ssh
docs.text:
With this key, you can bypass local PTY and process execution and directly connect via TCP/IP to a remote SSH server.

profiles:
  profile_name:
    ssh:
      host: remote-server.example.com
      port: 22
      user: "CustomUserName"
      private_key: "path/to/key"
      public_key: "path/to/key.pub"
      known_hosts: "~/.ssh/known_hosts"
      forward_agent: false

Note, only host option is required. Everything else is defaulted. Keep in mind, that the user's ~/.ssh/config will be parsed with respect to the supported options above. These values can be overridden in the local Contour configuration as follows:

ssh.host SSH server to establish the connection to. ssh.port SSH port (defaults to 22). Only specify this value if it is deviating from the default value 22. ssh.private_key Path to private key to use for key based authentication. ssh.public_key Path to public key that belongs to the private key. When using key based authentication, it depends on the underlying backend, if the public key is also required. OpenSSL for example does not require it. ssh.known_hosts Path to known_hosts file. This defaults to and usually is located in ~/.ssh/known_hosts. ssh.forward_agent Boolean, indicating whether or not the local SSH auth agent should be requested to be forwarded. Note: this is currently not working due to an issue related to the underlying library being used, but is hopefully resolved soon.

Note, custom environment variables may be passed as well, when connecting to an SSH server using this builtin-feature. Mind, that the SSH server is not required to accept all environment variables.

If an OpenSSH server is used, have a look at the AcceptEnv configuration setting in the sshd_config configuration file on the remote SSH server, to configure what environment variables are permitted to be sent.

docs.title: escape_sandbox
docs.text:
option in the configuration file allows you to control the sandboxing behavior when the terminal is executed from within Flatpak. This configuration is relevant only if the terminal is running in a Flatpak environment. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    escape_sandbox: true

docs.title: copy_last_mark_range_offset
docs.text:
configuration option is an advanced setting that is useful when using the CopyPreviousMarkRange feature with multiline prompts. It allows you to specify an offset value that is added to the current cursor's line number minus 1 (i.e., the line above the current cursor). 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    copy_last_mark_range_offset: 0

docs.title: copy_command_preserve_multiline
docs.text: Set copy_command_preserve_multiline: true to preserve internal line breaks and tabs when using Copy Command. The default is false, which keeps single-line copying. CR/CRLF are normalized to LF; trailing whitespace is removed. Unsafe controls are filtered in both modes. Pasting multiline text into a destination without bracketed paste may execute commands immediately.

docs.title: show_title_bar
docs.text:
configuration option determines whether or not the title bar will be shown when the terminal profile is activated. On Linux, false (the default) is Contour's own header bar with the desktop's window buttons; with true the window manager draws the frame (KWin, Mutter, or a tiling WM's border or none), and the header bar keeps the tabs, new tab, search and menu: only the window buttons move out of it. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    show_title_bar: true
With false, the header bar rounds the window's top corners while it is neither maximised nor full screen. Outside the corners the window is transparent, which takes a compositor: on X11 without one, the corners show black. Run a compositor there, or set show_title_bar: true.

docs.title: window_shadow
docs.text:
configuration option sets how far the drop shadow around a frameless window reaches. One of None, Small, Medium, Large or VeryLarge — the same names and sizes Breeze offers, so a Contour window matches the rest of a Plasma desktop. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    window_shadow: Large
Only KWin can act on this. With show_title_bar set to true the window manager draws its own shadow along with its decoration, and no other Wayland compositor or X11 window manager offers a way for an undecorated window to publish one — so everywhere else, every value behaves as None. Windows and macOS draw a system shadow of their own instead.

docs.title: dim_unfocused
docs.text:
configuration option dims a pane while it is not the focused one (an inactive pane of a split, or any pane of an unfocused window) by blending it toward its own background color. The value is the blend amount between 0.0 (dimming disabled; the classic default) and 1.0 (fully blended to the background). The native2026 default is 0.15. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    dim_unfocused: 0.3

docs.title: size_indicator_on_resize
docs.text:
configuration option determines whether or not the size indicator will be shown when terminal will resized. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    size_indicator_on_resize: true

docs.title: fullscreen
docs.text:
configuration option determines whether the terminal's screen should be put into fullscreen mode when the terminal profile is activated. Fullscreen mode expands the terminal window to occupy the entire screen, providing a distraction-free environment for your terminal sessions. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    fullscreen: false

docs.title: maximized
docs.text: configuration option determines whether the terminal window should be maximized when the specified profile is activated. Maximizing a window expands it to fill the entire available space on the screen, excluding the taskbar or other system elements.

docs.title: insert_after_yank
docs.text:
This configuration option determines whether the terminal should automatically switch from normal mode to insert mode after executing a yank command. When enabled, the terminal will enter insert mode, allowing for immediate text input. If disabled, the terminal will remain in normal mode, maintaining command functionality. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    insert_after_yank: false

docs.title: bell
docs.text:
Configuration section permits tuning the behavior of the terminal bell.

profiles:
  profile_name:
    bell:
      sound: "default"
      alert: false
sound This option determines the sound of BEL (also  or 0x07) to off or default or sound generated by a file located at path. alert This option determines whether or not a window alert will be raised each time a bell is ringed. Useful for tiling window managers like i3 or sway.

docs.title: notify_on_command_finish
docs.text:
configuration tells you when a command you are not watching finishes: a desktop notification, the bell, or both. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    notify_on_command_finish:
      when: unfocused
      min_duration: 10
      outcome: any
      action: notify
      clear_on: focus
Commands are known from the OSC 133 marks shell integration emits; a shell without it reports none, so nothing is notified. A notification reads ✓ make finished, ✗ make failed (exit 2) or ✗ make killed (SIGSEGV), with how long it took, where it ran and the tab's name below. A newer finish in the same pane replaces the older notification, and clicking it brings the pane forward where the desktop reports clicks. when never, unfocused (unless it is the focused pane of the active window), hidden (only while the pane is off screen: another tab is active, a sibling pane is zoomed, or the window is minimised) or always. min_duration Commands that ran for fewer seconds than this never notify. outcome any, or failure for commands that exited non-zero or died of a signal. action notify (a desktop notification), bell (the profile's bell sound and window alert) or notify_bell (both). clear_on When a notification still on screen is withdrawn: focus (the pane is focused), next (the pane's next command starts) or never. Only a desktop notification can be withdrawn, which is what Linux shows; on Windows and macOS the notice is a tray message, which stays until it times out whatever clear_on says.

docs.title: terminal_id
docs.text:
configuration option allows you to specify the terminal type that will be advertised by the terminal emulator. The terminal type indicates the set of capabilities and features that the terminal supports, enabling compatibility with different applications and systems.

profiles:
  profile_name:
    terminal_id: VT525

docs.title: pixel_reporting
docs.text:
Selects the unit Contour reports pixel sizes to applications in, via TIOCGWINSZ (ws_xpixel/ws_ypixel), CSI 14 t, CSI 16 t and XTSMGRAPHICS.

Applications derive the cell size by dividing a reported extent by the grid and size image canvases from it, so on a scaled display this decides how large an image an application draws into a given area.

A report is only usable if that division is exact, and Contour's cell is the font's advance in device pixels — at a fractional scale it has no exact logical counterpart (17 / 1.75 = 9.714). Valid values (ignore-case):

  • Device — report device pixels. The division is exact, so an image lands 1:1 on the display's own pixels and is never resampled — gapless and sharp. The cost is that the application draws as many times more pixels per axis as the display is scaled by. This is the default.
  • Logical — report logical pixels, matching the canvas size a terminal whose cell is integral in logical pixels (Konsole, for one) would report, which is useful when comparing the two on equal terms. Exact only where the scale divides both cell axes evenly (an unscaled display, or a 20x40 cell at scale 2). Otherwise each axis is floored on its own, which changes the cell's aspect ratio, and a full-page image is letterboxed by the difference — a few percent of unpainted space down one side.

On an unscaled display the two are identical.

docs.title: frozen_modes
docs.text: fmt formatted doc 0

docs.title: smooth_line_scrolling
docs.text:
Defines the number of milliseconds to wait before actually executing the LF (linefeed) control code in case DEC mode DECSCLM is enabled. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    slow_scrolling_time: 0

docs.title: smooth_scrolling
docs.text:
Enables pixel-based smooth scrolling. When enabled, scrolling will be performed in pixel increments rather than jumping by full lines, providing a smoother visual experience similar to GNOME Terminal/VTE. This applies to mouse wheel and trackpad scrolling on the primary screen. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    smooth_scrolling: true

docs.title: momentum_scrolling
docs.text:
Enables momentum (inertia) scrolling for touchpad gestures. When enabled, lifting your finger from the touchpad after a swipe will cause the terminal to continue scrolling with decelerating velocity, mimicking the natural scrolling behaviour of macOS and iOS. This governs touchpad finger-lift inertia only. Mouse-wheel smoothness is controlled by smooth_scrolling, which glides discrete wheel notches with the same physics. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    momentum_scrolling: true

docs.title: terminal_size
docs.text:
configuration option allows you to specify the initial size of the terminal window in terms of the number of columns and lines. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    terminal_size:
      columns: 80
      lines: 25
columns This option specifies the number of columns (characters) to be displayed in the terminal window. In the provided example, the value is set to 80. lines This option specifies the number of lines to be displayed in the terminal window. In the provided example, the value is set to 25.

docs.title: margins
docs.text:
Enforces a horizontal and vertical margin to respect on both sides of the terminal. This is particularly useful on operating systems (like MacOS) that draw the border frame into the main widgets space, or simply to create some artificial space to improve the user's focus.

profiles:
  profile_name:
    margins:
      horizontal: 5
      vertical: 0

docs.title: history
docs.text:
configuration allows you to customize the behavior and settings related to the terminal's history, including the number of preserved lines, auto-scrolling, and scroll events. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    history:
      limit: 1000
      hard_limit: 2000
      auto_scroll_on_update: false
      scroll_multiplier: 3
limit This option specifies the number of lines to preserve in the terminal's history. A value of -1 indicates unlimited history, meaning that all lines are preserved. In the provided example, the limit is set to 1000. hard_limit The upper bound on the scrollback, and what makes eviction command-aware. Anything above limit is headroom: the buffer is allowed to grow into it, and when it fills, whole (prompt, output) blocks are dropped from the top rather than a slice taken wherever limit fell. The oldest line kept is then a prompt with its command's output intact, instead of an orphaned tail. Block boundaries come from the OSC 133 marks a shell with shell integration emits, so with no such shell -- or for a single command whose output is larger than the whole headroom -- there is no boundary to honour and the buffer simply bounds at this value, evicting line by line as before. Values below limit are raised to it, which disables the feature; -1 means infinite, and an infinite limit makes this infinite too since nothing is ever evicted. Defaults to limit. auto_scroll_on_update This boolean option determines whether new output brings a view scrolled back into the history down to the bottom. Only output that adds lines counts: a prompt, a progress bar or a clock repainted in place does not, so a shell that redraws its prompt on a timer leaves the view where you put it. If set to false, the terminal maintains the current scroll position until you type, which always brings the view down. Defaults to false. scroll_multiplier This option defines the number of lines to scroll when the ScrollUp or ScrollDown events occur. By default, scrolling up or down moves three lines at a time. You can adjust this value as needed. In the provided example, scroll_multiplier is set to 3.

docs.title: scrollbar
docs.text:
configuration allows you to customize the appearance and behavior of the visual scrollbar in the terminal. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    scrollbar:
      position: Right
      mode: system
      hide_in_alt_screen: true
      marks: [failures, commands, running, user_marks, search_matches]
position This option specifies the position of the scrollbar in the terminal window. It can be set to one of the following values: Left, Right, Hidden. The default is Right for new configurations; a contour.yml written by an earlier version keeps Hidden, so set position: Right there to see the marks. Hidden turns the scrollbar, and with it the command marks, off. The scrollbar floats over the edge of the terminal, takes no column from it, and is shown only while there is history to scroll through. mode system follows the operating system's scroll bar setting; overlay hides the bar at the bottom of the scrollback, unless a failed or running command or a user mark is above the view; always shows it while there is scrollback. Defaults to system; a configuration written before the 2026 defaults keeps always. Where the system publishes no setting, system means overlay. hide_in_alt_screen This boolean option determines whether the scrollbar should be hidden when the terminal is in the alternate screen mode. If set to true, the scrollbar will be hidden when the terminal switches to the alternate screen. If set to false, the scrollbar will remain visible even in the alternate screen mode. marks Which marks the scrollbar shows as thin ticks; clicking a tick scrolls its line to the top of the view, opening it if it is folded. A list of failures (commands that exited with an error), commands (every command that did not fail; running is listed on its own), running (commands still running, drawn as hollow ticks), user_marks (lines marked with mm in vi normal mode) and search_matches (the rows the active search matches, in yellow); [] shows none. The default is [failures, running, search_matches], or, in a configuration written before the 2026 defaults, [failures, commands, running, user_marks]. Command ticks need the OSC 133 marks a shell with shell integration emits -- or, without one, systemd's OSC 3008 contexts. Ticks are hidden whenever the scrollbar is.

docs.title: sticky_header
docs.text:
configuration pins the command line of the block you are reading over the top row of the terminal, once that command has scrolled out of view above its own output. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    sticky_header:
      mode: scrolled
      show_evicted: true
mode When the header appears: never, scrolled (only while the viewport is scrolled back into history; the default) or always (also while following live output, so a long build keeps its command in view). It needs prompt marks (OSC 133;A), never appears on the alternate screen, shows the command's exit status and duration on its right, and a click on it scrolls to the command. A shell that marks only where its commands run (;C, ;D) gets no header. show_evicted Whether the header still names a command whose own line has already been dropped from the scrollback, as ⋯ <command> — earlier output evicted, so a long output does not lose its header when its prompt is evicted. At the very top of the scrollback it shows whatever mode says (even never); anywhere else it shows wherever mode would show a header.

docs.title: mouse
docs.text:
configuration allows you to control the behavior of the mouse in the terminal. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    mouse:
      hide_while_typing: true
hide_while_typing This boolean option determines whether the mouse cursor should be hidden while typing in the terminal. When set to true, the mouse cursor will be hidden when you start typing. When set to false, the mouse cursor will remain visible while typing.

docs.title: permissions
docs.text:
configuration allows you to control the access permissions for specific VT sequences in the terminal. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    permissions:
      change_font: ask
      capture_buffer: ask
      display_host_writable_statusline: ask
change_font This option determines the access permission for changing the font using the VT sequence OSC 50 ; Pt ST. The possible values are: allow, deny, ask. capture_buffer This option determines the access permission for capturing the screen buffer using the VT sequence CSI > Pm ; Ps ; Pc ST. The response can be read from stdin as the sequence OSC 314 ; <screen capture> ST. The possible values are: allow, deny, ask. display_host_writable_statusline This option determines the access permission for displaying the "Host Writable Statusline" programmatically using the VT sequence DECSSDT 2. The possible values are: allow, deny, ask.

docs.title: input_method_editor
docs.text: fmt formatted doc true

docs.title: input_method_editor_style
docs.text:
How text an input method is composing is drawn, at the cursor, or to its left when it would not fit.

Valid values are: - inline - in the terminal's default colours with a thin underline, as it will read once committed - highlighted - in the colour scheme's input_method_editor colours, bold and underlined

profiles:
  profile_name:
    input_method_editor_style: inline

docs.title: highlight_double_clicked_word
docs.text:
configuration option enables the highlighting of a word and its matches when double-clicked on the primary screen in the terminal. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    highlight_word_and_matches_on_double_click: true
change_font When this option is enabled (true), the following behavior occurs: - Double-clicking on a word in the primary screen will select and highlight the double-clicked word. - Additionally, all other occurrences of the same word will also be highlighted without being selected. - This feature is implemented by initiating a search for the double-clicked word. - You can use the FocusNextSearchMatch and FocusPreviousSearchMatch actions to navigate to the next or previous occurrence of the same word, even if it is outside the current viewport.

docs.title: fonts
docs.text:
section of the configuration allows you to customize the font settings for the terminal. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    font:
      size: 12
      locator: native
      text_shaping:
        engine: native
      builtin_box_drawing: true
      max_fallback_count: 16
      render_mode: gray
      strict_spacing: false
      regular:
        family: "monospace"
        weight: regular
        slant: normal
        features: []
      emoji: "emoji"
size Specifies the initial font size in pixels. The default value is 12, and 13 on macOS under the native2026 defaults. locator Determines the font locator engine to use for locating font files and font fallback. Possible values are native and mock. native will use the operating-system native font location service (e.g. CoreText on macOS and DirectWrite on Windows), whereas mock is solely used for testing the software (not recommended by end-users) text_shaping.engine Selects the text shaping and font rendering engine. Supported values are native, DirectWrite, CoreText, and OpenShaper. builtin_box_drawing Specifies whether to use built-in textures for pixel-perfect box drawing. If disabled, the font's provided box drawing characters will be used. The default value is true. max_fallback_count Maximum number of fallback fonts per font style. Set to -1 for unlimited, 0 to disable fallbacks entirely. The default value is 16. render_mode Specifies the font render mode, which tells the font rasterizer engine what rendering technique to use. Available modes are lcd, light, gray, color and monochrome. strict_spacing Indicates whether only monospace fonts should be included in the font and font fallback list. The default value is false. regular Defines the regular font style with the following parameters: regular.family Specifies the font family name, such as "monospace", "Courier New", or "Fira Code". regular.weight Specifies the font weight, such as thin, extra_light, light, demilight, book, normal, medium, demibold, bold, extra_bold, black, or extra_black. regular.slant Specifies the font slant, which can be normal, italic, or oblique. regular.features Sets optional font features to be enabled. This is usually a 4-letter code, such as ss01 or ss02. Refer to your font's documentation for supported features. By default, no features are enabled. emoji Specifies the font to be used for displaying Unicode symbols with emoji presentation. The default value is "emoji".

docs.title: draw_bold_text_with_bright_colors
docs.text:
Specifies whether bold text should be rendered in bright colors for indexed colors. If disabled, normal colors will be used for bold text. The default value is false. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
