   draw_bold_text_with_bright_colors: false

docs.title: search_case_sensitivity
docs.text:
Which case policy the find bar opens with.

  • smart (default): the search is case-insensitive until the term contains an uppercase letter, at which point it becomes exact. So error also finds Error, while Error finds only itself. The test is Unicode-aware, so it works for non-Latin scripts too.
  • insensitive: never case-sensitive.
  • sensitive: always case-sensitive.

The find bar's Aa button cycles the same three at any time; this only selects the one it starts from. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    search_case_sensitivity: smart

docs.title: blink_style
docs.text:
Determines the visual style of cell blink animation (SGR attributes 5 and 6).

Valid values are: - classic - abrupt on/off toggle - smooth - continuous cosine-based pulse - linger - like smooth but stays visible longer

profiles:
  profile_name:
    blink_style: smooth

docs.title: screen_transition_style
docs.text:
Determines the visual style of screen transitions between primary and alternate screens.

When switching between primary and alternate screen buffers (e.g. entering/leaving vim, htop), this setting controls whether the transition is instant or animated.

Valid values are: - classic - instant switch (no animation) - fade - smooth fade-out/fade-in (250ms by default; 150ms under the native2026 defaults)

profiles:
  profile_name:
    screen_transition: fade

docs.title: screen_transition_duration
docs.text:
Duration in milliseconds for the screen transition animation.

Only applies when screen_transition is set to fade.

profiles:
  profile_name:
    screen_transition_duration: 250

docs.title: cursor_motion_animation_duration
docs.text:
Duration in milliseconds for the cursor motion animation when the cursor moves between cells.

Set to 0 to disable cursor motion animation (instant jumps).

profiles:
  profile_name:
    cursor_motion_animation_duration: 100

docs.title: mode_insert
docs.text:
section of the configuration allows you to customize the appearance and behavior of the terminal cursor. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
   cursor:
    shape: "bar"
    blinking: false
    blinking_interval: 500
shape Specifies the shape of the cursor. You can choose from the following options: -block: A filled rectangle. -rectangle: Just the outline of a block. -underscore: A line under the text. -bar: The well-known i-Beam cursor. blinking Determines whether the cursor should blink over time. If set to true, the cursor will blink; if set to false, the cursor will remain static. blinking_interval Specifies the blinking interval in milliseconds. This value defines how quickly the cursor alternates between being visible and invisible when blinking is enabled.

docs.title: mode_normal
docs.text:
section in the configuration allows you to customize the appearance and behavior of the cursor specifically in vi-like normal mode. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    normal_mode:
      cursor:
        shape: block
        blinking: false
        blinking_interval: 500

docs.title: mode_visual
docs.text:
section in the configuration allows you to customize the appearance and behavior of the cursor specifically in vi-like normal mode. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    visual_mode:
      cursor:
        shape: block
        blinking: false
        blinking_interval: 500

docs.title: highlight_timeout
docs.text:
option in the configuration determines the duration in milliseconds for which the yank highlight is shown in vi mode. After yanking (copying) text in vi mode, the yanked text is typically highlighted momentarily to provide visual feedback. This configuration option allows you to specify the duration of this highlight. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    vi_mode_highlight_timeout: 300

docs.title: modal_cursor_scroll_off
docs.text:
option in the configuration sets the scrolloff value for cursor movements in normal and visual (block) modes. The scrolloff value determines the minimum number of lines to keep visible above and below the cursor when scrolling. In other words, it controls the amount of margin or padding around the cursor during scrolling operations. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    vi_mode_scrolloff: 8

docs.title: status_line
docs.text:
section in the configuration file allows you to customize the behavior and appearance of the status line in the terminal. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    status_line:
      display: none
      position: bottom
      sync_to_window_title: false
display specifies whether the status line should be shown or not. The possible values are none (status line is not shown) and indicator (status line is shown). In the example, the status line is set to none, meaning it will not be displayed initially. position determines the placement of the status line. It can be set to top or bottom. In the example, the status line is set to bottom, indicating that it will appear at the bottom of the terminal window if enabled. sync_to_window_title controls whether the window title should be synchronized with the Host Writable status line. If the Host Writable status line is denied, enabling this option will update the window title accordingly. By default, this option is set to false. extension names an entry of the profile's extensions section that takes the whole status line over. By default it is null, which keeps the template-driven status line.

docs.title: extensions
docs.text:
section in the configuration file declares the WebAssembly extensions that may draw into the status line of a profile. None is configured by default. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    extensions:
      git:    { run_command: ask }
      plasma: { config: { speed: "2" } }
      mine:   { path: ~/wasm/mine.wasm, run_command: deny }
    status_line:
      extension: plasma
      indicator:
        right: "{Extension:git} | {Clock:Bold}"
path is the module to load; a leading ~ is the home directory. Without it, the entry's name selects an extension bundled with Contour. config holds text values the extension reads by key. run_command decides whether the extension may run the commands its manifest declares: allow, deny or ask. The default is ask.

An extension is used by naming it in a status line template as {Extension:name}, or, with status_line.extension, by letting it take the whole line over.

docs.title: background
docs.text:
section in the configuration file allows you to customize the background settings for the terminal. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    background:
      opacity: 1.0
      blur: false
opacity specifies the background opacity to use. The value ranges from 0.0 to 1.0, where 0.0 represents fully transparent and 1.0 represents fully opaque. You can adjust this value to control the transparency level of the terminal's background. blur determines whether the transparent background should be blurred on platforms that support it. Currently, only Windows 10 is supported for background blurring. By default, this option is set to false, meaning no background blurring will be applied.

docs.title: colors
docs.text:
section in the configuration file allows you to specify the colorscheme to use for the terminal. You can use one of the predefined color palettes as a setting for colors entry. List of predefined colorschemes: contour(default colors), monokai, one-light, one-dark, gruvbox-light, gruvbox-dark, solarized-light, solarized-dark, papercolor-light, papercolor-dark.

Under defaults_edition: native2026, colors: default (the stock scheme, unmodified) means the pair contour-dark/contour-light, so the terminal follows the system's dark mode; naming another scheme keeps it fixed, and classic keeps default as one fixed scheme.

profiles:
  profile_name:
    colors: " default "

To make the terminal's color scheme dependant on OS appearance (dark and light mode) settings, you need to specify two color schemes:

profiles:
  profile_name:
    colors:
      dark: "some_dark_scheme_name"
      light: "some_light_scheme_name"

With this, the terminal will use the color scheme as specified in dark when OS dark mode is on, and light's color scheme otherwise.

A configuration reload applies the colors to running sessions too, replacing any a program set there (OSC 4, 10, 11 and friends), just as switching to another profile does.

docs.title: hyperlink_decoration
docs.text:
section in the configuration file allows you to configure the styling and colorization of hyperlinks when they are displayed in the terminal and when they are hovered over by the cursor.

Possible values: underline, dotted-underline, double-underline, curly-underline, dashed-underline, overline, crossed-out, framed, encircle (if implemented)

profiles:
  profile_name:
    hyperlink_decoration:
      mode: always
      normal: dotted-underline
      hover: underline

mode when links are decorated: always, hover (only the one under the pointer), modifier (all of them while the follow modifier is held), never.

docs.title: link_detection
docs.text:
section decides which links are found automatically in printed text, per screen. OSC 8 hyperlinks are always links, and hint mode always offers everything. primary_screen is the normal shell screen; other_screens is the alternate screen (vim, less, htop, ...) and every further page. urls also covers your own patterns, unless they open a file: URL, which follows file_paths.

profiles:
  profile_name:
    link_detection:
      primary_screen:
        urls: true
        file_paths: true
      other_screens:
        urls: true
        file_paths: false

docs.title: file_opener
docs.text:
opens detected file paths on Ctrl+click and with hint mode's Open. command is a command line with {path}, {line} and {column}, split into arguments once, with no shell involved; its program is written out, without a placeholder. placement is detached (default), split or tab. Without a command, a file opens with the system's default application; a directory always opens in the file manager.

profiles:
  profile_name:
    file_opener:
      command: 'code --goto {path}:{line}:{column}'
      placement: detached

docs.title: hint_patterns
docs.text: fmt formatted doc {}

docs.title: hint_scrollback_lines
docs.text: fmt formatted doc 1000

docs.title: wm_class
docs.text: Configuration option defines the class part of the WM_CLASS property of the terminal window. The WM_CLASS property is a standard X11 property used to identify and classify windows by their class and instance.

docs.title: tab_label
docs.text:
Default template for the text shown on each GUI tab. The value is a string with optional {Name} placeholders that are substituted per tab:

  • {TabName} — the tab name the application set with OSC 30, as the indicator status line shows it, or the window title when the application set none (or cleared it). This is the default.
  • {WindowTitle} — the active pane's window title (OSC 0/2), ignoring any tab name.
  • {TabPosition} — the tab's 1-based position in the window.

Literal text outside placeholders is kept verbatim, and an unknown placeholder is echoed verbatim (you see exactly the {Name} you typed). Renaming a tab overrides this default for that tab; the rename text may itself contain the same placeholders (so renaming a tab to {WindowTitle} tracks its title). A tab holding a split is shown as Multiple panes.

docs.title: tab_color
docs.text: Default tab color as '#RRGGBB', or null for no profile color. Layout, user and application colors override it. Split tabs keep the color of the profile that created the tab.

docs.title: option_as_alt
docs.text:
section tells Contour which Option keys act as Alt (Meta) on macOS: off, left, right or both. The other Option key keeps typing accents like é and ü. true and false are still read, as both and off. This value is ignored on other platforms. 

profiles:
  profile_name:
    option_as_alt: left

docs.title: The Settings Window
docs.text:
Settings opens in a window of its own, one per application, from Settings… in the Contour menu (⌘+, on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+, elsewhere), from the command palette, or with the OpenConfiguration binding. Asking for it again brings the open window forward, and it reopens on the page it was left on.

The sidebar lists five sections, then your profiles, then Edit contour.yml…, which opens the file in your editor. A search field above them finds a row by its label, then its help text, then its key, in any case.

Section What it holds General Windows, the command palette, and the advanced global options such as the rendering GPU. Appearance Window chrome and the tab bar. Keyboard Key bindings, as a list. Shell Integration What shell integration draws: the gutter, command blocks and folding. Profiles One page per profile: colors, window, text, scrolling, behaviour, cursor, bell, background, links, status line and more.

A profile's page has a live preview at its top: a small terminal that shows the profile's font, size and colors, and follows every change before it is written. Colors, Links and Status Line open as pages of their own from the profile, and the Status Line fields are on both the profile's page and the Status Line page.

docs.title: Every change applies at once
docs.text:
There is no Apply or Save button. A change takes effect in every terminal that uses the profile, in every window, and is written to disk within about 300 ms of the last edit. Revert Changes, at the top right, undoes everything changed since the window opened, and is disabled until something has.

Settings writes only the files it owns: settings.yml for the global options, profiles/<name>.yml for each profile it edits, and colorschemes/<name>.yml for each color scheme. It never writes contour.yml. Each write replaces the whole file at once, so a crash never leaves half of one.

  • A file you edited meanwhile is never overwritten. If an editor saves a profile while Settings has it open, Settings writes nothing, shows the version on disk, and says which file changed. That includes a file saved in a state that does not parse: it stays as you left it until you fix it.
  • Profiles and color schemes defined in contour.yml are read-only. The page says "Defined in contour.yml" and offers Duplicate to Edit, which makes a copy Settings can change.
  • With gui_config_locked: true every control is disabled and nothing is written; a banner says why.
  • A change that cannot be applied (a value the loader would reject, or a folder you cannot write to) is refused with the reason, and the control goes on showing the value in effect.

Names for new profiles and color schemes follow the rules of every system the configuration may travel to, so they cannot contain path separators or .. and, because a configuration directory may be copied to Windows, may not be one of its reserved device names such as con, aux or nul. A profiles/aux.yml or nul.yml you already have on Linux still loads, can be edited and deleted.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text:
The Colors page picks the color scheme (one for both appearances, or one for light and one for dark) from a gallery of every scheme with its eight ANSI colors. New scheme and Duplicate to Edit create a scheme; a scheme made in Settings can be renamed and deleted. Renaming moves every profile that draws with it. A scheme a profile defined in contour.yml draws with cannot be renamed or deleted here, and neither can one that is still in use.

Every color well shows its contrast against the background and says whether it passes, so a scheme whose ink does not read is found while you make it. A scheme file that does not parse is never renamed over: open it and fix it first.

docs.title: Links and Status Line
docs.text: The Links page edits hint_patterns with a preview line that shows what each pattern underlines, as described in Links. The Status Line page edits the indicator status line's segments with a preview of the bar, as described in the indicator status line.

docs.title: Option as Alt on macOS
docs.text: option_as_alt takes off, left, right or both, so that one Option key can type accents (é, ü) while the other acts as Alt. In Settings it is the Use Option as Meta row on the Keyboard group of a profile. true and false in an existing file are still read, as both and off.

docs.title: Command blocks
docs.text:
With shell integration installed, every command you run becomes a command block: the prompt you typed it at and the output it printed. For each block Contour remembers the command line, how it ended, when it started, how long it took and the directory it ran in — for the last 1000 commands by default (command_blocks.max_records), even after their output has scrolled out of the history.

Most of this page is built on those records. Without shell integration — and without OSC 3008, which systemd 258 and later send on their own — there are no command blocks: no block marks in the gutter or on the scrollbar, no sticky header and no finish notifications. Line numbers, timestamps and user marks work either way.

docs.title: The gutter
docs.text:
The strip left of the grid holds up to three columns, each switched on by configuration. Its width depends only on the configuration, never on what is on screen — a gutter that grew would resize the page mid-command. On the alternate screen of a full-screen program such as vim, less or htop it keeps its width and stays empty.

Column Shows Configured by Default Timestamps when each line was first reached gutter.timestamps, gutter.timestamp_format off Line numbers absolute, relative or hybrid numbers gutter.line_numbers, gutter.line_number_width off Block column fold controls, exit status, user marks folding.show_markers, gutter.exit_status, gutter.user_marks on 
gutter:
  exit_status: true
  user_marks: true
  line_numbers: hybrid
  line_number_width: 6
  timestamps: true
  timestamp_format: "%H:%M:%S"

docs.title: The block column
docs.text:
One cell per line, beside the grid, showing the first of these that applies:

Mark Where Meaning boxed minus / boxed plus a prompt line the block's output is shown / collapsed; click to toggle ◆ any other line a user mark (mm in Vi normal mode) │, ┕ the output the extent of the block ▸ a prompt line the command is still running ● a prompt line the command finished without output to fold — or, with folding.show_markers: false, finished at all

A block's marks take the color of how its command ended, from the color scheme's block_status colors: neutral for success, red for a failure, yellow while it runs. With gutter.exit_status: false the column keeps the plain fold-marker color and draws neither ▸ nor ●; with gutter.user_marks: false it draws no ◆. The column is there while any of the three is on.

Hover the block column to see the block's exit code (and the signal that ended it, named by OSC 3008 or by a 128 + n exit status), its duration, start time, directory and command line.

docs.title: Line numbers
docs.text:
gutter.line_numbers works like vim's number and relativenumber:

Value vim Cursor line Other lines off nonu nornu — — absolute nu its number their numbers relative rnu 0 distance from the cursor line hybrid nu rnu its number distance from the cursor line
  • An absolute number counts rows from the first row of the session, including rows that have since left the history, so a row keeps its number while the history scrolls away. Resizing the window re-wraps the lines and renumbers the rows below the top.
  • A relative distance counts the rows you see: a collapsed block counts as one row, exactly as j and k do, so 12k lands on the row labeled 12.
  • The cursor is the Vi-mode cursor while Vi mode is on, and the terminal's cursor otherwise.
  • gutter.line_number_width (3 to 10, default 6) is the column count; a longer number shows its last digits after ….

docs.title: Timestamps
docs.text: gutter.timestamps: true shows beside each line the local time output first reached it. gutter.timestamp_format is a std::format chrono format such as %H:%M:%S (the default) or %H:%M. It must begin with a % conversion, and every character it spells must take exactly one column; a format that cannot be used is reported when the configuration loads, and the default is kept. A line shows its time only where it differs from the line above, so a burst of output does not repeat the same second all the way down. Recording the time costs no memory per line.

docs.title: Folding
docs.text:
A finished command's output can be collapsed to its prompt line (see folding): click its fold control in the block column, or use the ToggleFold, ToggleLastFold, CollapseLastFold, CollapseAllFolds and ExpandAllFolds actions. A collapsed block says how much it hides — 1,234 lines hidden ⌄ — after its prompt; that chip is drawn over the page and is never selected or copied. In Vi normal mode, vim's fold keys work:

Key Action za toggle the block under the cursor zo open it zc close it zM close every block zR open every block

Unlike vim's, these know one fold level only, take no count, and work in normal mode alone; zn, zN and zi do not exist. With folding.enabled: false, za, zc and zM do nothing, while zo and zR still open what is collapsed.

docs.title: The rail, the chip and the block menu
docs.text:
On the native chrome styles each block gets a rail: a thin strip after the line numbers and timestamps, beside the block's rows. It is neutral for a success (a ✓ appears while the pointer is over the block), red with a ✗ for a failure, and the accent colour with a ▸ while the command runs. The strip has a fixed width, so the page never changes size when a block starts or ends. The ui_style: terminal row keeps the block column described above.

  • The chip. Right of a finished command's prompt, in cells that are blank, a small pill says how it went — Failed · exit 1 · 0.0 s — and a running command's pill ticks. The pill is placed only where it covers nothing: a prompt with an RPROMPT keeps it, and a prompt filling the whole row shows the rail's mark alone, with the details in the block menu and read out by screen readers. A folded block's chip says 80 lines hidden ⌄; clicking it expands the block.
  • The menu. A ⋯ button beside the block, or a right-click on it, opens a native menu whose header names the command and how it ended, above Copy Output, Copy Command, Rerun, Open in Pager and Collapse Output. The block's tooltip is gone; the header carries what it said.
  • Keyboard. Cmd+Up and Cmd+Down (macOS) step through the blocks and announce each one; Shift+Cmd+Up and Shift+Cmd+Down also select its output. Ctrl+Enter or Shift+F10 opens the focused block's menu, Enter toggles its fold, Escape leaves the block, and typing reaches the shell again. The actions are FocusPreviousCommand, FocusNextCommand, SelectPreviousCommandOutput, SelectNextCommandOutput, OpenBlockMenu, ClearCommandBlockFocus and ToggleCommandFold, and the keys are free to rebind; while a block holds the focus the input mode BlockFocus is on.
  • Ending a session with a command still running closes its block as abandoned: no ▸, no tick and no finish notification stay behind, and a restarted pane starts with no blocks.

docs.title: Scrollbar marks
docs.text:
The scrollbar marks where commands are, so a failure far up the history is one glance — and one click — away. Clicking a mark scrolls its line to the top, opening its block if that was collapsed. Marks that fall on the same pixel merge, the most important winning: a failure, then a running command, then a user mark, then any other command. A failure is a solid tick, a running command a hollow one, and a search match (search_matches) a yellow one. A command's mark takes its block_status color.

profiles:
  main:
    scrollbar:
      marks: [failures, commands, user_marks, running, search_matches]   # [] turns the marks off

The scrollbar is shown on the right by default, so the marks are there from the start. It floats over the edge of the terminal without taking a column away, and appears only once there is history to scroll through.

That default applies to new configurations. Contour writes out its full default configuration on first run, so a contour.yml written by an earlier version still says position: Hidden and shows neither the scrollbar nor its marks. Set position: Right to see them, or pick right for Scrollbar position on the settings page:

profiles:
  main:
    scrollbar:
      position: Right      # Left | Right (the default) | Hidden

The marks hide whenever the scrollbar does: on the alternate screen (hide_in_alt_screen, on by default), and with position: Hidden, or hidden on the settings page.

docs.title: Sticky command header
docs.text:
Scrolled back into a long output, the command that produced it stays pinned above it — in the pane header of a split, in the title band of a single pane, and in the grid's own band under show_title_bar: true — with its exit status and duration — or running 12s while it runs. Click the header to jump to the command.

profiles:
  main:
    sticky_header:
      mode: scrolled       # never | scrolled | always
      show_evicted: true
  • scrolled (the default) shows the header only while you are scrolled back into the history; always also shows it while following live output, so a running make stays labeled above its own output; never turns it off. It never shows on the alternate screen.
  • The header needs prompt marks (OSC 133 ; A): a shell that marks only where its commands run gets none.
  • When a command's own line has already been evicted from the history, the header names the command instead — ⋯ make -j8 — earlier output evicted — so its remaining output still says where it came from. It does so wherever the header would show, and at the very top of the history even with mode: never; show_evicted: false turns it off.

The header is drawn over the page: selection, copying and screen readers see only the page. Its colors: sticky_header.

docs.title: Acting on a block
Finish notifications
docs.text:
When a command that took a while finishes somewhere you are not looking, Contour posts a desktop notification — ✓ make finished, ✗ make failed (exit 2) or ✗ make killed (SIGSEGV) — with how long it took, where it ran and which tab it is in. Clicking it brings that pane forward where the desktop reports clicks, and a newer notification from the same pane replaces the older one.

profiles:
  main:
    notify_on_command_finish:
      when: unfocused      # never | unfocused | hidden | always
      min_duration: 10     # seconds; quicker commands never notify
      outcome: any         # any | failure
      action: notify       # notify | bell | notify_bell
      clear_on: focus      # focus | next | never
Key Meaning when unfocused: unless the pane is the focused one of the active window (the default); hidden: only while the pane is off screen (another tab, a zoomed sibling, a minimized window); always; never min_duration commands quicker than this many seconds never notify (default 10) outcome notify for any command, or only for a failure (a non-zero exit or a signal) action a desktop notification (notify), the profile's bell (bell), or both (notify_bell) clear_on withdraw the notification when you focus the pane (focus), when the next command there starts (next), or never. Only a desktop notification can be withdrawn (Linux); a tray message elsewhere stays until it times out

It is on by default because the case it serves — a build in a background tab — is exactly when nobody thinks to turn it on; the 10-second floor keeps ordinary commands quiet.

docs.title: User marks
docs.text: mm in Vi normal mode marks the cursor line, and clears the mark again. A user mark is drawn as ◆ in the gutter and as a tick on the scrollbar, and [m / ]m jump between marks of both kinds. Unlike a prompt, it never starts a command block: folding and block-wise history eviction ignore it. See Line marks.

docs.title: Daemon sessions
docs.text: All of this works in a contour client session attached to a daemon: the daemon sends the block records along with the screen. Reattaching does not replay notifications for commands that finished while you were away. OpenCommandOutput opens no pane there — the pane would run on the daemon's side, which never sees the file — so bind it with placement: detached instead.

docs.title: Restored sessions
docs.text: When the daemon brings a workspace back after a restart, each pane's history comes back above a dimmed "Restored · session ended hh:mm" row, which names the day too when it is not today. A command that was still running when the snapshot was taken is shown as abandoned: its chip stops counting, since the program it belonged to is gone. The first window to attach also shows one toast, such as "Restored 2 windows, 7 tabs".

docs.title: Installing shell integration
docs.text:
Contour offers to turn shell integration on when a bash, zsh or fish session needs it. After you have entered three commands in a pane whose shell writes no prompt marks, a card appears in the pane's bottom rows: Turn on command blocks, with Install and Not Now. Install shows the one line it would add to the shell's startup file (~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile on macOS, or ~/.config/fish/config.fish) and nothing is written yet. Add Line appends it and says so in a toast; new sessions of that shell then show command blocks. Cancel hides the card for this run, and Not Now is remembered for that shell, in gui-state.yml beside contour.yml.

The line runs contour generate integration shell <shell> from the binary that is running, and only in a shell Contour started (TERM_PROGRAM is contour). Contour only ever appends: it never rewrites or replaces the file, a file that is a symlink is appended through, and the line is not added twice. It adds nothing when Contour runs as root, when the file changed while it was being read, or when an earlier append was cut short and left half a Contour line at the end of the file: delete that line, then install again. The card is not offered in a window attached to another host.

Shell Integration on the settings page starts with an Install group: one row per shell, saying Installed in ~/.zshrc, Not installed or why the file cannot be read. Install… asks the same question, with the same line, and adds it the same way, also for a shell you declined at the card. A row whose file ends in a cut-short Contour line shows that exact line to delete.

docs.title: Settings page
docs.text:
Every setting above but the key bindings can also be changed on the settings page:

  • Global settings has the rows named Gutter: …, Command blocks: … and Folding: … (configuration). Each saves the one key it edits to settings.yml, and the rest of its section keeps what contour.yml says. Command blocks: pager format picks sgr or plain. Command blocks: pager cannot be left blank; Reset goes back to the pager contour.yml names.
  • A profile's page has a Command blocks group (profiles): the three Scrollbar marks: … rows, Sticky command header, Name evicted commands, Notify on finish and the Notify: … rows. Scrollbar position is under History & scrollbar. A profile defined in contour.yml is read-only there; Save As makes an editable copy.
  • A color scheme's page has the swatches Block status: success, failure and running, Gutter text, and Sticky header: background and separator (colors). A swatch the scheme leaves unset says that it follows the scheme's other colors, and shows the color they give it. Typing a new color pins the swatch, and so does Enter in its field, which keeps the color it shows now; tabbing through the field pins nothing. Each of these swatches that the scheme sets has a ↺ button, which makes it follow the other colors again.
  • Keybindings lists the bindings without editing them: the input_mapping of contour.yml, then the built-in bindings none of its rows takes, such as Ctrl+triple-click and Ctrl+Shift+G, marked built-in. A binding that runs several actions names them all.

When the page refuses a value, a message above the rows says why, and screen readers announce it. The message goes away with the next change that goes through, or when you open another page.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
• Global: gutter, command_blocks, folding
  • Profile: scrollbar, sticky_header, notify_on_command_finish
  • Color scheme: block_status, gutter_text, sticky_header
  • Actions and bindings: Key mapping

docs.title: Drag and drop
docs.text: Contour accepts drops on a pane. What happens depends on what you drag: a pane or a tab moves, files and text are typed into the pane's shell (below).

docs.title: Moving panes and tabs
docs.text: You can pick up any pane, or any tab, and put it anywhere a terminal can live: elsewhere in its tab, in another tab, in another window, in a tab of its own, or in a window of its own. The shells inside keep running through the move. Nothing is restarted and nothing is lost: scrollback, the running program, the cursor, the selection and any search move with the pane, and output keeps arriving while you drag.

docs.title: The two handles
docs.text:
You pick up By a pane its header (the buttons on its right keep their click). The header is shown inline in Comfortable density; in Minimal density it is shown while you hold the reveal modifier. a tab the tab itself, in any window's tab bar.

A tab with a single pane is that pane: dragging it behaves exactly as dragging the pane does, including the swap below. A pane whose header is hidden because the pane is too short to spare the row has no handle of its own; drag its tab instead.

While you drag a pane, a translucent card (its header, with a grip and the pane's name, and its last few lines) follows the pointer, and the pane's place shows a dashed outline reading "name's place", so you can see what will close up behind it. Dragging a tab keeps the tab's own drag image.

docs.title: Where you can drop
docs.text:
Every target works for both handles, unless the table says otherwise.

# Release on What happens T1 the edge band of a pane (the outer 20 % of each side) the dragged pane or tab splits beside, above or below that pane, taking half of it. The same tab, another tab, or another window. T2 the middle of a pane, with a single pane dragged the two panes swap places. T3 the middle of a pane, with a tab of several panes dragged nothing: a whole layout cannot trade places with one pane. No ghost is drawn. T4 hovering a tab in any tab bar for 600 ms that tab becomes the visible tab of its window, with the drag still in your hand, so T1 and T2 then apply to its panes. T5 a tab, released on it (its middle, clear of the gaps) the dragged pane or tab is added to that tab, as a split to the right of the tab's active pane. T6 a gap of a tab bar: between two tabs, before the first, after the last, or in the empty bar the dragged pane or tab becomes a new tab at that place. For a tab this is the reorder, or the move into another window's tab bar. T7 outside every Contour window a new window with the dragged pane or tab as its only tab.

What you will get is drawn before you let go:

  • Over a pane, a ring in the accent colour marks the pane, and a ghost shows the part of it the dragged node would take: the half beside the edge you are nearest (a corner goes to the edge you are proportionally nearer to; a tie goes to left or right), or the whole pane for a swap. A label on the ghost says what happens: Pane → split left, Pane → split right, Pane → split up, Pane → split down or Swap with <pane name>. A dragged tab of several panes says Tab → split left and so on.
  • Over a tab, the tab is outlined in the accent. If hovering would open it, a bar fills along the tab's foot during the 600 ms, and it stays full once the tab has opened.
  • In a gap, a dashed, tab-shaped slot named for what you carry shows where the new tab will stand. Between two tabs, the tabs after the gap move aside to make room for it.
  • Dropping a pane on itself, or on the empty place it left, does nothing, and nothing is drawn. Dropping a pane on the only other pane of its own tab is a legal swap or re-dock. Dropping a tab onto a pane of its own tab does nothing either.

Hover-to-open never moves the wrong thing. It opens only another tab: never the tab you are dragging, never the tab the drag came from, and never a tab of a window that would refuse the drop.

Gaps versus tabs. Each boundary between tabs counts as a gap for 10 px to either side (at most a quarter of a narrow tab), so a gap is easy to aim at and a tab keeps a middle to rest on. The tab strip does not reorder by where you drop along it any more; you reorder by dropping in the gap you want.

docs.title: Out to a new window
docs.text:
Release outside every Contour window (T7) and the pane or tab opens as a window of its own, at the cursor position when you let go, on the screen you released on. On Wayland, which does not tell an application where the pointer is outside its windows, the window opens at the last position the drag was seen inside a Contour window, on that window's screen, and the compositor places it as it places every Wayland window. The platform cannot draw outside Contour's windows, so the drag image alone shows what is happening until you let go.

A tab of several panes behaves as it always has: it tears off into a new window. A pane dragged out of a tab of several panes now does the same, and leaves its place to its sibling.

Press Escape during a drag to cancel it: nothing moves and no window opens, even when the pointer is inside Contour. The same goes for a release inside one of Contour's windows that no target takes.

docs.title: What a move does
docs.text:
• The new split divides the target pane in half, exactly as the ghost showed. In the tab the pane left, its sibling takes over the space. A swap trades the two places, and each place keeps its size.
  • Focus follows the moved pane into its new tab and window, and that window is raised. Zoom is cleared on both the tab it left and the tab it entered.
  • A tab left empty closes, and so does a window left empty, without asking: a move loses no session, and the question exists to protect running sessions. Moving the last pane of the last tab of a window out closes that window; the moved shell keeps running, and Contour does not quit.
  • A screen reader announces the move ("Pane moved", "Pane moved to new tab", "Pane moved to window name", "Panes swapped", "Pane moved to new window").
  • Daemon-hosted layouts are saved as they are after the move, so restoring a workspace brings the new arrangement back.
  • If the shell in the pane you carry exits before you let go, the drop does nothing.

docs.title: Between windows
docs.text:
Where the windows are Moving a pane or tab between them two windows of the same Contour process works, every target above two windows hosted by the same daemon, even when different Contour processes show them (see Persistent sessions) works, every target above a window of another Contour process that shares no daemon with this one refused a window whose daemon is older than this one's pane-move support refused for panes; see below a tmux window (contour client --tmux) refused

A refused target is not silent. The ring turns amber, and a note on the pane says why and names what to do instead. Releasing there does nothing at all: it is accepted as a no-op, so it never tears off a window by accident, and everything stays where it was. The three notes, under the title Can't move a pane here:

  • another process: This window belongs to another Contour process. Run Contour in daemon mode to move panes between any windows.
  • an older daemon: This window's daemon is too old to move panes. Update Contour on the daemon side.
  • tmux: Panes can't be moved into a tmux window yet.

Older daemons. A daemon that predates pane moves keeps serving what it always did: reordering tabs, moving a tab to another window's tab bar, tearing a tab off into a new window, and dropping a tab on a pane of its own window to split it. Dragging a pane, and every tab target that needs more than those, shows the second note above. Nothing is ever half done: a move happens completely or not at all.

docs.title: Dragging files onto a pane
docs.text:
Drop files from your file manager onto a pane, and their paths are typed at the cursor, escaped for the program in the foreground, and not run. A trailing space lets you keep typing.

Foreground program Quoting a known POSIX shell (bash, zsh, fish, sh, dash, ksh, ...) each special character, and spaces, escaped with a backslash PowerShell (pwsh, powershell) single quotes, ' doubled cmd double quotes anything else: Windows, a pane hosted by the daemon, a multiplexer (tmux, screen, zellij), a transport (ssh, mosh, docker exec, su, sudo, wsl), nushell, elvish, vim double quotes, and a name holding any character one of those shells reads as syntax is refused

The text arrives as a paste, so an application that enabled bracketed paste receives it wrapped. Web links are typed the same way as file names, each one a quoted word, so a link a web page chose cannot run anything. Dropping plain text pastes it as text, as Ctrl+V does, except that text with a line break is refused where the program has not enabled bracketed paste: without it each line would run as it arrives, and the page that started the drag chose the text, not you.

Quoting assumes the drop starts a new word. If you have an open quote at the prompt (a " or ' you typed and have not closed), a dropped name can close it, and what follows runs as syntax. Contour cannot see the state of your shell's line editor, so finish or clear the line before you drop a file onto it.

docs.title: What is refused
docs.text:
• A file name holding a control character (a newline, an escape, and the like) or a character that makes the typed text look other than it runs (a text-direction control such as U+200E or U+202E, U+2028, U+2029) refuses the whole drop with "Not inserted: a file name holds a control or text-direction character.", because such a name could run as a command in the shell.
  • Under cmd, a name holding %, " or ! cannot be quoted safely and is refused too.
  • Where the shell is not known, a name holding any of $ ` ; & | < > ( ) ' " \ ! % ^ is refused, and the window says its shell is not known.
  • A name or link starting with - would be read as an option: a local file is typed as ./-name, and a link (which has no path to put ./ in front of) is refused except for a POSIX shell, which gets ./ too.
  • A pane whose program has ended ignores drops.

docs.title: Font Ligatures
docs.text: Contour renders your font ligatures out of the box. If you font supports them, Contour will render them.

docs.title: Git Branch Drawings
docs.text:
Contour implements rendering of git branch characters used by e.g. vim-flog and gitgraph.nvim. Initially introduced to kitty the symbol set was later expanded to support more commit options.

The symbols use codepoints U+F5D0 ... U+F60D.

Note

U+F5D2 ... U+F5D5 are supposed to be fading out symbols but currently are rendered as simple lines.

The symbols may be customized via config options: 

# Controls how git branch drawings are rendered.
# `branch_style` controls style of connecting branches. May be on of `none`,`thin`,`thick`,`double. The default value is `thin`.
# `arc_style` controls style of arcs. May be one of `round`,`ellips`. `arc_style` has effect only if `branch_style` is `thin`. The default value is `round`.
# `merge_commit_style` controls style of merge commits. May be one of `solid`,`bullet`. The default value is `bullet`.

git_drawings:
    branch_style:       thin
    arc_style:          round
    merge_commit_style: bullet

docs.title: Hint Mode
docs.text:
Hint mode lets you quickly act on clickable elements visible in the terminal — URLs, file paths, git commit hashes, IP addresses — using only the keyboard. When activated, Contour scans the visible screen for recognized patterns, overlays a short alphabetic label on each match, and waits for you to type a label to perform an action on that match.

Think of it like Vimium for your terminal.

docs.title: Activating Hint Mode
docs.text: There are two ways to enter hint mode:

docs.title: Via Key Binding (from any mode)
docs.text:
The default key binding activates hint mode for URLs:

input_mapping:
    - { mods: [Control, Shift], key: U, action: HintMode, patterns: url, hint_action: Open }

Press Ctrl+Shift+U to scan for URLs and open the selected one in your browser.

docs.title: Via Vi Normal Mode
docs.text:
When in normal mode, you can use:

  • gh — activate hint mode with Copy action (yank the match to clipboard)
  • gH — activate hint mode with Open action (open the match, e.g. URL in browser)

These commands scan with the profile's patterns: the builtins (URLs, file paths, git hashes, IPs) and your own hint_patterns.

docs.title: Using Hint Mode
docs.text:
Once hint mode is active:

  1. Labels appear — Each detected match gets a short label (a, b, ..., z; or two-character labels aa, ab, ... for more than 26 matches).
  2. Type the label — Type the label characters to select a match. Labels are case-insensitive.
  3. Auto-select — As soon as your typed characters uniquely identify a match, the action is performed automatically.
  4. Cancel — Press Escape to exit hint mode without selecting anything.
  5. Backspace — Press Backspace to undo the last typed label character.

docs.title: Recognized Patterns
docs.text:
Contour ships with the following builtin pattern detectors:

Pattern Examples Description url https://example.com, http://localhost:8080 http, https, ftp, file and mailto URLs filepath /home/user/file.txt, ./src/main.cpp, src/main.cpp:12:5, C:\Users\me\notes.txt, Makefile Absolute, relative, home-relative (~/...) and Windows paths, and bare file names; a :line[:column] or (line[,column]) after one is kept as its location githash a1b2c3d, abc1234567890def1234567890abcdef12345678 7–40 character hex strings (git commit SHAs) ipv4 192.168.1.1, 10.0.0.1:8080 IPv4 addresses, optionally with port ipv6 ::1, fe80::1, 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334 IPv6 addresses

docs.title: Smart File Path Detection
docs.text:
Hint mode and the links Contour underlines in output share one path grammar, which takes bare names and a location printed after a path (main.cpp:42:10). When the terminal knows the current working directory, or the directory a command ran in (via shell integration), file path detection also matches:

  • Bare filenames with extensions — main.cpp, README.md
  • Extensionless files — Makefile, LICENSE, Dockerfile, CHANGELOG
  • Directory names — src, build, docs

These bare names are validated against the filesystem: only entries that actually exist in that directory are shown as hints. This means you can look at ls output, compiler errors, or git status and jump directly to the referenced files.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
The hint_action parameter controls what happens when you select a match:

Action Description Copy Copy the matched text to the system clipboard (default); a path, resolved to its absolute form Open Open the match as Ctrl+click opens it — web URLs in the browser, directories in the file manager, and files (a file:// URL among them) with file_opener at the line they were printed with Paste Paste the matched text into the terminal input CopyAndPaste Copy to clipboard and paste into the terminal Select Enter vi visual mode with the match range pre-selected for manual adjustment

docs.title: Key Bindings
docs.text:
You can create multiple hint mode bindings for different pattern sets and actions:

input_mapping:
    # Open URLs in browser
    - { mods: [Control, Shift], key: U, action: HintMode, patterns: url, hint_action: Open }

    # Copy file paths to clipboard
    - { mods: [Control, Shift], key: F, action: HintMode, patterns: filepath, hint_action: Copy }

    # Copy git hashes to clipboard
    - { mods: [Control, Shift], key: G, action: HintMode, patterns: githash, hint_action: Copy }

    # Scan for all patterns and copy
    - { mods: [Control, Shift], key: H, action: HintMode, patterns: all, hint_action: Copy }

The patterns parameter accepts:

  • A single pattern name: url, filepath, githash, ipv4, ipv6
  • Multiple pattern names separated by |: filepath|githash
  • all or empty: scan for all builtin patterns at once

docs.title: Scope: Reaching Into Scrollback
docs.text:
By default hint mode scans only what is on screen. The scope parameter widens that to the scrollback history:

input_mapping:
    # Scan the visible page (the default — may be omitted)
    - { mods: [Control, Shift], key: U, action: HintMode, patterns: url, hint_action: Open, scope: Visible }

    # Scan the visible page *and* scrollback history
    - { mods: [Control, Shift], key: Y, action: HintMode, patterns: url, hint_action: Open, scope: Scrollback }

Under scope: Scrollback, labels are assigned once when hint mode is activated and then stay put: scrolling reveals the labels on other rows rather than renaming the ones you have already read. So the workflow is: activate, scroll to the output you want, then type its label. A label acts on its match even while it is off screen.

scope: Visible behaves the other way round, because its scan region is the viewport: scrolling re-scans and re-labels.

How much history a Scrollback activation reads is capped per profile, so a very large scrollback does not turn one keystroke into a long scan:

profiles:
  main:
    # Maximum scrollback rows a `scope: Scrollback` activation scans (default: 1000).
    hint_scrollback_lines: 1000

docs.title: Wrapped Lines
docs.text:
A pattern is matched against the logical line, so a URL that the terminal broke across two or more rows because the window was too narrow is still found as a single hint, and selecting it yields the whole URL rather than the fragment on one row. The label sits at the start of the match, and the highlight follows the match across the line break.

A hint is only offered where its label can be drawn. A match that begins above the scanned region — so that its label would be invisible — is not offered, since a label you cannot see is a label you cannot type. A match that begins inside the region and runs past its end is offered, and still yields its complete text.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text:
Hint mode label and match colors are configured in the color scheme section of your configuration:

color_schemes:
    default:
        # Colors for the short alphabetic labels overlaid on matches.
        hint_label:
            foreground: '#000000'
            foreground_alpha: 1.0
            background: '#E5C07B'
            background_alpha: 1.0

        # Colors for the matched text behind the labels.
        hint_match:
            foreground: '#ABB2BF'
            foreground_alpha: 1.0
            background: '#3E4452'
            background_alpha: 0.8

docs.title: Custom Patterns
docs.text:
You can define your own hint patterns in the profile configuration. Each pattern needs a name (used to reference it in key bindings) and a regex (ECMAScript syntax):

profiles:
  main:
    hint_patterns:
      - name: uuid
        regex: '\b[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}\b'
      - name: docker_id
        regex: '\b[0-9a-f]{12,64}\b'

Custom patterns with the same name as a builtin override the builtin definition. You can then reference custom patterns in key bindings just like builtins:

input_mapping:
    - { mods: [Control, Shift], key: I, action: HintMode, patterns: uuid, hint_action: Copy }

Back-references (\1 to \9) are not supported; a pattern using one is reported when the configuration is loaded and disabled.

docs.title: Clickable Patterns
docs.text:
Links in Terminal Output describes the links Contour finds in output, and how they open, in full.

A pattern can also be found in the terminal's output without entering hint mode: with clickable: true its matches are decorated as links are (see hyperlink_decoration) and opened with Ctrl+click. url says what is opened, with {0} standing for the whole match and {1} to {9} for its capture groups. Without url, the match is opened as printed.

Where the printed text chooses the scheme (no url, or a url that does not start with a scheme of its own, such as {0}), a match opens only with a scheme Contour opens in URLs it finds itself: http, https, ftp, mailto or file. Any other is no link: it is not underlined, and hint mode offers it to copy and opens nothing. A url that writes its scheme itself may open any.

Only what a URL cannot hold is percent-encoded as a group is put in: spaces, control characters and "#<>[\]^`{|}. Characters such as / ? & = + @ : % pass through, so a group placed in a query can add parameters, and one placed before the host can change it. Write the scheme and the host in the template itself, as the examples below do, and put groups after them.

profiles:
  main:
    hint_patterns:
      - name: jira
        regex: '\b[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\d+\b'
        clickable: true
        url: 'https://jira.example.com/browse/{0}'
      - name: github_issue
        regex: '\b([\w.-]+)/([\w.-]+)#(\d+)\b'
        clickable: true
        url: 'https://github.com/{1}/{2}/issues/{3}'
      - name: commit
        regex: '\b[0-9a-f]{7,40}\b'
        clickable: true
        url: 'https://github.com/contour-terminal/contour/commit/{0}'

The builtins url and filepath are clickable, and githash, ipv4 and ipv6 are offered in hint mode only. An entry named like a builtin changes only the keys it gives, so it may leave out its regex:

    hint_patterns:
      - name: filepath
        clickable: false   # stop underlining paths; hint mode still offers them

A url template applies to your own patterns only: a builtin opens what it finds, and a url given to one is reported and ignored. So clickable: true on githash, ipv4 or ipv6 alone makes no link, as a bare hash or address names no scheme; to link commits to their page, write a pattern of your own with a url, as commit above does.

A url that names a capture group the regex does not have, such as {2} for a regex with one group, is reported when the configuration is loaded and disables the pattern.

A regex that overrides filepath must say which part of its match is the path: capture group 1 is the path, groups 2 and 3 a :line[:column] printed after it, and groups 4 and 5 a (line[,column]). An override of filepath without a capture group is reported and disabled. Every other pattern's link is its whole match, {0}.

docs.title: Path Resolution
docs.text:
When copying or opening file paths, Contour resolves relative paths to absolute using the directory the command that printed them ran in, as shell integration recorded it, so a cd since then does not change what an earlier command's output names. Outside any command's output, the terminal's current working directory is used. For example, copying a hint for src/main.cpp gives you /home/user/project/src/main.cpp in the clipboard, and opening it passes the full path to your editor or file manager. Ctrl+clicking a path resolves it the same way.

A command that changes directory itself, such as cd build && make, prints paths relative to where it went. The shell reports that directory only at the next prompt, so a path not found where the command started is looked up there too.

Paths printed by a command that ran on another machine (over ssh, in a container) name files there, so they are neither offered as hints nor opened here. That includes the output of an ssh session whose remote shell reports its directory but marks no commands of its own: everything it printed belongs to the local ssh command, and stays refused after you return to the local prompt.

Home-relative paths (~/...) are expanded using the HOME environment variable.

docs.title: Tips and Tricks
docs.text:
• Shell integration matters — Ensure your shell reports the current working directory via OSC 133 for the best file path detection. Without it, only paths containing a / separator are matched.

  • Combine with Vi mode — In normal mode, gh (copy) and gH (open) are quick ways to enter hint mode without reaching for modifier keys.

  • Works with scrollback — Hint mode scans the currently visible viewport. Scroll to the area of interest first, then activate hint mode.

  • Compiler errors — When viewing build output with file paths like src/main.cpp:42:10: error: ..., hint mode detects the file path portion, making it easy to copy or open the referenced file.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Input Modes — Vi-like input modes including normal mode, where gh/gH trigger hint mode
  • Key Mapping — How to customize key bindings
  • Shell Integration — Enables smart bare filename detection

docs.title: Image Support
docs.text:
Contour implements first-class Sixel image support.

Most notably supporting libraries, are notcurses and libsixel.

Also, libsixel does provide a CLI to convert well known image formats (like PNG) to Sixel format and have them printed to the terminal.

docs.title: Input method editor (IME)
docs.text: An input method (or input method editor, commonly abbreviated IME) is an operating system component or program that enables users to generate characters not natively available on their input devices by using sequences of characters (or mouse operations) that are available to them. Using an input method is usually necessary for languages that have more graphemes than there are keys on the keyboard. More info can be found on wikipedia and with more info how to setup it and use here wiki.archlinux

docs.title: Example of emoji input in contour using ibus
docs.text:
List of emoji from unicode

You can insert any unicode character using ibus IME by pressing Ctrl+Shift+u (default) and then insert unicode code for the emoji or other character.

docs.title: Example of input using pinyin via ibus
Input Modes
docs.text: Just like with the power of Vi-like modes in some editors, Contour Terminal comes with so called vi-like modes to empower the advanced user with very fast access to the screen and its history.

docs.title: Select, Yank, Paste
docs.text:
Your browser does not support the video tag.

This little videos shows how to get into normal mode (Ctrl+Shift+Space) and move to the text that is to be yanked (y) into the clipboard. Mind, the clipboard is being pasted with newlines being stripped off (<Shift-p>).

Note how the statusline at the bottom is reflecting the current input mode.

For more information on what motions Contour supports, please refer to its documentation here.

docs.title: Line Marks
docs.text: Ever wanted to jump quickly to the top of the previous prompt? With a little bit of shell integration, you can make the shell tell the terminal which lines in your screen and scrollback buffer to remember.

docs.title: Setting a line mark
docs.text:
This is what a shell integration would do, but you can simply mark lines yourself by trivially writing to stdout, as follows:

printf "\033]133;A\033\\"

This will tell the terminal to remember the line as a jump-target. Being a prompt mark, it also starts a new command block; to mark a line without that, see Bookmarking a line in Vi normal mode.

OSC 133 ; A is the shell-integration sequence for "a new prompt starts here". Contour also accepted a dedicated SETMARK sequence (CSI > M) for this until 0.8.0, when it was removed in favour of this one.

docs.title: Jump via shortcut
docs.text:
Ensure you have a similar configuration set as follows to relatively jump up or down of your marked lines.

input_mapping:
    - { mods: [Control, Alt], key: K, action: ScrollMarkUp,   mode: "~Alt" }
    - { mods: [Control, Alt], key: J, action: ScrollMarkDown, mode: "~Alt" }

docs.title: Jump extension to Vi-like Normal Mode
docs.text:
Use [m and ]m to jump to the next line mark up and down when being in normal input mode.

Please see Input Modes for more information.

docs.title: Bookmarking a line in Vi normal mode
docs.text:
In Vi-like normal mode, mm toggles a user mark on the line the cursor is on. A user mark is a bookmark, not a prompt: [m/]m, the im/am text objects and ScrollMarkUp/ScrollMarkDown visit user marks and prompt marks alike, but a user mark never starts a command block, so it neither splits a fold nor decides where old output is dropped from the scrollback.

A user mark is drawn as ◆ in the gutter and as a tick on the scrollbar; see Command blocks.

docs.title: Line marks as text objects
docs.text:
In Vi-like normal mode, you can span a text object in between two line marks, as follows:

  • vim - visual select within two line marks (excluding marked lines)
  • vam - visual select around two line marks (including marked line)
  • yim - yank within two line marks (excluding marked lines)
  • yam - yank around two line marks (including marked line)

Please see Input Modes for more information.

docs.title: ReGIS Vector Graphics
docs.text:
Contour implements ReGIS (Remote Graphics Instruction Set), DEC's vector-graphics language introduced with the VT330/VT340 terminals. Where Sixel transmits a raster (a grid of pixels), ReGIS transmits drawing instructions — lines, circles, arcs, curves, filled polygons and text — which the terminal rasterises. This makes ReGIS compact and resolution-independent: a circle is a few bytes, not a bitmap.

This page is a practical reference for people who script and program terminals. It matches Contour's implementation; where Contour deviates from the VT340 it is called out explicitly.

Authoritative reference

The behaviour here follows the VT330/VT340 Programmer Reference Manual, Volume 2: Graphics Programming. That manual is the ground truth for ReGIS semantics.

docs.title: Entering and leaving ReGIS
docs.text:
ReGIS is carried inside a DCS (Device Control String):

ESC P p  <ReGIS commands>  ESC \

ESC P (0x1B 0x50) is the DCS introducer, the letter p selects ReGIS, and ESC \ (String Terminator) ends it. An optional numeric parameter before p controls state carry-over:

Introducer Meaning ESC P p or ESC P 0 p Resume: position, colours, write controls and the addressing window carry over from the previous ReGIS string. ESC P 1 p / ESC P 3 p Reset the graphics state and clear the canvas before drawing.

From a shell you can emit ReGIS with printf:

# Draw a diagonal line from the top-left toward the middle of the screen.
printf '\033PpP[100,100]V[400,300]\033\\'

docs.title: Detecting ReGIS support
docs.text:
ReGIS-capable terminals advertise feature 3 in their primary Device Attributes reply. Send CSI c (ESC [ c) and look for ;3 in the response:

printf '\033[c'    # Contour replies e.g. ESC [ ? 65 ; ... ; 3 ; 4 ; ... c   (3 = ReGIS, 4 = Sixel)

You can also query the ReGIS graphics geometry with XTSMGRAPHICS (CSI ? 3 ; 1 S); Contour reports the fixed VT340 addressing area of 800 x 480.

docs.title: The coordinate system
docs.text:
ReGIS addresses an 800 × 480 pixel screen. The origin [0,0] is the top-left corner and Y increases downward, so [799,479] is the bottom-right. Contour rasterises the ReGIS canvas and scales it across the terminal window, drawing it above the text so that painted pixels overlay the cells and untouched areas remain transparent.

Coordinates are written in brackets, [x,y]. Each axis is independent and may be:

Form Meaning [100,50] Absolute position. [+30,-10] Relative to the current position (signed). [100] X only; Y unchanged. [,50] Y only; X unchanged. [] The current position (used by V to plot a dot).

docs.title: Pixel vectors
docs.text:
Outside brackets, a run of the digits 0–7 moves in one of eight compass directions, each step scaled by the pixel-vector multiplier W(M...):

    3   2   1
      \ | /
   4 -- + -- 0
      / | \
    5   6   7

0 = right, 2 = up, 4 = left, 6 = down, and the odd digits are the diagonals. For example V0000 draws a line four pixels to the right.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Every ReGIS command is a single, case-insensitive letter, optionally followed by parenthesised options ( ... ), bracketed coordinates [ ... ], pixel-vector digits, and quoted strings. A ; ends a command. Whitespace is ignored between tokens.

docs.title: P — Position
docs.text:
Moves the graphics cursor without drawing.

printf '\033PpP[400,240]\033\\'     # move to the centre
  • [x,y] or pixel-vector digits move the cursor.
  • (B) / (S) begin a bounded / unbounded position stack, (E) ends it.
  • (W...) applies temporary write controls (see W).

docs.title: V — Vector
docs.text:
Draws straight lines from the current position, honouring the current colour, line pattern and width.

printf '\033PpP[100,100]V[400,100]V[400,300]V[100,300]V[100,100]\033\\'   # a rectangle
  • [x,y] draws a line to that point and moves there.
  • [] plots a single dot at the current position.
  • Pixel-vector digits draw along each step.

docs.title: C — Curve
docs.text:
Circles, arcs and interpolated curves.

printf '\033PpP[400,240]C[500,240]\033\\'      # circle of radius 100, centred at the cursor
  • C[x,y] — a circle whose centre is the current position and whose radius reaches [x,y].
  • C(C)[x,y] — the bracket is the centre; the current position lies on the circumference.
  • C(A<degrees>)[x,y] — an arc; a positive angle sweeps counter-clockwise, negative clockwise.
  • C(S)[...]...(E) — an open interpolated curve through the listed points.
  • C(B)[...]...(E) — a closed interpolated curve (the cursor returns to the start).

docs.title: W — Write controls
docs.text:
Sets the state that governs all drawing. Options combine inside one W( ... ).

Option Effect I<n> / I(<spec>) Foreground colour: a register index, or a colour spec (see Colour). V R C E Writing mode: V overlay (default), R replace, C complement, E erase. P<n> Line pattern 0–9 (see Patterns); P(M<n>) sets the pattern multiplier. M<n> Pixel-vector multiplier (pixels per PV step). L<n> Line width in pixels. N<0/1> Invert (negate) the line pattern. S... Shading (see Shading).

When written inside another command as (W...), the controls apply only to that command.

docs.title: T — Text
docs.text:
Draws text with anti-aliased glyphs. In the GUI, ReGIS text is shaped by the same font engine as normal terminal text; the terminal engine itself ships a self-contained bitmap font as a fallback (headless use, or before a font is configured). An injected interface keeps the terminal engine free of any font-stack dependency.

printf "\033PpP[100,100]T(S2)'Hello, ReGIS'\033\\"
  • 'text' or "text" — the string to draw at the current position.
  • (S<0-16>) — a standard cell size (0 = 9×10, up to 16 = 144×240); (S[w,h]) a custom cell.
  • (M[wf,hf]) — width/height multipliers; (H<n>) a height multiplier.
  • (D<degrees>) — writing direction in 45° steps (0 = rightward, 90 = up).
  • (I<degrees>) — italic slant.

docs.title: S — Screen
docs.text:
Screen-wide operations.

Option Effect (E) Erase the canvas to the background. (A[ul][lr]) Set the addressing window (defaults to [0,0][799,479]). (I<n>) / (I(<spec>)) Background colour. (M<i>(<spec>)...) Program colour registers (the colour map). 
printf '\033PpS(E)S(A[0,0][799,479])\033\\'    # clear and reset the coordinate window

Page selection, scrolling, output scaling, hardcopy and time-delay sub-options are accepted but have no effect in Contour (they describe hardware Contour does not emulate).

docs.title: F — Polygon fill
docs.text:
Fills the region enclosed by a set of vectors or a curve.

printf '\033PpP[300,100]F(V[500,100][400,280])\033\\'   # a filled triangle
  • F(V...) fills the polygon traced by the vector operations (the current position is the first vertex).
  • F(C...) fills a curved region.

docs.title: R — Report
docs.text:
Queries state and sends a reply to the host application.

Request Reply R(P) The graphics cursor position, as [x,y]. R(P(I)) The interactive locator (mouse) position, as <button>[x,y]. Contour reports it immediately rather than blocking. R(E) The last error code (0 = none). R(L) The current alphabet.

docs.title: @ — Macrographs
docs.text:
Stores and replays command strings.

# Define macro A as a box, then invoke it twice at different positions.
printf '\033Pp@:AV[+100,0]V[0,+100]V[-100,0]V[0,-100]@;P[100,100]@AP[300,100]@A\033\\'
  • @:X ... @; defines macro X.
  • @X invokes macro X (expanded recursively; Contour bounds the depth and output size).
  • @. clears all macros.

docs.title: L — Load character set
docs.text: Down-loadable custom character sets are recognised but not rendered in Contour (as in several other ReGIS implementations); text uses the built-in font.

docs.title: Colour
docs.text:
Contour keeps 16 colour registers, initialised to the VT340 default palette. A colour is named in three ways:

  • Register index — W(I5) selects register 5.
  • Named colour — W(I(R)), where D=dark, R=red, G=green, B=blue, C=cyan, Y=yellow, M=magenta, W=white.
  • HLS or RGB spec — W(I(H<0-360>L<0-100>S<0-100>)) for hue/lightness/saturation, or W(I(R<0-100>G<0-100>B<0-100>)). On the DEC hue wheel 0° is blue, 120° red, 180° yellow, 240° green.

Registers are reprogrammed with S(M<index>(<spec>)), e.g. S(M1(H240L50S100)) makes register 1 green.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
W(P<n>) selects one of ten standard line patterns:

n Pattern n Pattern 0 (none) 5 dash-dot-dot 1 solid (default) 6 sparse dot 2 dash 7 asymmetric sparse dot 3 dash-dot 8 sparse dash-dot 4 dot 9 sparse dot-dash

A custom pattern is a bit string, e.g. W(P11110000).

docs.title: Shading
docs.text:
Shading fills the area between a drawn primitive and a reference line:

  • W(S1) turns shading on (reference defaults to the cursor's current Y); W(S0) turns it off.
  • W(S[,Y]) sets a horizontal reference at Y; W(S(X)[X]) a vertical reference at X.
# Shade the area under a line down to y=300.
printf '\033PpW(S[,300])P[100,100]V[400,200]\033\\'

docs.title: Example programs
docs.text:
Contour ships four ReGIS demos under examples/:

  • regis-primitives.cpp — a static showcase of every primitive (lines, circles, arcs, curves, fills, patterns, colours and text). A good visual conformance check.
  • regis-plot2d.cpp — a labelled 2D plot of a mathematical function with axes and a grid.
  • regis-animation.cpp — an animated analog clock, redrawing each frame with S(E) + redraw.
  • regis-plot3d.cpp — an interactive 3D plot of the complex function |z² − 1|; drag with the mouse to rotate it (horizontal = yaw, vertical = pitch), press q to quit.

Build them with the test build enabled and run them inside Contour:

cmake --build --preset clang-release --target regis-primitives regis-plot3d
./out/clang-release/examples/regis-primitives
./out/clang-release/examples/regis-plot3d      # then drag with the mouse

docs.title: Size indicator
docs.text: On resize window with current terminal size will appear

docs.title: Statusline
docs.text: The Statusline in Contour is an implementation of the DEC VT320 statusline feature. We aim to revive this feature as we see great use to it.

docs.title: Indicator Statusline
docs.text:
This is the most obvious and probably most used one. It's the statusline as you may be used to it.

Contour shows relevant contextual information on it, such as:

  • the clock,
  • current VT emulation mode,
  • input mode

and much more, depending on the context.

This line can be actively toggled by the user via configuration, e.g. via:

input_mapping:
    - { mods: [Control, Alt],   key: '.',           action: ToggleStatusLine }

docs.title: Host Programmable Statusline
docs.text:
This statusline can be alternatively displayed and can be written to and fully controlled like the main display.

There are not many applications yet doing so, but there would be a great use to such a feature by any application that has fast output but a rarely updating status line, maybe even tmux or screen could make use of it to trivialize the common use-case.

If you consider playing around with it, have a look at the VT sequences

  • DECSASD - Select Active Status Display
  • DECSSDT - Select Status Display (Line) Type

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
docs/             - Contour documentation and website
cmake/            - CMake helper modules
scripts/          - general development assisting and CI helper scripts
src/              - Contour source code
  contour/        - GUI terminal emulator application (business logic)
  coro/           - C++23 coroutine vocabulary types
  crispy/         - fundamentals library
  net/            - coroutine reactor, sockets and TLS
  text_shaper/    - font location and text shaping & rasterization library
  vtbackend/      - core terminal library
  vthost/         - Qt-free session daemon and both protocol engines
  vtparser/       - VT parser library
  vtpty/          - PTY library
  vtrasterizer/   - frontend independent Terminal rendering library
  vtworkspace/    - Qt-free tab/split-pane tree model
test/             - Contains a set of test scripts.

Listed alphabetically above; the dependency order is crispy → coro → net → text_shaper/vtparser → vtpty → vtbackend → vtrasterizer/vtworkspace → vthost → contour. Lower layers must not depend on higher ones, and the GUI must not reach around vtbackend/ vtworkspace into rendering internals.

The daemon and its protocols are documented separately in Multiplexer & daemon mode, and measuring where the time goes in Profiling with Tracy and what the daemon costs in latency.

The application's own chrome (title band, tabs, panes, menus, Settings) and the token tables behind it are described in The native chrome.

docs.title: crispy library
docs.text: This library contains super generic helper functions that are too small to be their own library and ease general development.

docs.title: text_shaper library
docs.text: This library abstracts font location service, text shaping, as well as glyph rasterization into a platform independent API.

docs.title: vtpty library
docs.text: vtpty provides an abstract API to construct a PTY handle to communicate between a terminal emulator (master) and a connected application (slave).

docs.title: vtparser library
docs.text: vtparser library provides an API to parse VT sequences. This library can be used on the master side (terminal emulator) as well as slave side (terminal application, e.g. the shell).

docs.title: vtbackend library
docs.text: Here we implement the actual terminal emulation. This is a headless library and cannot just be used for a GUI terminal emulator software. In order to render the screen state of a terminal to pixels, the vtrasterizer library can be used.

docs.title: vtrasterizer library
docs.text: vtrasterizer implements rasterizing the screen state into a bitmap. This is done target independent, which means, that the caller must provide the respective implementation to decide how the pixels are being stored (or rendered).

docs.title: Process Threading Model
docs.text:
Contour Terminal Emulator is multithreaded. The main thread is solely for receiving user input events and displaying screen updates plus some necessary administrative tasks.

The slave application will be spawned as a process and a thread is being associated with it to exclusively read the application's output, which will be processed inside the same thread. That thread is responsible for updating the internal terminal state.

docs.title: How terminal input is being processed
docs.text:
The user can send keyboard and mouse input which the connected slave (application) will read from its stdin.

  1. The native OS will emit an event, which will be intercepted by GLFW3 (the OpenGL Framework)
  2. The target GUI input events are being mapped to terminal API input events (see InputGenerator)
  3. The terminal::InputEvent objects are send to the respective terminal_view::TerminalView, which will apply key binds, if applicable, or pass the events to terminal::Terminal.
  4. The terminal::Terminal instance will use terminal::InputGenerator to generate VT sequences depending on current mode flags.
  5. The generated VT sequences are being transmitted to the slave application.

docs.title: How terminal output is being processed
docs.text:
The connected slave (application) may write a stream of characters to stdout or stderr, which will be read by the terminal.

  1. The VT stream is being parsed by a VT Parser that emits raw events
  2. These events are taken by the OutputHandler, and translated to Command variant types - in case of a VT function (such as ESC, CSI, OSC) a unique ID is being constructed. This unique ID is then mapped to a FunctionDef with a FunctionHandler whereas the latter will perform semantic analysis in order to emit the higher level Command variant types.
  3. The Command variant types are then processed in order by the Screen instance, that ultimatively interprets them.
  4. A callback hooks is being invoked to notify about screen updates (useful for displaying updated screen contents).

docs.title: Coding Style Guidelines
docs.text:
• Prefer CppCoreGuidelines if possible.
  • Avoid friend keyword.
  • Use signed integers unless the integer is holding a bit pattern.
  • Use the smallest integer type that is required to hold all desired values.
  • Do not cast from signed to unsigned unless you want the bit pattern, prefer to cast from unsigned to signed instead.

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
These are enforced by readability-identifier-naming in ./.clang-tidy, which is the single config for the whole tree — there are no module-local overrides. Where this file and .clang-tidy disagree, .clang-tidy wins; please fix this file.

  • namespaces: snake_case
  • types (class, struct, enum, enum constants): UpperCamelCase
  • temporary variable: lowerCamelCase
  • private member variables: lowerCamelCase with leading underscore
  • public member variable: lowerCamelCase
  • constexpr variable: UpperCamelCase
  • function names: lowerCamelCase
  • function parameters: lowerCamelCase, no underscore
  • Template parameter name: UpperCamelCase
  • preprocessor definitions: SCREAMING_CASE
  • east const instead of west const

docs.title: Exception: names the standard library binds to by spelling
docs.text: Member typedefs (value_type, iterator, const_iterator, difference_type, reference, pointer, iterator_category, …), nested iterator classes, container methods (begin, end, push_back, emplace_back, …) and std::formatter/std::hash specializations keep their standard spelling — renaming them silently breaks concept satisfaction and ADL. crispy::Ring is vtbackend::Lines and is driven through std::rotate and range-for, so its iterator surface is load-bearing. Mark each such declaration with // NOLINT(readability-identifier-naming).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
namespace org::coding_style::naming_conventions
{
    void eastConst() {
        int const a = 42;        // a is const
        int const* p = &a;       // value in p is const, p is not const.
        int const *const p = &a; // both value and p are const.
    }

    enum class Role { Employed, Unemployed };

    struct User
    {
        std::string firstname;
        std::string lastname;
        Role role;
    };

    class Actor
    {
      public:
        Actor(std::string _firstname, std::string _lastname, Role _role) :
            user_{ std::move(_firstname), std::move(_lastname), _role },
            credits_{ 0 }
        {}

        void giveOrTakeCredits(int _amount) noexcept
        {
            constexpr auto Scalar = 2;
            credits += Scalar * _amount;
        }

        std::string name() const
        {
            auto const result = user.firstname + " " + user.lastname;
            return result;
        }

      private:
        User user_;
        int credits_;
    };
}
