docs.title: Build times
docs.text: How long Contour takes to compile, measured the same way every time so a change can prove its gain.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
cmake --build out/clang-release          # compile_commands.json and generated sources must be current
python3 scripts/measure-compile-times.py --build-dir out/clang-release --jobs 16 --out build-times-out
python3 scripts/measure-compile-times.py --aggregate-only build-times-out/traces --out build-times-out

The script runs every .cpp command of compile_commands.json directly (any ccache/sccache/pace-cc launcher is dropped) with -ftime-trace, and writes report.md: total CPU seconds split into frontend and backend, a per-module table, the slowest TUs, the headers with the highest summed inclusive parse time (#TUs and ms/TU alongside), and the most expensive template instantiations. --filter REGEX limits the run to matching sources; --self-test (ctest measure_compile_times_selftest, label lint) checks the aggregator on embedded traces.

Caveats:

  • Per-TU wall time is measured with --jobs compiles in parallel, so it includes CPU contention. Compare runs only at the same --jobs on the same machine.
  • Header times are inclusive and overlap (a header's time contains the headers it includes); do not sum them across headers.
  • The release preset compiles with a launcher-free command, so no cache hides work.

docs.title: Baseline
docs.text:
out/clang-release (Clang 22, RelWithDebInfo), master at 4de2e780a, 16 jobs, 32-core machine: 1212 TUs, 4511 CPU-s in total (5m19s wall), of which frontend 3136 s and backend 1300 s.

Module TUs CPU-s Frontend s Backend s src/contour 396 2374 1682 651 src/vtbackend 200 660 425 226 src/vthost 169 599 394 197 generated (moc/autogen, in build tree) 130 237 206 26 src/vtextension 53 148 98 48 vendor/core-cpp 74 89 64 23 src/vtrasterizer 29 89 61 26 src/vtpty 47 80 52 26 src/vtcontrol 22 61 37 23 src/vtconformance 22 61 47 13 src/text_shaper 14 29 19 10 src/testing 16 26 15 11 src/crispy 17 25 16 8 src/vtworkspace 10 18 11 7 examples 10 9 5 3 src/vtparser 3 7 4 3

Top 10 headers by summed inclusive parse time:

Header Total s #TUs ms/TU src/contour/config/Config.hpp 298 142 2098 src/contour/ContourGuiApp.hpp 269 41 6551 src/vtbackend/screen/Terminal.hpp 260 214 1217 libstdc++ <format> 245 1137 216 src/contour/display/TerminalDisplay.hpp 180 60 3006 src/contour/session/TerminalSessionManager.hpp 166 49 3395 src/contour/config/Actions.hpp 125 156 804 libstdc++ <chrono> 122 956 128 Qt qqmlprivate.h 113 182 620 Qt qjsprimitivevalue.h 106 182 581

docs.title: Where a CI build's time goes
docs.text:
One Linux Clang 22 job, read from its log: ubuntu-24.04 (Clang 22, C++23, Qt6) of the pull-request run 41084258466 (job 124161606673, 2026-10-30), a 4-vCPU, 15 GiB runner with 3 GiB of swap.

Phase Wall time cmake --build (-j4, 1498 ninja steps) 69 m 44 s --target test 18 m 14 s (the four contour_gui_test* runs alone: 16 m 05 s) Whole job 91 m 50 s

The 1498 steps are 1211 C++ compiles, 44 C compiles, 9 WebAssembly compiles, 62 links, and a few rcc/MOC steps.

  • Compiling dominates. ccache -s at the end of the job: 1285 cacheable calls, 517 hits (40.2 %), 768 misses; the cache held 0.3 GB of a 0.3 GB limit (124 %) and had run 643 cleanups. Misses are full compiles, and the local baseline above puts the whole tree at 4511 CPU-s -- 19 minutes on four ideal cores. The runner is not ideal: its four vCPUs are two cores with SMT at a lower clock, and 70 min x 4 vCPU = 280 vCPU-min is 3.7x the baseline's 75 CPU-min, which is the whole difference between "about 20 minutes of compute" and the 70 observed. A cache that hit 90 % instead of 40 % would leave about a sixth of the compiles, about 12 minutes if a miss costs the average.
  • Linking does not. ninja prints only completions, so a link has no duration of its own, but the bound is tight where it matters: the last step, the link of contour_gui_test, completed 7 s after the last compile before it. Static libraries and test binaries link inside the seconds between neighbouring steps; CONTOUR_LINK_JOBS=1 serialises them without ever being the critical path.
  • Memory does not. The sampler logged 419 points, one per 10 s: peak 9502 MB used of 15 GiB, never less than 6485 MB available, so the swap was not a factor.

So the gap is cache misses on slow vCPUs, and the cache is the lever. Why it missed:

  • The cache directory was capped at 256 MB while a tree needs about twice that (below); at 124 % full, ccache evicts entries the same build is about to need.
  • Every run of every job saved a new, timestamped entry, pull requests included. A pull request can restore caches made on master but master cannot restore a pull request's, so those saves served one PR only -- and filled the repository's 10 GB quota (11.3 GB in use across 30 entries on 2026-10-30, 18 of them from one PR), evicting the master entries that every PR would have hit.
  • Windows had no persistent compiler cache at all: its sccache steps were gated on SCCACHE_GHA_ENABLED, which the workflow set to "false", so they never ran. The 102-minute build compiled every file on every run.

docs.title: The compiler cache
docs.text:
Rules, in .github/workflows/build.yml:

  • master pushes save, pull requests only restore (save: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' }}). hendrikmuhs/ccache-action restores by key prefix, so a pull request takes the newest entry master saved under the same key. Merge-queue runs restore too and save nothing.
  • evict-old-files: job drops every cached object the saving job did not touch, so an entry is one working set -- the current tree -- and does not accumulate dead objects up to max-size.
  • Keys are stable: one per job, the action appends the timestamp.
  • Hit-defeating inputs are neutralised workflow-wide: CCACHE_BASEDIR (the checkout), CCACHE_NOHASHDIR, and CCACHE_SLOPPINESS=include_file_mtime,include_file_ctime. There is no pch_defines because there is no PCH.
  • The tidy-diff job has no cache. It builds generated headers only and compiles nothing.

docs.title: Sizes
docs.text:
Measured with ccache 4.9.1 (the version the Ubuntu 24.04 runner installs), compression on, a clean RelWithDebInfo build of the whole tree into an empty cache:

Tree Compiles cached Cache size Clang 22, clang-release 1289 0.50 GB (497 MB on disk) GCC 16.2, gcc-release 780 of ~1290 before a -Werror=bidi-chars stop in ExtensionConsent_test.cpp 0.53 GB, about 0.9 GB extrapolated to the full tree

The brief expected 2-3 GB; the real figure is a fifth of that, because ccache compresses and debug info compresses well. max-size is about 1.3x the tree:

Job Key max-size Linux matrix, Clang (x86, arm) ccache-<runner>-Clang 22-... 700 MB each Linux matrix, GCC (x86, arm) ccache-<runner>-GCC 15-... 1200 MB each Packaging, Ubuntu 26.04 ccache-ubuntu-26.04 1200 MB check_clang_tidy (push/merge group) ccache-ubuntu2404-clang-tidy 700 MB build_no_extensions ccache-ubuntu2404-no-extensions 700 MB build_headless ccache-ubuntu2404-headless 500 MB macOS (arm) ccache-macosArm-r1 800 MB Windows (MSVC) ccache-windows-msvc-release 1500 MB

The caps sum to 9.5 GB; the entries should settle near 70 % of that, about 6.7 GB, beside roughly 1.5 GB of Qt, vcpkg, FreeBSD and apt caches. That is inside the 10 GB quota with little to spare: a second master push before the first generation is evicted costs the oldest entries first. The guard jobs (build_headless, build_no_extensions, tidy) were not turned into read-only restorers of the Linux Clang key as the plan suggested: they compile with a different preset, so their command lines differ and a restored Clang-matrix entry would hit almost nothing. If eviction churn shows, drop the tidy cache first -- it caches compiles only, and the tidy runs themselves are not cacheable. The Windows and GCC figures are estimates, not measurements; revisit them from the first master run's ccache -s.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: The MSVC build is cacheable. cmake/CompileCache.cmake selects the ccache on PATH (the log reads [cache] Enabling ccache (C:/Strawberry/c/bin/ccache.exe)) and, whenever a launcher is in use under MSVC, sets CMAKE_MSVC_DEBUG_INFORMATION_FORMAT=Embedded with CMAKE_POLICY_DEFAULT_CMP0141=NEW -- /Z7 instead of /Zi -- and rewrites a legacy /Zi in the flag variables; the project requires CMake 3.25, which has both. What was missing was a persisted cache directory, so the job now runs hendrikmuhs/ccache-action like the Linux jobs, and its final step prints the binary CMake used, its configuration and ccache -s; "Uncacheable calls" there would mean /Zi survived. The dead sccache steps and SCCACHE_* environment are gone.

docs.title: What a pull request runs
docs.text:
A pull request runs the platform builds and tests -- Windows, macOSArm (build and tests, no signing, no packaging) and one Linux leg (Clang 22 on x86, built with -Werror) -- plus the guard builds, the lint jobs and clang-tidy on the changed lines. Master pushes and the merge queue run the rest: the other three compiler legs, packaging, valgrind, conformance, bench-headless, notcurses, FreeBSD and the full-tree clang-tidy. The release branch's pull request runs all of those except FreeBSD and the full-tree clang-tidy (both are github.event_name != 'pull_request'); the static build runs on master pushes and the release pull request, never in the merge queue.

A required status check is never gated off pull requests. tests matrix and Ubuntu Linux 24.04 post-check always run and treat a skipped dependency as passed (a failed or cancelled one still fails them). scripts/check-workflows.py enforces both rules, and its --self-test pins them against fixtures. A master run is never cancelled by the next push (cancel-in-progress is off on master), so it finishes and saves the compiler cache.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Measured on 2026-10-31 with scripts/measure-compile-times.py --jobs 16, the merge base and this branch built back to back on the same idle machine (Clang 22, RelWithDebInfo), so contention is equal on both sides:

Base (4de2e780a) This branch Change Total CPU-s, 1220 TUs 4832 4218 −12.7 % Frontend CPU-s 3388 2947 −13.0 % Backend CPU-s 1360 1203 −11.5 %

The slowest translation units fall by a quarter to a third: SettingsController_test.cpp 34.7 → 23.6 s, TerminalSessionManager_test.cpp 30.3 → 22.2 s, TerminalSessionPermissions_test.cpp 29.7 → 21.9 s, Config.cpp 42.2 → 33.1 s.

What a change to a central header rebuilds (translation units depending on it, ninja -t deps):

Header Base This branch vthost/SessionHost.hpp 115 37 contour/config/Actions.hpp 172 113 vtbackend/screen/Terminal.hpp 234 202 contour/config/Config.hpp 158 138 contour/session/TerminalSession.hpp 79 67 contour/window/WindowController.hpp 65 53

The single largest gain is Action: a std::variant of 129 alternatives whose copy, move and destruction every translation unit holding an Action used to instantiate. It is now a class deriving from that variant with its special members defined once, in Actions.cpp; the variant's instantiation cost fell by 88 %. Forward declarations alone moved cost between headers more than they removed it, because the slowest translation units — the GUI tests — genuinely need the application they drive. scripts/include-budget.txt keeps the cuts that were made from coming back.

Pull-request CI, warm cache, a change that touches no central header (wall clock per job):

Job Before After Linux Clang 22 92–107 min 23.5 min Windows ~134 min 31 min macOS ~125 min 19–23 min Guard builds (GUI off, no extensions) 25–60 min 3–6 min clang-tidy 160+ min (full tree) 14 min (changed lines)

A change that touches a header half the tree includes still rebuilds what depends on it: with this branch's own header churn the platform jobs took 40–58 min. A cold cache costs what it did before.

docs.title: Latency: what the daemon costs
docs.text: Running a terminal through contour daemon must not feel different from running it in-process. This page defines what is measured, what the budgets are, and how to run the gate. For where the time goes inside one frame, see Profiling with Tracy; for the daemon itself, see Multiplexer & daemon mode.

docs.title: The budgets
docs.text:
Both are relative to in-process on the same machine and the same build, with the daemon already running, and inclusive:

Metric Budget Launch to first prompt pixel at most +10 ms (median over in-process) Keystroke to pixel over the local socket at most +1 ms at the median

A cold launch (no daemon running, so the client spawns one) is measured and reported as startup-cold, never gated. The first spawn after an upgrade stages a copy of the install; it is reported apart as startup-cold-staging and is not part of startup-cold.

Bulk output keeps coalescing at 20 ms (FlushPolicy::coalesceDelay); the gate says nothing about throughput, but bench-latency headless workload NAME reports MiB/s and Deltas per second of both modes beside it.

docs.title: What is timed
docs.text:
The application behind the terminal is always the echo child (bench-latency echo-child): it prints the prompt >, then echoes every byte it reads, wrapping to a fresh prompt after 60 columns, and ends on ^D. What a frame shows of that is the cursor column, not the glyph, so the probes detect the column the echo of key k leaves the cursor at (vthost/latency/EchoProtocol.hpp).

Launch to first prompt.

  • bench-latency headless: t0 is read just before createTab() (in-process) or just before the connect (daemon); t1 is when the terminal's, or the mirrored screen's, cursor reaches column 2.
  • bench-latency e2e: t0 is the benchmark's steady_clock just before it spawns contour; t1 is the steady_clock read in the frameSwapped handler of the first frame that drew the cursor at column 2, reported by the GUI through --latency-probe. steady_clock is one system-wide clock on all three platforms, and the benchmark refuses a report whose process start is before its spawn or after its first prompt ("steady clocks disagree").

Keystroke to pixel.

  • bench-latency headless: t0 is read by the probe immediately before the key is handed to SessionHost::writeInput (in-process) or NativeClient::sendInput (daemon); t1 is when the cursor column reaches the key's expected column. Keys are typed 25 to 35 ms apart, so each finds the host idle.
  • bench-latency e2e: t0 is read on the GUI thread immediately before the key press event is delivered to the window; t1 is read in the frameSwapped handler of the first frame whose prepareFrameRhi drew the cursor at the expected column. It includes key translation, the PTY write (in-process) or the Input PDU (daemon), the echo, parsing (in-process) or the Delta and mirror apply (daemon), and render plus swap. It excludes the OS input stack, which is identical in both modes.

Swaps are unpaced by default (--latency-probe selects swap interval 0), because a 60 Hz vsync quantizes every sample to 16.7 ms, which hides a 1 ms difference. vsync on the e2e command turns the pacing back on.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
bench-latency is built with -DVTHOST_BUILD_BENCH_LATENCY=ON (on in every preset but macos-package; it is never installed and never packaged).

# Without a GUI: both modes behind the same SessionHost / daemon code.
bench-latency headless                       # 10 runs of 50 keys per mode
bench-latency headless runs 20 keys 100 record latency-headless.tsv
bench-latency headless workload ascii seconds 3   # throughput instead of keystrokes

# With the real GUI: `contour terminal` against `contour client`. Needs a display.
bench-latency e2e contour PATH-TO-contour gate
bench-latency e2e contour PATH-TO-contour cold record latency-e2e.tsv

e2e writes a configuration with one profile (bench: the echo child as shell, 120x40, a steady cursor), starts contour daemon on a socket of its own, and alternates contour terminal and contour client launches, each with --latency-probe. Every client launch uses a unique --label, so no registered service of yours answers for it. With cold, the benchmark stops its daemon itself before each cold launch (the daemon's 10 s idle grace would otherwise make it warm).

On Linux the GUI needs a compositor that delivers frame callbacks. The CI-grade choice is a headless weston: scripts/run-display-tests.sh --run COMMAND... runs a command under one (and under a private session bus). Qt's offscreen platform draws no frames, so a probe under it times out and the benchmark names the column it waited for.

docs.title: Reading the table
docs.text:
metric          mode         count     p50 us     p90 us     p99 us     max us
startup         in-process      10     2620.1     3106.5     3384.2     3384.2
startup         daemon          10     3065.9     3651.7     3944.2     3944.2
keystroke       in-process     500       85.7      120.5      134.9      142.9
keystroke       daemon         500      134.1      202.4      243.0      297.4
gate: startup +0.4 ms (budget +10.0 ms) PASS; keystroke p50 +0.05 ms (budget +1.00 ms) PASS

Times are microseconds. The gate line compares the medians; a verdict is INCONCLUSIVE, not PASS, with fewer than 10 startup or 200 keystroke samples per mode (the defaults give 10 and 500). headless marks its gate line (informational): the gate is e2e gate, whose exit status is 0 only if both budgets pass.

A probe that never sees its cursor column ends the run with probe timed out waiting for cursor column N and a non-zero exit; it never hangs. Typical causes are a blinking cursor, an unexposed window, or a platform that schedules no frames.

docs.title: The gate
docs.text:
The gate is a reproducible local run on a Windows, a Linux and a macOS machine before the default is flipped to daemon mode and before each release:

Platform Command Linux cmake --build --preset clang-release --target contour bench-latency then scripts/run-display-tests.sh --run out/clang-release/src/vthost/bench-latency e2e contour out/clang-release/src/contour/contour gate Windows cmake --build --preset clangcl-release --target contour bench-latency then out\build\clangcl-release\bin\bench-latency.exe e2e contour out\build\clangcl-release\bin\contour.exe gate (in the desktop session) macOS cmake --build --preset appleclang-release --target contour bench-latency then out/appleclang-release/src/vthost/bench-latency e2e contour out/appleclang-release/src/contour/contour.app/Contents/MacOS/contour gate (in the desktop session)

CI runs the same benchmark on all three platforms in the latency_trend job and records the numbers as a workflow artifact and a step summary. It never fails on them: shared runners are too noisy to gate on, but a trend across commits shows a regression early.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Each row is one run of the gate command above, gate cold, 10 runs of 50 keys per mode (500 keystroke samples). A FAIL or INCONCLUSIVE is recorded as such: the budgets and the sample minimums are not tuned to fit.

Date Commit OS CPU GPU Startup delta Keystroke p50 delta Cold startup (p50) Verdicts 2026-10-24 d9878cde (before the resync fix) Fedora 44, Linux 7.2.9, Xephyr (X11, no compositor), clang-release AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D none: Mesa software GL (llvmpipe) -0.9 ms +0.10 ms 296.2 ms (first staging spawn 295.0 ms) startup PASS, keystroke PASS 2026-10-24 257505a7 (resync snapshots coalescing) Fedora 44, Linux 7.2.9, Xephyr (X11, no compositor), clang-release AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D none: Mesa software GL (llvmpipe) -0.2 ms +0.09 ms 293.4 ms (first staging spawn 297.8 ms) startup PASS, keystroke PASS pending Windows (clangcl-release) to be run on the owner's machine pending macOS (appleclang-release) to be run on the owner's machine

The Linux run used a nested Xephyr server in place of the headless weston run-display-tests.sh starts when it finds weston (not installed on that machine). It renders in software, so absolute times (6.5 ms keystroke-to-pixel, 255 ms to the first prompt) are those of a software renderer; the deltas between the two modes are what the gate judges.

docs.title: Bulk output after the flush change
docs.text:
bench-latency headless runs 5 workload ascii seconds 2, this tree against the same tree with the commit that flushes an echo at once (b7edc5ce) reverted, both clang-release, two alternating runs:

MiB/s in-process MiB/s daemon Deltas/s without the flush change 317 / 324 313 / 316 47.9 / 48.0 with it, first version (d9878cde) 309 / 330 296 / 296 217.1 / 217.4 with it, resync snapshots coalescing (257505a7) 320 / 322 312 / 313 48.4 / 48.4

The first version flushed 4.5 times as often. The flood scrolls, so nearly every flush is a resync snapshot (412 snapshots, 411 of them resyncs, in a 2 s run); a snapshot cleared the follow's increment history, and the next screen update counted as the first one after an attach and flushed at once (422 such flushes beside 1505 coalesced). Only the attach snapshot now leaves the next increment to flush at once; a resync keeps the history, and Deltas per second are back at the coalescing rate.

Callgrind of the daemon (valgrind --tool=callgrind --trace-children=yes bench-latency headless runs 1 workload ascii seconds 2, the serve process) shows the same profile with and without the flush change: 829 M instructions against 846 M, with streamSnapshots at 37 % and buildPush at 15 % in both and no new hot spot.

The keystroke gate was rerun with the fix; that run is the 257505a7 row of the results table above.

docs.title: macOS code signing, notarization and packaging
macOS code signing, notarization and packaging
docs.text:
Shipping a macOS app that opens on someone else's Mac takes four things, and missing any one of them produces the same unhelpful Gatekeeper dialog:

  1. The bundle is self-contained — every library it loads is inside it.
  2. Every Mach-O in it is signed with a Developer ID, inside-out, under the hardened runtime.
  3. The disk image is signed too.
  4. Both the app and the image are notarized by Apple and have the ticket stapled.

A correct signature alone is not enough. spctl says so plainly:

$ spctl --assess --type install Contour-0.7.0-Darwin.dmg
Contour-0.7.0-Darwin.dmg: rejected
source=Unnotarized Developer ID

All four steps run automatically from cpack. The mechanics live in scripts/macos-bundle.py, which is driven by the install(CODE …) block in src/contour/CMakeLists.txt and by the two CPack hooks cmake/MacOSNotarizeApp.cmake and cmake/MacOSSignDmg.cmake.

docs.title: Building a distributable .dmg
docs.text:
The macos-package preset is the only configuration that produces a .dmg, and CI uses it too — there is deliberately no second definition of "a shippable macOS build" to drift out of sync:

export QT_ROOT_DIR=$HOME/Qt/6.11.1/macos
export VCPKG_ROOT=$HOME/vcpkg          # git clone microsoft/vcpkg && ./bootstrap-vcpkg.sh
cmake --preset macos-package           # also builds the vcpkg dependencies, once
cmake --build --preset macos-package
ctest --preset macos-package           # what CI runs, same configuration
cpack --preset macos-package

The first configure builds openssl, libssh2, yaml-cpp, freetype, harfbuzz and cairo from source — about 5 minutes, cached in ~/.cache/vcpkg/archives afterwards. install-deps.sh provides the autotools those ports need on the build host.

The image contains contour.app and the /Applications symlink, nothing else. That is not luck: contour-common turns CONTOUR_INSTALL_TOOLS on, and src/vtbackend installs bench-headless straight into contour.app/Contents/MacOS when it is set — so the packaging preset turns it back off, and CI asserts the mounted image's contents. Tests are built (CONTOUR_TESTING=ON, inherited) but no test target has an install rule, so building them cannot affect what ships.

Stale build directories lie. Subproject test options are cached on first configure and are not revisited when CONTOUR_TESTING changes, so a directory first configured with tests off keeps most suites disabled even after the preset turns them on. If ctest --preset macos-package reports far fewer than the full suite, delete out/macos-package/ and configure again.

That runs, in order: macdeployqt → prune → verify → sign → notarize+staple the app → build the image → sign the image → notarize+staple the image → spctl. Every step is fatal on failure, so a broken bundle stops the build instead of becoming a release.

Two knobs control the Apple round trips, which cost a minute or more each:

option effect CONTOUR_MACOS_NOTARIZE Notarize and staple the .dmg. This is the one Gatekeeper demands on a downloaded file. CONTOUR_MACOS_STAPLE_APP Additionally notarize and staple the .app inside the image, so it launches offline after being dragged to /Applications.

Both are ON in the macos-package preset. CI enables the first for master and the second only for release, so an ordinary push pays one wait instead of two.

docs.title: Why not Homebrew's Qt
docs.text:
Homebrew ships Qt as roughly forty separate per-module formulae (qtbase, qtdeclarative, qtmultimedia, …), each in its own prefix. macdeployqt resolves QML modules and plugins relative to a single Qt prefix, so it silently misses everything in the other thirty-nine: it prints ERROR: Cannot resolve rpath to stderr, exits 0, and leaves frameworks whose LC_ID_DYLIB still points into /opt/homebrew. Release builds therefore use the official Qt binaries, which live under one prefix and are built to be relocated — the same Qt the Linux and Windows CI jobs already use.

Homebrew's Qt remains perfectly fine for the appleclang-debug / appleclang-release dev presets, which are never packaged. scripts/install-deps.sh no longer installs it by default; pass CONTOUR_INSTALL_BREW_QT=ON if you want it.

Install the official Qt with:

pip install aqtinstall
aqt install-qt mac desktop 6.11.1 clang_64 \
    -m qtmultimedia qt5compat qtshadertools qtspeech -O ~/Qt

docs.title: One-time credential setup
docs.text: Two independent credentials are needed: a certificate to sign with, and an API key to notarize with. Neither can substitute for the other.

docs.title: 1. Developer ID Application certificate (signing)
docs.text:
Check whether you already have a usable one — an "identity" means the certificate and its private key are present, which is exactly what is needed:

security find-identity -v -p codesigning
# 1) 8E5F... "Developer ID Application: Christian Parpart (6T525MU9UR)"

If it is listed, nothing needs to be recreated for local signing.

If it is missing or expired, create one at https://developer.apple.com/account/resources/certificates:

  1. Keychain Access → menu Certificate Assistant → Request a Certificate From a Certificate Authority. Enter your email and name, choose Saved to disk, and keep the resulting CertificateSigningRequest.certSigningRequest. This also creates the private key in your login keychain — the half Apple never sees and never sends back.
  2. On the certificates page: + → Developer ID Application → Profile Type: G2 Sub-CA → upload the CSR → Download the .cer.
  3. Double-click the .cer to install it. security find-identity -v -p codesigning should now list it.

Note: creating Developer ID certificates requires the Account Holder role, and a team is limited to a small number of them — so revoke an unused one rather than accumulating.

For CI, export the identity as a .p12 (certificate + private key in one file):

  1. Keychain Access → login keychain → category My Certificates → find Developer ID Application: … → expand it and confirm a private key sits underneath.
  2. Right-click → Export "Developer ID Application: …" → format Personal Information Exchange (.p12) → choose a password. That password becomes the P12_PASSWORD secret.

Then encode it and set three repository secrets:

base64 -i DeveloperID.p12 | pbcopy      # -> secret BUILD_CERTIFICATE_BASE64
openssl rand -base64 24                 # -> secret KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD (any random string)
secret value BUILD_CERTIFICATE_BASE64 base64 of the .p12 P12_PASSWORD the password chosen during export KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD any random string; it only protects the runner's throwaway keychain

The old BUILD_PROVISION_PROFILE_BASE64 secret is no longer used — provisioning profiles belong to App Store and ad-hoc distribution, not to Developer ID. It can be deleted.

docs.title: 2. App Store Connect API key (notarization)
docs.text:
Preferred over an Apple ID plus app-specific password: it is tied to no personal account, is scoped by role, and can be revoked on its own.

  1. https://appstoreconnect.apple.com → Users and Access → Integrations tab → App Store Connect API → Team Keys → +.
  2. Name it (e.g. contour-notary), set Access to Developer, generate.
  3. Download AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8 immediately — Apple allows it exactly once.
  4. Note the Key ID (10 characters, in the key's row) and the Issuer ID (a UUID shown above the table, shared by all of the team's keys).

Store it locally under the profile name the build expects:

xcrun notarytool store-credentials contour-notary \
    --key ~/Downloads/AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8 \
    --key-id XXXXXXXXXX \
    --issuer aaaaaaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddd-eeeeeeeeeeee

# confirm it works (empty history is a success; an auth error is not)
xcrun notarytool history --keychain-profile contour-notary

Override the profile name with -DCONTOUR_MACOS_NOTARY_PROFILE=… if you use another.

For CI, set three more secrets:

secret value APPLE_API_KEY_P8 base64 -i AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8 \| pbcopy APPLE_API_KEY_ID the 10-character Key ID APPLE_API_ISSUER_ID the Issuer UUID

Keep the .p8 somewhere safe. It cannot be downloaded again, and losing it means generating a new key and updating the secrets.

docs.title: Why not codesign --deep
docs.text:
--deep is what the earlier attempts here used, and Apple documents it as unsuitable for distribution signing. It applies the top-level entitlements to nested code, and it does not guarantee that nested code is sealed before its container — so the outer seal can end up covering a signature that was replaced afterwards. macos-bundle.py sign walks the bundle deepest-first instead: loadable dylibs in Frameworks/, PlugIns/ and Resources/qml/, then each framework's versioned directory, then helper executables, then the main executable, then the bundle. Only the outermost signature carries entitlements.

--deep is right for verification, where it means "check every nested signature too":

codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=4 contour.app

docs.title: Entitlements
docs.text:
support/macOS/entitlements.plist is applied to the app bundle only. It carries no explanatory comments, because the kernel's entitlements parser (AMFI) rejects XML comments outright — Failed to parse entitlements: AMFIUnserializeXML: syntax error — so the reasoning lives here:

  • com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit — the QML engine's V4 JIT needs MAP_JIT, which the hardened runtime otherwise denies.
  • com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation — insurance for Qt plugin loading. Everything Contour bundles is re-signed with the same Team ID, which library validation already permits, so this is a candidate for removal; verify a notarized build launches and loads its plugins before dropping it.

docs.title: Inspecting a signature
docs.text:
# Identity, hardened runtime flag, timestamp, team ID
codesign -dv --verbose=4 contour.app

# Hardened runtime shows as flags=0x10000(runtime). Its absence is invisible to --verify
# and is a hard notarization rejection.
codesign -dv --verbose=4 contour.app 2>&1 | grep -E 'Authority|flags='

# Entitlements actually embedded
codesign -d --entitlements - --xml contour.app | plutil -p -

# What Gatekeeper will decide
spctl --assess --verbose=4 --type exec contour.app
spctl --assess --verbose=4 --type install contour.dmg
xcrun stapler validate contour.dmg

docs.title: Reproducing what a user sees
docs.text:
spctl is an assessment, not the real thing: Gatekeeper only engages when a file carries the quarantine attribute a browser sets. To test the actual download path:

xattr -w com.apple.quarantine "0081;00000000;Safari;" contour.dmg
open contour.dmg          # then drag Contour to /Applications and launch it

Launching again with networking disabled proves the stapled ticket works. Without a staple, first launch silently depends on Gatekeeper reaching Apple — which is why the app inside the image is notarized and stapled separately from the image itself.

docs.title: Minimum macOS version
docs.text:
verify reports the oldest macOS the bundle can run on, computed as the highest minos across every bundled Mach-O:

macos-bundle: verify: bundle requires macOS 26.0 or newer, set by 14 binary/binaries

The floor is 13.3, and it is enforced rather than hoped for.

docs.title: Why the dependencies come from vcpkg, not Homebrew
docs.text:
Homebrew ships one prebuilt bottle per macOS release and installs the one matching the build machine. A bundle assembled from Homebrew dylibs therefore inherits the builder's macOS as its minimum — on a developer's up-to-date Mac that meant a .dmg requiring macOS 26, and in CI it meant the floor moved silently whenever GitHub rotated the runner image. Nothing surfaced it: the app was correctly signed, correctly notarizable, and simply refused to start.

So the six libraries Contour links — openssl, libssh2, yaml-cpp, freetype, harfbuzz, cairo — are built from source by vcpkg against CMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET. The whole mechanism is one triplet file, cmake/vcpkg-triplets/arm64-osx-contour.cmake, whose VCPKG_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET is the single knob. This is not a new mechanism: the Windows job has always built its dependencies with vcpkg from the same vcpkg.json.

A side benefit: vcpkg's cairo does not drag in the X11 stack that Homebrew's does, so libX11, libXext, libXrender, libXau and libxcb no longer ship at all.

docs.title: Two macdeployqt details this depends on
docs.text:
• Homebrew dylibs carry an absolute install name, so macdeployqt resolved them without help. vcpkg's carry @rpath/libfoo.dylib, and macdeployqt expands @rpath using only the binary's own LC_RPATH — its -libpath option is not consulted for this. The vcpkg library directory is therefore added to CMAKE_INSTALL_RPATH for the deployment step, and removed again afterwards so no build-machine path ships in a release binary.
  • macdeployqt usually strips the rpaths it consumed itself, so that removal is conditional; an unconditional install_name_tool -delete_rpath fails hard on a missing LC_RPATH.

docs.title: The promise is checked
docs.text:
CONTOUR_MACOS_MIN_SUPPORTED (13.3 in the macos-package preset) is compared against what the bundled binaries actually demand. If anything exceeds it, verify fails and no package is produced:

- the bundle requires macOS 26.0, but this build promises support down to 13.3 --
  users below 26.0 would be unable to launch it

It defaults to empty (report only) for the dev presets, which still use Homebrew and whose floor is whatever the developer's bottles happened to be — a fact, not a promise.

LSMinimumSystemVersion in Contents/Info.plist is the same number. Qt's Info.plist template — which qt_add_executable() installs, in place of CMake's MacOSXBundleInfo.plist.in — substitutes CMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET into it, and that is what the vcpkg triplet pins. So the version macOS shows in a "requires a newer macOS" dialog and the version verify measures across the bundled binaries come from one source and cannot drift apart. Were they allowed to, a too-low declaration would be worse than none: macOS would launch the app and let dyld fail on a missing symbol instead of refusing it with a clear message.

NSHighResolutionCapable is likewise absent from the shipped Info.plist, and that is the enabled state, not a gap. Measured on a Retina display: an absent key and an explicit <true/> both give an NSWindow a backingScaleFactor of 2.0, and only an explicit <false/> drops it to 1.0. Apple's own bundled apps set the key nowhere, and Qt ships a separate Info.plist.disable_highdpi precisely because opting out is the case that needs saying. Declaring it would mean forking Qt's template — and forgoing whatever Qt adds to it next — to restate a default.

The CI runner image is pinned (runs-on: macos-15) for toolchain reproducibility. The floor no longer depends on it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause resource fork, Finder information, or similar detritus not allowed Extended attributes; sign runs xattr -cr first for this reason. The signature of the binary is invalid from notarytool Something was modified after signing — install_name_tool invalidates a signature, so any relinking must precede signing. The executable does not have the hardened runtime enabled Missing --options=runtime on some nested binary. codesign hangs in CI The key's ACL does not permit codesign; needs security import -T /usr/bin/codesign and security set-key-partition-list. ERROR: Cannot resolve rpath from macdeployqt Split-prefix Qt (see above). It exits 0 anyway; verify is what catches it.

docs.title: The native chrome
docs.text: This page is for maintainers who change the application's own chrome: the title band, the tab well, pane cards, menus, dialogs, the Settings window and the small overlays around the grid. It records the design rules the chrome is built to and where each one lives in the tree, so a change can respect them without rediscovering them. The code wins over this page; where they disagree, fix the page.

docs.title: Purpose and principles
docs.text:
The chrome looks native on each platform and is still one component tree. macOS came first, then Windows 11, then one Linux design that serves every desktop; there is no GNOME-specific or KDE-specific variant. A fourth look, the Terminal (TUI) style, is a first-class row of the same components, not an afterthought.

  1. The chrome is data-driven. Every extent, radius, colour role, type size, duration and glyph comes from a token row (src/contour/config/UiStyle.hpp, src/contour/config/ChromeTokenGroups.hpp) or from the terminal's colour scheme. QML interprets tokens and holds no literals. Two lint gates enforce this: scripts/check-qml-colors.py (no hex colours, no all-literal Qt.rgba) and scripts/check-qml-sizes.py (no numeric size literals, with a shrinking baseline in scripts/qml-size-literal-baseline.txt). Both run under ctest -L lint.
  2. There is one component tree. Platforms differ through token rows plus a handful of layout switches (LayoutTokens: caption buttons, tab shape, header-bar arrangement, profile dropdown, Settings layout, and a few more). There are no per-platform QML forks. A visual change lands in the Terminal row in the same change, not later.
  3. Pure decisions are headless. Which badge wins, whether a pane shows a header, which menu rows exist, where the find bar goes, how a status segment collapses: each is a dependency-free header under src/contour/window/, src/contour/command/, src/contour/session/ or src/vtbackend/, with Catch2 tables. QML renders the answer and decides nothing.
  4. The OS is reached through interfaces. Everything that asks the OS lives behind an interface in src/contour/platform/ with a null implementation and a test double, injected at construction.
  5. Nothing is drawn over non-blank cells. Badges, chips, toasts, banners, link pills and block chips go into chrome bands, pane headers, gutters or blank cells only. The one exception is the hint labels, which by definition sit over the first cells of the match they label.
  6. Glass and material are chrome only, never behind terminal text. The chrome's light or dark appearance follows the terminal background (theme: terminal, the default; the luminance threshold is in colorSchemeOfBackground), unless the configuration carries a dual light/dark colour scheme, in which case it follows the OS.
  7. Existing users keep their look. New defaults sit behind DefaultsEdition (src/contour/config/DefaultsEdition.hpp), see below.
  8. Contrast is a rule, not a taste. Chrome text must reach 4.5:1 against what it sits on (MinimumTextContrast), marks such as dots and status glyphs 3:1 (MinimumMarkContrast). The built-in contour-dark and contour-light schemes keep every colour except black and white at 4.5:1 against their background, bright black on dark at 5.0. The OS selected-row colour pair is exempt only while it already reads: legibleHighlight in src/contour/config/HighlightPair.hpp keeps the OS hue and swaps the text to white or black when the pair falls under 4.5:1. This is the Breeze fallback: KDE's default #3DAEE9 under white reads about 2.5:1, under black 8.6:1, so the text flips and the fill stays.

Other fixed rules of the look:

  • Status colours are semantic. "Running" and "working" use the accent, never yellow or green; yellow means search. In the Terminal row, yellow appears as a glyph only, never as a fill.
  • Tabs live in the title band. Settings is a separate window (Cmd+, / Ctrl+,), never a tab.
  • A single pane runs edge to edge with no focus frame. Pane cards with headers appear only once a tab is split, and focus is shown by dimming the others, not by an outline (except under increased contrast).
  • Shortcuts render per platform: modifier glyphs on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+P elsewhere (src/contour/command/Shortcut.hpp).
  • Command blocks never draw UI over non-blank cells.

docs.title: Architecture: rows, token groups and styles
UiStyle, ChromeStyle and the token table
docs.text:
UiStyle is what the user asks for (ui_style: native | terminal). resolveChromeStyle(UiStyle, HostPlatform) turns it into a ChromeStyle, the row the chrome is actually painted with:

Row Where it applies MacOS native on macOS Fluent native on Windows ContourLinux native on KDE Plasma and every other host Terminal ui_style: terminal, on every OS

Enumerator order is the row order of the table. Two tables are indexed by it:

  • UiStyleTokenTable in UiStyle.hpp, the older UiStyleTokens (units, corner radius, border width, popup shadow and scrim, tab metrics, glyph vocabulary, quickControlsStyle).
  • ChromeTokenRows in ChromeTokenGroups.hpp, one ChromeTokenRow per style, composed of groups: size, space, radii, type, motion, elevation, material, contrast, tui, layout, tint, colors (a ChromeColorSource per ChromeColorRole), statusInk, dim, minimal, blockChips and settings.

Both carry a static_assert that every ChromeStyle has exactly one row, so a sixth row is one table edit: add the enumerator, add a row to each table, and the compiler names whatever else is missing. The exception is the Qt Quick Controls half, below.

Rules for token groups:

  • A group is added by the first change that consumes it, never ahead of need. Component extents quoted in a design are named tokens (size.toast, size.palette, space.blockGutter, ...), so the size-literal gate never has to flag them.
  • Enums used by tokens have an explicit underlying type and put the default at zero.
  • A colour is a source, not a value: an OS palette slot, a scheme slot, a derivation. The chrome resolves it against the active scheme at provider-build time (chromeSchemeColorsOf), so a scheme change recolours the chrome without touching QML.
  • Counted-in-cells extents (LengthUnit::Cell) are how the Terminal row snaps to the grid. Never mix a pixel literal into a cell row.

docs.title: Resolution and the provider
docs.text:
resolveChromeTokens(style, accessibilityPreferences, density, materialSupport) applies, in order: the Minimal density sub-row, Reduce Motion (durations collapse to a short cross-fade, travel to zero), Reduce Transparency or an OS that cannot draw the material (materials become Solid), and Increased Contrast (separators double, the active pane card gets a ring, the pane dim drops). It is a pure constexpr function with a test row per rule (ChromeTokenGroups_test.cpp).

UiStyleProvider (src/contour/window/UiStyleProvider.hpp) exposes the resolved row to QML as grouped Q_PROPERTY objects (chromeStyle.size.tab, ...). Its properties are constant. When any input changes (an OS accessibility or appearance change, a reload, a light/dark flip, the density) ChromeStyleHost builds a new provider and republishes it; the old one is deleteLater()ed because the change often arrives from a signal the old provider is still on the stack for. Never add change notification to provider properties.

docs.title: The Qt Quick Controls styles
docs.text:
Qt resolves a Quick Controls style by name, once per process, before the first control exists. So a row also names its style (quickControlsStyle) and each style needs real control files:

Row Controls style MacOS Fusion, with the chrome drawn by the shared QML Fluent FluentWinUI3 ContourLinux src/contour/styles/ContourLinux/ Terminal src/contour/styles/ContourTui/

The two first-party modules are built the same way (src/contour/CMakeLists.txt) and must implement the same set of controls; their *_test.cpp (ContourTuiStyle_test.cpp, ContourLinuxStyle_test.cpp) load every control. A change of ui_style takes effect on the next start for this reason.

The hand-drawn chrome in src/contour/qml/ never learns which style is active.

docs.title: Config and defaults
docs.text:
Config keys you will touch: ui_style, chrome_density (comfortable | minimal), theme (terminal follows the background), show_title_bar, defaults_edition, scrollbar.mode and the window-control style (src/contour/config/WindowControlStyle.hpp).

DefaultsEdition { Classic = 0, Native2026 } exists because a configuration that sets only profiles.main.font would otherwise inherit every new default. A fresh install is Native2026 by virtue of the generated file carrying defaults_edition: native2026. A file that sets nothing is Classic. The edition is read by a pre-scan (settings.yml wins over contour.yml) because Config and the seed TerminalProfile are constructed before the YAML is parsed. Classic users get a one-time offer (NewDefaultsOffer.hpp, window/NewDefaultsNotice.hpp): Use New writes native2026 through the Settings session, Keep Mine remembers the dismissal. Every default lives in one table per edition, not in scattered ifs.

docs.title: Title band and tab well
docs.text:
The top of every window is one band (TitleBar.qml, TabStrip.qml, TabItem.qml) whose arrangement is decided by pure code: window/TitleBandLayout.hpp (which frame, window mode, tab-strip gate and bar edge combine to which layout), window/HeaderBarLayout.hpp (items, menus and slots of the Linux header bar), window/TabWellLayout.hpp and window/TitleBandGeometry.hpp. Keep the keying of those tables (shape-or-any, frame, gate-or-any, position): new cases are new rows.

  • Tabs are pills in a well; the badge slot is resolved by window/TabBadge.hpp with the fixed priority Blocked > Error > Working > Done > Output. OSC 7501 program status, the unseen-output dot and the finished-command badge share that one slot.
  • Host chip (HostChip.qml, window/HostChipState.hpp): Connected, Reconnecting, Disconnected. The daemon drift chip lives in the band's trailing area, never over the cells.
  • Notices: window/NoticeModel.hpp queues Toast (a transient pill) and Banner (a band below the title band that pushes the content down once). Config reload errors, "Copied N lines" and restore summaries all arrive here. Toasts persist while hovered and are announced politely through platform/Announcer.hpp.
  • Dialogs are KitDialog.qml, an in-scene sheet-styled Dialog (a Quick Controls Dialog never becomes an NSWindow sheet, so it is styled as one). Placement is a token (layout.dialog).
  • Menus are data: command/MenuTree.hpp, command/ContextMenu.hpp, command/TabMenus.hpp, command/MenuBarTable.hpp, command/BlockMenu.hpp. layout.menu picks the presenter: Native realises the tree as a QMenu (an NSMenu on macOS), InScene uses the QML menus. The QMenu realisation is only exercised by display tests; the tree builder is unit tested.
  • Command palette (CommandPalette.qml, command/CommandPaletteTree.hpp): rows grouped by category, parameterised actions collapse to one drill-in row.
  • No title bar and full screen: with show_title_bar: true the server frame is used and the tabs sit in a strip below it; in full screen the band reveals when the pointer reaches the top edge.

docs.title: Panes, densities and cards
docs.text:
There are two densities, Comfortable and Minimal. chrome_density selects the minimal sub-row, which resolveChromeTokens copies over the pane extents, so a density change rebuilds the provider.

  • PaneNode.qml draws splits; the visual gap is space.paneGap and the grab area space.splitHit is a transparent item that overlaps the cards and never changes layout. The window-size solver reads the same gap, so the two cannot drift (vtworkspace::DefaultPaneGap).
  • window/PaneHeaderPolicy.hpp decides, from density, held modifier, pointer, focus, pane count and size, whether a header shows its name, name and working directory, or nothing, and whether its actions show. An inline header that would leave less than one cell row of content hides.
  • Per-pane data (displayWorkingDirectory, foregroundProcessName, programStatus) is exposed by session/PaneProxy.hpp. Process-name polling runs only while a header is visible.
  • A reconnecting pane dims by the dim token and shows a static toast pill. A disconnected or exited pane gets ExitedFooter.qml in its bottom chrome, never over the cells.
  • The Terminal row draws everything in cells: one-row headers, | and - cell lines for splits, inactive panes at reduced opacity, a hard one-cell shadow, menus in-scene on every OS, the find bar in the pane header row, and ui_font_family / ui_font_size applying to the chrome font.

docs.title: Window controls and frame
docs.text: Window controls are chosen by WindowControlStyle (Auto matches the host) and only drawn while the window is frameless. On macOS AppKit's real traffic lights are kept; the Terminal row snaps them to the first cells of the bar row. Windows draws 46-wide caption buttons with Segoe Fluent glyphs. Linux uses client-side decorations by default with a 46 high header bar; the button order follows the desktop's layout. With show_title_bar: true the server draws the frame and only the window buttons move out of the tab row. The Terminal row on Linux and Windows draws coloured cell dots from the scheme.

docs.title: Platform integration seams
docs.text:
Every seam has the same shape: a decision that is pure and tested everywhere, and an adapter that asks the OS, behind an interface with a null implementation. The adapters that cannot run on CI are thin; the decision is never inside them. Look in src/contour/platform/:

Concern Interface Notes Reduce motion, transparency, contrast IAccessibilityPreferenceSource Cocoa, Windows and portal backends Accent colour, corner radius, button layout IPlatformAppearance the Linux backend reads the XDG Settings portal; fallback accent #3584E4 Title band material ITitleBandMaterial null implementation and a Solid fallback Global hotkey IGlobalHotkey Carbon hot key, RegisterHotKey, GlobalShortcuts portal Secure input ISecureInput EnableSecureEventInput on macOS Shell rc editing IShellRcEditor shows the line before it appends it Notifications IUserNotificationCenter, Notifier decision vs adapter: NotificationRouter vs FreeDesktopNotifier Dock, taskbar, launcher counts TaskbarProgressSink and friends the tally is pure (window/TaskbarAttentionTally.hpp)

Platform notes that are easy to get wrong:

  • macOS. The window keeps the full-size content view. As shipped the title band is the client's own tint over a compact toolbar (Solid): with AppKit's transparent title bar the NSTitlebarView took the band's clicks. Glass remains a possible follow-up as a within-window NSVisualEffectView behind the Qt content. nativeControlsInset() stays the horizontal inset for the traffic lights; the band's height comes from the safe area. Alpha-capable surfaces can clear hasShadow, so it is re-asserted after the frame is applied. On macOS QWindow::setBaseSize hard-resizes the NSWindow, and the OpenGL RHI backend maps a window that never composites; both are avoided in the code and must stay so. The application menu bar is built from command/MenuBarTable.hpp once per app and rebuilt on reload.
  • Windows 11. Mica through DWMWA_SYSTEMBACKDROP_TYPE = DWMSBT_TABBEDWINDOW with the frame extended into the client area on an alpha-capable surface; the band is Solid when that fails or under Reduce Transparency. background.blur turns the whole window Acrylic and replaces Mica. Snap Layouts need the maximise button to answer WM_NCHITTEST with HTMAXBUTTON, plus the non-client mouse messages to drive the QML button's hover; all of it sits in the hit-test table (platform/CaptionHitTest.hpp) so it is testable off Windows. Menus stay in-scene on Windows: a native menu is an HMENU, which draws no swatch row, ignores the terminal scheme the chrome follows and has no supported dark mode. A Windows contrast theme overrides theme: terminal. The Settings window keeps the system title bar with Mica. The caption, Mica and Settings objects check the platform when called, not at construction, because construction runs before QApplication exists.
  • Linux. One design for all desktops. Accent and light/dark come from the XDG Settings portal through PortalCall; the button layout comes from the first source that answers (GNOME's button-layout, KWin's ButtonsOnLeft/ButtonsOnRight, else close on the right). Window shadows are drawn client-side per windowing system (X11WindowShadow, WaylandWindowShadow) using Breeze's own parameters so a Contour window and a Breeze one cast the same shadow. Selected rows use the legible highlight rule from the principles above.

docs.title: The Settings window and its one save model
docs.text:
Settings is a separate QQuickWindow, one per application (window/SettingsWindowHost.hpp), opened by OpenConfiguration and by the application menu, and focused if already open. Its sections (General, Appearance, Keyboard, Shell Integration, Profiles, then an "Edit contour.yml..." entry) come from the table in window/SettingsSections.hpp; a test requires every field group to appear in exactly one section, so a new group that is not mapped fails the build's tests. Field groups are data (window/SettingsFields.hpp, profileFieldGroups, globalFieldDescriptors), and the controls are the Kit* components, so a new setting is a row, not a layout.

There is one save model:

  • Every commit (a control change, leaving a field) is staged and written by a debounced save, 300 ms, atomically, to the side file it belongs to: profiles/<name>.yml for profiles, settings.yml for globals. contour.yml is never written.
  • The controller keeps a draft of settings.yml, so two global changes inside one debounce both land.
  • "Revert Changes" restores every side file as it was when the session first touched it, and never writes anything itself. Closing Settings or quitting flushes what is staged.
  • Read-only profiles offer "Duplicate to Edit".
  • Fallible setters return std::expected<void, SettingsError>, not bool.
  • Profile pages preview against an offscreen TerminalDisplay rendering a canned transcript (window/SettingsPreview.hpp).
  • option_as_alt is an enum (Off | Left | Right | Both); the YAML boundary still accepts the old boolean and converts it, so the enum stays inside the boundary.

docs.title: The moments
docs.text:
Each moment is a decision header plus, where the OS is involved, one interface from the table above.

  • Shell integration card. After three prompts without OSC 133 a dismissible card offers to append the one-line source to the shell rc file, showing the line first. The edit goes through IShellRcEditor and is reversible.
  • Restore. A restored session gets a "Restored" divider and one toast; a process that ended while the daemon was down shows the exited footer instead of silently restarting.
  • Drag and drop. Dropped files insert shell-escaped paths. A tab dropped on a pane's outer 20 % splits it (window/DropZonePolicy.hpp).
  • Finished elsewhere. A command that ran for 10 s or longer while the window was unfocused raises a notification and sets the Done or Error badge. On macOS this requires running from an app bundle with a bundle identifier, otherwise the tray notifier is used.
  • Secure input. When the PTY echo is off a lock badge shows (SecureInputPolicy, SecureLockPlacement), and macOS secure event input is enabled for as long as it holds.
  • Quick terminal. A global hotkey slides a window down from the top (full width, 40 % of the height, Minimal density). It is a tool window that does not accept focus on show, which Qt maps to a non-activating panel on macOS. The hotkey, its refusals and the window each have a policy header (window/QuickTerminalPolicy.hpp, window/HotkeyRefusals.hpp).
  • Keyboard to chrome. Ctrl+F6 cycles focus terminal, tabs, toolbar (window/ChromeFocus.hpp, window/ChromeKeys.hpp). A test requires every default chord to be unique.
  • Bell, dock, taskbar. A visual bell is a tab badge plus a dock bounce or taskbar flash. The dock, taskbar and Linux launcher show how many tabs are Blocked (TaskbarAttentionTally).
  • IME. The candidate window anchors at the cursor cell and preedit is drawn inline with a one-point underline (display/ImeQueryRect.hpp).

docs.title: Terminal-side pieces
docs.text:
These live below the chrome but are part of the same design:

  • Status line is on by default, cell-drawn and scheme-coloured. Its placeholders (Cwd, Git, LastCommand, Selection, Scroll, ...) are each four edits (struct, variant, ItemTraits, serializer) in vtbackend/screen/StatusLineBuilder.hpp; role colours (Color=accent|success|...) and Hide=Insert are flags. Git reads .git/HEAD through a narrow filesystem seam off the terminal's lock; a collapse step drops low-priority segments when the line is too narrow.
  • Command blocks draw a rail in the gutter (RailSegment { None = 0, Head, Body, Tail }), a status chip only over blank cells (vtbackend/shell/BlockChipPlacement.hpp), a block menu from command/BlockMenu.hpp, a fold chip and scrollbar ticks. The glyph column stays for the Terminal row. Running uses the accent, ColorPalette::blockStatusColor's fallback is blue.
  • Find bar has literal/regex and whole-word options; an invalid regex is an std::expected error shown in the count slot; the walk is chunked so the lock is released between chunks.
  • Permissions are one two-button dialog with a remember checkbox, (PermissionDecision, PermissionMemory) instead of two bools (session/Permission.hpp).
  • Hint labels, link target pill, scrollbar follow the "blank cells only" rule, hint labels aside.

docs.title: Testing strategy
docs.text:
• Pure decisions are Catch2 tables next to the header.
  • QML components are loaded against mocks (test/Qml*_test.cpp, test/QmlMocks.hpp) and asserted through objectName and findChild; every element a test needs gets an objectName.
  • Acceptance is property tests, not images. test/MainWindowQml_test.cpp asserts token-driven values (the tab well's height equals chromeStyle.size.tabWell, a radius equals its token). A change that moves geometry on purpose updates those assertions in the same commit.
  • Style variants in ctest. The QML tests run once per controls style, because Qt picks it once per process: contour_gui_test, _fluent, _contourlinux and _contourtui, selected with CONTOUR_TEST_CONTROLS_STYLE. A control added to one style module must be added to both.
  • Widgets in tests. contour_gui_test builds a QGuiApplication, not a QApplication, so code that needs QMenu splits into a pure tree builder (tested) and a thin realisation (display smoke tests).
  • Snapshots are review artefacts. test/ChromeSnapshot_test.cpp and test/ChromeSnapshotPlan.hpp render named scripts (single-tab, split-three, palette, settings, ...) per chrome row, edition and appearance; scripts/run-chrome-snapshots.sh <contour_gui_test> <out-dir> runs one pass per controls style under a headless compositor and checks the PNG count against manifest.tsv. CI uploads them. Nothing compares them against a baseline.
  • Display passes. Tests tagged [display] drive a real TerminalDisplay through RHI and are skipped offscreen. scripts/run-display-tests.sh runs them under headless weston (CI) or an existing X11 session. Run them once per body of work, not per edit.
  • Pixel tests for in-grid visuals. Anything drawn in or over the grid (rails, chips, the cursor, hint labels) gets a [display] test that grabs a real frame and samples pixels (test/DisplayPixels.hpp, display/CommandBlockRendering_test.cpp, display/InGridVisualsRendering_test.cpp). Chrome snapshots cannot see the grid.
  • Offscreen verification of QML. Use QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen and grabWindow(); OS-level screen capture needs a permission nobody may be there to grant.
  • Accessibility. Every control sets Accessible.role and Accessible.name; a table-driven test walks the chrome's accessible tree (test/Accessibility_qml_test.cpp).

docs.title: Decisions that are easy to undo by accident
docs.text:
• Putting a literal in QML "just this once". The gates exist because nobody notices the third one.
  • Adding change notification to a provider property instead of rebuilding the provider.
  • Adding a style row without the controls module (or only to one of the two token tables).
  • Switching Windows to native menus. They cannot show the swatch row or follow the terminal scheme.
  • Drawing a chip, toast or pill over cells that might hold text. Use the placement policy, which collapses to a glyph when the blank space is not there.
  • Using green or yellow for "running". It is the accent.
  • Moving the OS highlight pair into a surface without legibleHighlight.
  • Making a new default unconditional rather than a Native2026 row; existing configurations change look.
  • Reading the OS from a constructor that runs before QApplication, or from a decision header.
  • Letting the pane-gap token and the window-size solver disagree.
  • Treating snapshot PNGs as acceptance, or skipping the Terminal row because "it is only the TUI".
  • Re-enabling the OpenGL RHI backend or setBaseSize on macOS.
  • Changing a config enum's spelling after release; the spelling is the file format.

docs.title: Profiling with Tracy
docs.text:
Contour is instrumented for the Tracy frame profiler, so the whole pipeline — PTY read → VT parse → grid write → render buffer → frame — can be measured rather than guessed at, and two commits can be compared mechanically.

Call sites use Tracy's own macros directly. There is deliberately no first-party profiling abstraction: ZoneScoped and TracyPlot mean exactly what Tracy's documentation says they mean.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
All default to OFF, and with all of them off nothing is fetched and no compiled output changes — contour::tracy merely puts a no-op header on the include path.

Option Builds Cost CONTOUR_TRACY Instrumentation compiled into contour (the client). Fetches TracyClient (a single source file). CONTOUR_TRACY_TOOLS tracy-capture, tracy-capture-daemon, tracy-csvexport. Tracy CPM-fetches capstone, zstd, PPQSort and json. Minutes, once. CONTOUR_TRACY_GUI The tracy-profiler GUI. Adds glfw, freetype, imgui, nativefiledialog, md4c, base64, tidy, usearch, pugixml and libcurl, and needs EGL/Wayland (or X11) development packages. CONTOUR_TRACY_GUI_X11 Selects X11 over Wayland for the GUI. —

The tool options are independent of CONTOUR_TRACY: build the viewer and the exporter once and keep them, and rebuild only contour when you want a different instrumented binary. Neither tool is packaged on Arch, which is why they are buildable from this tree at all.

TRACY_VERSION in cmake/Tracy.cmake pins all three. The client and the tools must be the same version — Tracy's capture protocol is version-specific.

docs.title: Building a profiling tree
docs.text:
cmake --preset clang-release -B out/clang-tracy \
    -DCONTOUR_TRACY=ON -DCONTOUR_TRACY_TOOLS=ON
cmake --build out/clang-tracy -j4

Do not profile the default preset. clang-asan is Debug plus AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer; its timings say nothing about release behaviour. clang-release is RelWithDebInfo, which keeps the symbols Tracy needs.

The tools are not part of all — build them by name:

cmake --build out/clang-tracy -j4 --target tracy-tools   # capture + csvexport
cmake --build out/clang-tracy -j4 --target tracy-gui     # the profiler GUI

Both land in out/clang-tracy/tracy-tools/bin/. If the GUI's configure step fails with No package 'egl' found (or wayland-egl, wayland-cursor, xkbcommon), install those development packages or reconfigure with -DCONTOUR_TRACY_GUI_X11=ON.

docs.title: Taking a capture
docs.text:
Live, with the GUI. Start tracy-profiler, run the instrumented contour, and connect. The frame view shows the terminal's real frame rate, because there is exactly one FrameMark in the tree.

Scripted, to a file. tracy-capture waits for a client, so start it first. Give it -s so the capture ends on its own rather than waiting for the client to disconnect:

out/clang-tracy/tracy-tools/bin/tracy-capture -o /tmp/notcurses.tracy -f -s 50

then, in another terminal, a workload — notcurses-demo is a good one, since -c pins its PRNG seed and -d 0 removes its pacing delays, making the run repeatable and parse/render-bound:

out/clang-tracy/src/contour/contour early-exit-threshold 0 \
    execute sh -c 'notcurses-demo -c -d 0 -p /usr/share/notcurses ixetun'

The client listens on 127.0.0.1:8086 from process start, so the two can be started in either order. TRACY_NO_EXIT=1 in the environment makes the client hold its data until a profiler has collected it — use it for a run too short to attach to, but not together with -s, or the two wait on each other. The same recipe profiles bench-headless, which inherits every backend zone by linking vtbackend.

docs.title: Reading a capture
docs.text:
out/clang-tracy/tracy-tools/bin/tracy-csvexport /tmp/contour.tracy

One row per zone: name, source location, total time, share of the whole, call count, and mean/min/max/stddev. This is the terminal-readable form — no GUI needed — and it is how two commits are compared: capture the same workload on each, export both, and diff the totals for the zones you changed.

Two things to know when reading it:

  • readFromPty will dominate every capture. It is the blocking read, so its total is mostly idle. That is the point of zoning it — the wait is accounted for rather than sitting in an unexplained gap — but it means the interesting number is everything below it.
  • A zone in a template appears once per instantiation, with the same name and source line. Both Parser::parseFragment rows come from Parser-impl.hpp; they are different instantiations of the parser, not a double count.
  • A zone that was never entered is simply absent from the export.

docs.title: Self time, and counting frames
docs.text:
Two flags decide what a number means, and mixing them up produces confident nonsense:

  • -e gives self time. Nested totals double-count: shapeRunWithFallback once reported 81 seconds in a 30-second capture because it recurses. Reach for -e whenever the question is "where did the time go".
  • -u gives one row per event, which is the only way to count how many frames missed the budget rather than look at a mean. prepareFrameRhi's duration is the frame's CPU cost, and a frame is prepareFrameRhi → paint → renderImpl → recordFrameRhi, with the only FrameMark at the end of recordFrameRhi.
  • -p (with -u) exports plot data, which is how pty.read.bytes answers what the PTY actually delivered.

Per-cell zones are compiled out unless CONTOUR_TRACY_CELL_ZONES=ON (@see Options). They cost about 20 ns each to record and nothing to leave off, but a full-screen workload emits tens of millions of them, and every export has to decode all of them to answer a question about frames.

docs.title: Measuring pipeline latency
docs.text:
Frame cost and pipeline latency are different questions and need different arithmetic. Latency is a join over two zone streams: for each parseFragment event, the first prepareFrameRhi that starts after it ends is the earliest frame that could carry that output, and the delta is the latency. tracy-csvexport -u -f <zone> gives the two streams cheaply — the filter matters, since a notcurses-demo capture can hold tens of millions of zones.

Two traps, both easy to fall into:

  • parseFragment fires on the GUI thread too. Terminal::updateIndicatorStatusLine re-parses the three status-line segments through writeToScreenInternal, so a capture has three GUI-thread parseFragment events per frame that are output of the frame, not input to it. Counting them as PTY input turns a p50 of 0.14 ms into 16.6 ms, because each is matched to the next frame. Filter on the thread: the parser thread is the one that is not prepareFrameRhi's.
  • parseFragment nests, so drop any event contained in the previous one on the same thread.

The result is a lower bound on felt latency: it ends at the frame's start, so it excludes the frame's own CPU cost, GPU time, the swap and the compositor, and it begins at the PTY parse, so it excludes the keyboard leg entirely. For latency measured to the swapped frame, from the keystroke and from the launch, and compared between in-process and daemon mode, see Latency.

docs.title: Measuring key press latency under output load
docs.text:
That keyboard leg is what bench-headless keypress measures: how long a key press takes from Terminal::sendCharEvent() until its bytes are written to the PTY, while an application floods the terminal. It is the question to ask of any lock change on either side of input, because a key press and the parser compete for the terminal's locks. The application is a real process on a real PTY, reading the keys in raw mode.

out/clang-tracy/tracy-tools/bin/tracy-capture -o /tmp/keypress.tracy -f &
TRACY_NO_EXIT=1 out/clang-tracy/src/vtbackend/bench-headless keypress seconds 10
wait   # tracy-capture writes the file only once the client has gone
out/clang-tracy/tracy-tools/bin/tracy-csvexport -u -f bench.keyPress /tmp/keypress.tracy

A key press's time includes whatever it writes along with its key, such as a reply the parser queued since the last write. A press that falls behind schedule is not made up for, so a stall shows as one long press rather than a burst of short ones after it.

It prints its own percentiles, and those are the ones to quote: Tracy's per-sequence zones make every parse slower, and with it every lock the parser holds, so take the headline numbers from a build without Tracy and the explanation from one with it. There, each key press is the zone bench.keyPress. Beside it, pty.readSome shows how long each read holds the PTY's own lock, which a key press's write needs as well, and parseFragment how long each parse holds the state lock, which a key press would wait for if it took that lock. bench-headless help lists the options: the flood can be dropped, laced with queries that make the terminal reply, or read in larger or smaller pieces.

docs.title: Two rules worth stating outright
docs.text:
• Do not record on a busy machine, and prefer a paired run — the same workload recorded on both builds back to back — over a solo run on a quiet one. Background load that is common to both cancels; load that differs between them does not.
  • A workload driven by synchronized output does not have a frame rate you can read off our frame count. Count block closes (syncOut.refreshed + syncOut.dropped.*) instead: the cap can expire mid-body and draw the same application frame several times.

docs.title: Parser thread (Terminal.Loop)
docs.text:
Zone Where Terminal::processInputOnce vtbackend/screen/Terminal.cpp Terminal::readFromPty The blocking read — what separates idle from busy. Terminal::writeToScreen Locally injected text only; PTY input does not pass through it. Terminal::parseFragmentChunked Same — the injection path, not the PTY path. Parser::parseFragment vtparser/Parser-impl.hpp — the state machine. Screen::writeText The bulk overload; carries its cell count as the zone value. Screen::writeTextEnd Screen::executeControlCode One per control byte (LF, CR, BEL …). Screen::processSequence One per escape sequence, named after the sequence (see below). Screen::processAPC Screen::scrollUp / scrollDown / clearScreen Terminal::screenUpdated The parser thread's hand-off to the GUI. Terminal::resizeScreen Screen::applyPageSizeToMainDisplay The main grid's reflow. Terminal::fillRenderBufferInternal Grid::resize vtbackend/grid/Grid.cpp — reflow. Three call sites aggregate here: the main display and the two one-line status grids. applyPageSizeToMainDisplay is what separates them.

Screen::processSequence renames its zone to the sequence's mnemonic, so the timeline reads SGR, CUP, ED rather than a wall of identical rows. Two caveats: the rename is visible only in the GUI — tracy-csvexport aggregates by source location, so the CSV keeps one processSequence row — and it costs about 12 ns per sequence, which is measurable against a ~20 ns dispatch but negligible in absolute terms (~4 ms across 324k sequences).

Screen::writeText(char32_t) and writeTextInternal are deliberately not instrumented: they run once per codepoint, so a zone there would cost more than the work it measures and would bury the trace. The bulk writeText(string_view, size_t) overload above is the instrumented one.

Plots: pty.read.bytes (bytes returned by each PTY read) and pty.parse.bytes (bytes handed to the parser). Together they show throughput and how the stream is chunked.

docs.title: GUI / render thread
docs.text: Zone Where TerminalDisplay::prepareFrameRhi Pipeline build and resource uploads (before beginPass). TerminalDisplay::paint Called from prepareFrameRhi; drives Renderer::render. TerminalDisplay::recordFrameRhi Draw-command recording. Ends with the frame's FrameMark. Renderer::renderImpl Opens before _applyMutex is taken, so the wait is inside the zone. Renderer::renderCells / renderLines / renderGutter TextRenderer::beginFrame / endFrame OpenShaper::shape / rasterize Shaping and rasterization — where a cache miss becomes a hitch.

docs.title: Lock contention
docs.text: Terminal::_stateMutex is declared through TracyLockable, so Tracy's lock view shows how long the render path waits on the parser thread and vice versa. That is the cross-thread question the per-thread zones cannot answer on their own.

docs.title: Adding instrumentation
docs.text:
Use Tracy's macros directly — #include <tracy/Tracy.hpp> and ZoneScoped;.

Any macro you use must also be defined in src/crispy/tracy-stub/tracy/Tracy.hpp, the no-op header that stands in when CONTOUR_TRACY=OFF. ctest -R check_tracy_stub enforces this, and it matters: a macro missing from the stub breaks the default build — the one CI and every packaging job run — while the profiling build stays green.

The stub is a faithful proxy, not merely a permissive one: it declares the same ___tracy_scoped_zone name the real macros declare, so two zone macros in one scope collide and ZoneText/ZoneValue without a zone in scope fail, exactly as they do with Tracy enabled. It is constexpr and odr-used only inside sizeof, so no storage is emitted and disabled macros never evaluate their arguments.

That fidelity is not complete, though — the stub models the macros, not the library. Build with -DCONTOUR_TRACY=ON before pushing instrumentation changes.

docs.title: Session OOM isolation
docs.text: An out-of-memory kill of a process running inside Contour — a compiler, a language server — must end that process and nothing else. This page explains why that took code, and how it works.

docs.title: Why Contour died with its children
docs.text:
Desktops start applications as systemd units (app-org.contourterminal.Contour@….service). Every process a session spawns lands in that unit's cgroup, beside Contour. Two things then act on the unit as a whole:

  • OOMPolicy=stop (systemd's DefaultOOMPolicy): when the kernel OOM-kills any process in the unit, systemd stops the whole unit — Contour and every tab.
  • systemd-oomd kills whole cgroups under memory pressure, so a session's cgroup that contains Contour makes Contour a candidate.

docs.title: What happens now
docs.text:
vtpty::Process::start() forks the child and parks it on a gate — a socket pair — before exec. The parent hands the child, as a ParkedChild, to the injected ProcessPlacement:

  • SystemdScopePlacement (Linux, CONTOUR_WITH_SYSTEMD=ON) asks the user's systemd, over sd-bus, for a transient contour-session-<contour pid>-<child pid>-<n>.scope in app.slice with OOMPolicy=continue, waits for the job, and releases the child. Everything the child forks from then on is born in that scope. Every placed process's scope is named so, and described -- as the log names it -- by what the process is to Contour (ProcessRole): a session's shell, a program a session started, the daemon, or the tmux client. systemd before 253 knows neither PIDFDs nor OOMPolicy= on scopes and refuses a request carrying either, so the first such refusal switches the connection to PIDs= and no OOMPolicy=. Its scopes do not react to an out-of-memory kill at all, which is what we want. A child released unplaced because the bus fell silent -- its request timed out, or the breaker held requests off -- is placed late: once a request may be sent again, the worker asks for a scope for the running process (by pidfd; by pid only where systemd takes no pidfd). What the child started in the meantime stays in Contour's unit. A refusal is not asked again, and neither is a child released while there is no systemd user instance at all: that is a configuration, not an outage, so its children run unplaced, quietly, with nothing kept to ask again.
  • NoPlacement (other platforms, Flatpak, builds without systemd) releases at once.

What became of each child is told through an injected PlacementReporter, which Contour logs. Every child released unplaced for a fault is logged where a user sees it, with its pid and why -- each one, not only the first -- and so is its late placement.

Before parking, the child also sets the oom_score_adj its placement supplies -- Contour's own plus 100 -- so in a global out-of-memory the kernel picks a session's process before Contour.

The programs a session starts outside its terminal go through the same placement: the opener of a local file a link names (xdg-open), the viewer OpenCommandOutput hands a command's output to, the second Contour that follows a link to an executable file or opens one in $EDITOR, and the one spawn_new_process starts. ExternalLauncher starts each through vtpty::startDetached(), which double-forks -- the program is not Contour's child, and outlives it -- and parks the program's process on a gate exactly as Process::start() parks a shell. ContourGuiApp hands the sessions' factory and the launcher one placement. Windows starts them through QProcess, having no placement. The daemon contour client spawns, and the one contour daemon --background starts, go through startDetached() and a placement too: the daemon holds every hosted session's scrollback, and must live in neither the client's unit nor the scope of the tab it was typed into. --background's placement lasts only as long as the command does, which returns once the daemon accepts: a daemon deferred there because systemd fell silent is never placed late, and stays where it was started.
